05

React Fundamentals

5.1 Introduction to React Fundamentals

Simple Explanation

React Fundamentals are the building blocks of every React application. Think of them as the ABCs of React - once you master these concepts, you can build anything from a simple button to a complex enterprise application. These fundamentals include JSX (the HTML-like syntax), Components (the building blocks), Props (data passing), State (component memory), and the Component Lifecycle (birth, life, and death of components).

Imagine building with LEGO blocks: - JSX is how you describe what each block looks like - Components are the individual LEGO blocks - Props are like the instructions for how blocks connect - State is like the memory of what's been built - Lifecycle is the process of building, changing, and dismantling

Technical Explanation

React Fundamentals form the core API and patterns of React. These include:

  1. JSX: A syntax extension that allows writing HTML-like code in JavaScript
  2. Components: Functions or classes that return UI elements
  3. Props: Read-only data passed from parent to child
  4. State: Mutable data that triggers re-renders when changed
  5. Lifecycle: The sequence of events from component creation to destruction
  6. Rendering: The process of converting components to DOM elements
  7. Conditional Rendering: Showing different UI based on conditions
  8. Lists and Keys: Rendering collections of elements with unique identifiers

Professional Explanation

In enterprise React development, mastering fundamentals is crucial for:

  • Performance Optimization: Understanding rendering cycles and memoization
  • Architecture Decisions: Choosing between patterns and approaches
  • Code Quality: Writing maintainable and testable components
  • Team Collaboration: Following consistent patterns and best practices
  • Debugging: Understanding the component tree and data flow
  • Scalability: Building components that grow with the application

5.2 JSX (JavaScript XML)

Simple Explanation

JSX allows you to write HTML-like code inside your JavaScript files. It's a syntax extension that makes React code look like HTML, making it easier to understand and write. Under the hood, JSX gets transformed into regular JavaScript function calls.

Think of JSX as a bridge between HTML and JavaScript - it lets you write what looks like HTML but with the full power of JavaScript embedded within.

Technical Explanation

JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that resembles HTML. It allows you to write markup and logic together in a single file. JSX is transformed by tools like Babel into React.createElement() calls.

Key characteristics: - HTML-like syntax: Closer to what you see in the browser - JavaScript expressions: Embed JavaScript inside {} - Self-closing tags: Tags can be self-closed like <img /> - Fragments: Empty tags <> for grouping without extra DOM nodes - Attributes: camelCase for properties (e.g., className instead of class)

Professional Explanation

JSX is a compile-time syntactic sugar that follows the XML/HTML syntax. It provides type safety and linting capabilities when used with TypeScript and ESLint plugins. The JSX transform converts JSX to React.createElement calls, enabling React's virtual DOM reconciliation.

JSX features for enterprise: - TypeScript integration: Type checking for props and attributes - Custom components: Capitalized names distinguish from HTML elements - Expression interpolation: Full JavaScript expressions in {} - Spread attributes: {...props} for passing multiple props - Conditional rendering: Using JavaScript expressions

JSX Examples

// Basic JSX
const element = <h1>Hello, World!</h1>;

// JSX with JavaScript expression
const name = "John";
const greeting = <h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>;

// JSX with multiple elements
const div = (
    <div>
        <h1>Hello World</h1>
        <p>This is a paragraph</p>
    </div>
);

// JSX with attributes (camelCase)
const input = <input type="text" className="form-control" />;

// JSX with self-closing tags
const image = <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description" />;

// JSX with conditional rendering
const isLoggedIn = true;
const message = (
    <div>
        {isLoggedIn ? <h1>Welcome back</h1> : <h1>Please login</h1>}
    </div>
);

// JSX with list rendering
const items = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Orange'];
const list = (
    <ul>
        {items.map((item, index) => (
            <li key={index}>{item}</li>
        ))}
    </ul>
);

// JSX with event handlers
const button = (
    <button onClick={() => console.log('Clicked!')}>
        Click me
    </button>
);

// JSX with inline styles
const styledDiv = (
    <div style={{ 
        color: 'blue', 
        fontSize: '20px',
        padding: '10px',
        backgroundColor: '#f0f0f0'
    }}>
        Styled div
    </div>
);

// JSX with fragments
const fragment = (
    <>
        <h1>Title</h1>
        <p>Paragraph</p>
    </>
);

// JSX with spread attributes
const props = { className: 'container', id: 'main' };
const container = <div {...props}>Content</div>;

// JSX with custom components
function Welcome(props) {
    return <h1>Hello, {props.name}!</h1>;
}

const customComponent = <Welcome name="John" />;

// How JSX transforms to React.createElement
// JSX:
const jsxElement = <h1 className="title">Hello</h1>;

// Transpiled to:
const reactElement = React.createElement(
    'h1',
    { className: 'title' },
    'Hello'
);

JSX Rules and Best Practices

// ✅ DO: Use camelCase for attributes
<input type="text" className="input" htmlFor="name" />

// ❌ DON'T: Use HTML attribute names
<input type="text" class="input" for="name" />

// ✅ DO: Use expressions for dynamic content
const message = <h1>{dynamicContent}</h1>;

// ❌ DON'T: Use plain JavaScript in JSX
// This is incorrect:
// const message = <h1>if (condition) { 'Hello' }</h1>;

// ✅ DO: Use conditional operators
const result = <div>{condition ? 'Yes' : 'No'}</div>;

// ✅ DO: Use fragment for multiple elements
return (
    <>
        <Header />
        <Content />
        <Footer />
    </>
);

// ✅ DO: Use self-closing for empty elements
<Image src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" />

// ❌ DON'T: Use non-self-closing for empty elements
// <Image src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo"></Image>

// ✅ DO: Use {props.children} for child content
function Card({ children }) {
    return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
}

// JSX with complex expressions
const complexJSX = (
    <div>
        {user && (
            <div className="user-info">
                <Avatar src={user.avatar} />
                <h2>{user.name}</h2>
                <p>{user.email}</p>
                {user.isAdmin && <AdminBadge />}
            </div>
        )}
        {!user && <LoginPrompt />}
    </div>
);

5.3 Components

Simple Explanation

Components are the heart of React. They are reusable pieces of UI that can be combined to build complex interfaces. Think of them as custom HTML elements that you create - each component has its own structure, style, and behavior.

A React application is a tree of components, starting from a root component and branching out into smaller, more specialized components.

Technical Explanation

Components are JavaScript functions or classes that accept inputs (props) and return React elements (JSX). They follow the principle of composition - building complex UIs from smaller, focused pieces.

Component types: 1. Functional Components: Simple functions that return JSX 2. Class Components: ES6 classes with lifecycle methods (legacy) 3. Pure Components: Components that implement shallow comparison 4. Higher-Order Components (HOCs): Functions that wrap components 5. Render Props: Components that accept a function as a prop

Professional Explanation

In enterprise React, components are the primary unit of code organization. They follow the Single Responsibility Principle, each handling a specific piece of UI and logic.

Component architecture considerations: - Component Categories: Presentational vs Container components - Component Hierarchy: Smart vs Dumb components - Component Reusability: Designing for reuse across the application - Component Composition: Building complex components from simpler ones - Component Testing: Unit testing components in isolation - Component Documentation: Documenting props and usage

Functional Components

// Basic functional component
function Greeting() {
    return <h1>Hello, World!</h1>;
}

// Functional component with props
function Welcome({ name, age }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>
            <p>You are {age} years old</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Functional component with default props
function UserCard({ name = 'Guest', role = 'User' }) {
    return (
        <div className="user-card">
            <h3>{name}</h3>
            <p>Role: {role}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Functional component with children
function Card({ title, children }) {
    return (
        <div className="card">
            <h2>{title}</h2>
            <div className="card-body">
                {children}
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}

// Functional component with event handlers
function ClickCounter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    const handleClick = () => {
        setCount(count + 1);
    };

    return (
        <button onClick={handleClick}>
            Clicked {count} times
        </button>
    );
}

// Functional component with conditional rendering
function StatusMessage({ isLoggedIn }) {
    return (
        <div>
            {isLoggedIn ? (
                <p>Welcome back!</p>
            ) : (
                <p>Please log in</p>
            )}
        </div>
    );
}

// Functional component with list rendering
function TodoList({ todos }) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {todos.map(todo => (
                <li key={todo.id}>
                    <input type="checkbox" checked={todo.completed} />
                    {todo.text}
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// Functional component with multiple responsibilities
function UserProfile({ user, onSave, onDelete }) {
    const [isEditing, setIsEditing] = useState(false);
    const [formData, setFormData] = useState(user);

    const handleSave = () => {
        onSave(formData);
        setIsEditing(false);
    };

    if (isEditing) {
        return (
            <div className="edit-form">
                <input 
                    value={formData.name}
                    onChange={e => setFormData({ ...formData, name: e.target.value })}
                />
                <input 
                    value={formData.email}
                    onChange={e => setFormData({ ...formData, email: e.target.value })}
                />
                <button onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>
                <button onClick={() => setIsEditing(false)}>Cancel</button>
            </div>
        );
    }

    return (
        <div className="user-profile">
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p>
            <button onClick={() => setIsEditing(true)}>Edit</button>
            <button onClick={() => onDelete(user.id)}>Delete</button>
        </div>
    );
}

Class Components (Legacy)

// Basic class component
class Greeting extends React.Component {
    render() {
        return <h1>Hello, World!</h1>;
    }
}

// Class component with props
class Welcome extends React.Component {
    render() {
        return (
            <div>
                <h1>Hello, {this.props.name}!</h1>
                <p>You are {this.props.age} years old</p>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

// Class component with state
class ClickCounter extends React.Component {
    constructor(props) {
        super(props);
        this.state = {
            count: 0
        };

        // Bind methods
        this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this);
    }

    handleClick() {
        this.setState({
            count: this.state.count + 1
        });
    }

    render() {
        return (
            <button onClick={this.handleClick}>
                Clicked {this.state.count} times
            </button>
        );
    }
}

// Class component with lifecycle methods
class DataFetcher extends React.Component {
    constructor(props) {
        super(props);
        this.state = {
            data: null,
            loading: true,
            error: null
        };
    }

    componentDidMount() {
        this.fetchData();
    }

    componentDidUpdate(prevProps) {
        if (prevProps.url !== this.props.url) {
            this.fetchData();
        }
    }

    componentWillUnmount() {
        // Cleanup subscriptions
        if (this.abortController) {
            this.abortController.abort();
        }
    }

    async fetchData() {
        try {
            this.setState({ loading: true, error: null });
            const response = await fetch(this.props.url);
            const data = await response.json();
            this.setState({ data, loading: false });
        } catch (error) {
            this.setState({ error: error.message, loading: false });
        }
    }

    render() {
        const { data, loading, error } = this.state;

        if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
        if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;
        return <div>{JSON.stringify(data)}</div>;
    }
}

// Class component with default props
class UserCard extends React.Component {
    static defaultProps = {
        name: 'Guest',
        role: 'User'
    };

    render() {
        return (
            <div className="user-card">
                <h3>{this.props.name}</h3>
                <p>Role: {this.props.role}</p>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

Component Composition

// App component composed of multiple components
function App() {
    return (
        <div className="app">
            <Header />
            <MainContent />
            <Footer />
        </div>
    );
}

// Header composed of smaller components
function Header() {
    return (
        <header>
            <Logo />
            <Navigation />
            <UserMenu />
        </header>
    );
}

// Navigation composed of links
function Navigation() {
    const links = [
        { href: '/', label: 'Home' },
        { href: '/about', label: 'About' },
        { href: '/contact', label: 'Contact' }
    ];

    return (
        <nav>
            <ul>
                {links.map(link => (
                    <li key={link.href}>
                        <a href={link.href}>{link.label}</a>
                    </li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </nav>
    );
}

// Component composition with children
function Layout({ header, sidebar, main, footer }) {
    return (
        <div className="layout">
            <header>{header}</header>
            <div className="main-content">
                <aside>{sidebar}</aside>
                <main>{main}</main>
            </div>
            <footer>{footer}</footer>
        </div>
    );
}

// Using the Layout component
function HomePage() {
    return (
        <Layout
            header={<Header />}
            sidebar={<Sidebar />}
            main={<HomeContent />}
            footer={<Footer />}
        />
    );
}

// Component composition with slots
function Card({ header, footer, children }) {
    return (
        <div className="card">
            {header && <div className="card-header">{header}</div>}
            <div className="card-body">{children}</div>
            {footer && <div className="card-footer">{footer}</div>}
        </div>
    );
}

// Using the Card component
function ProductCard({ product }) {
    return (
        <Card
            header={<h3>{product.name}</h3>}
            footer={<button>Add to Cart</button>}
        >
            <img src={product.image} alt={product.name} />
            <p>{product.description}</p>
            <span className="price">${product.price}</span>
        </Card>
    );
}

5.4 Props

Simple Explanation

Props (short for properties) are how components communicate with each other. They are like arguments you pass to a function - you send data from a parent component to a child component, and the child component uses that data to render itself.

Think of props as the ingredients you give to a recipe. The recipe (component) uses these ingredients (props) to create the final dish (UI).

Technical Explanation

Props are read-only inputs to React components. They flow from parent to child (unidirectional data flow). Props can be any JavaScript value: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects, functions, or even React components.

Key characteristics: - Read-only: Components cannot modify their own props - Immutability: Props should never be mutated - Type checking: PropTypes or TypeScript for validation - Default values: Can be defined for optional props - Children: Special prop for nested content

Professional Explanation

Props are the primary mechanism for data flow in React applications. They implement a unidirectional data flow pattern, making the application predictable and easier to debug.

Prop management strategies: - Prop Types: Runtime type checking with PropTypes - TypeScript: Compile-time type checking - Default Props: Default values for optional props - Prop Drilling: Passing props through multiple levels - Context API: For props needed in many components - Composition: Using children instead of passing many props

Props Examples

// Passing and receiving basic props
function Parent() {
    const user = {
        name: 'John',
        age: 30,
        email: 'john@example.com'
    };

    return (
        <Child
            name="John"
            age={30}
            isActive={true}
            user={user}
            onUpdate={() => console.log('Updated')}
        />
    );
}

function Child({ name, age, isActive, user, onUpdate }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <p>Name: {name}</p>
            <p>Age: {age}</p>
            <p>Active: {isActive ? 'Yes' : 'No'}</p>
            <p>Email: {user.email}</p>
            <button onClick={onUpdate}>Update</button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Default props
function UserProfile({ name, age, role = 'User', email = 'Not provided' }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h3>{name}</h3>
            <p>Age: {age}</p>
            <p>Role: {role}</p>
            <p>Email: {email}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Using UserProfile with and without default props
function Users() {
    return (
        <div>
            <UserProfile name="John" age={30} email="john@example.com" />
            <UserProfile name="Jane" age={25} />
            <UserProfile name="Bob" age={40} role="Admin" />
        </div>
    );
}

// Props with children
function Container({ children, className = '' }) {
    return <div className={`container ${className}`}>{children}</div>;
}

function Page() {
    return (
        <Container className="main-container">
            <h1>Welcome</h1>
            <p>This content is passed as children</p>
            <button>Click me</button>
        </Container>
    );
}

// Spread props
function Button({ variant = 'primary', size = 'medium', ...props }) {
    const classes = {
        primary: 'bg-blue-500 text-white',
        secondary: 'bg-gray-500 text-white',
        danger: 'bg-red-500 text-white'
    };

    const sizes = {
        small: 'px-2 py-1 text-sm',
        medium: 'px-4 py-2 text-base',
        large: 'px-6 py-3 text-lg'
    };

    return (
        <button
            className={`${classes[variant]} ${sizes[size]} rounded`}
            {...props}
        />
    );
}

// Using spread props
function Form() {
    const handleClick = (event) => {
        console.log('Button clicked', event);
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <Button 
                type="submit"
                disabled={false}
                onClick={handleClick}
                aria-label="Submit form"
            >
                Submit
            </Button>

            <Button 
                variant="danger"
                size="small"
                onClick={() => console.log('Delete clicked')}
            >
                Delete
            </Button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Prop types with validation
import PropTypes from 'prop-types';

function UserList({ users, isLoading, onSelect }) {
    if (isLoading) return <div>Loading users...</div>;

    return (
        <ul>
            {users.map(user => (
                <li 
                    key={user.id}
                    onClick={() => onSelect(user)}
                    className="cursor-pointer hover:bg-gray-100"
                >
                    {user.name} - {user.email}
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

UserList.propTypes = {
    users: PropTypes.arrayOf(
        PropTypes.shape({
            id: PropTypes.number.isRequired,
            name: PropTypes.string.isRequired,
            email: PropTypes.string.isRequired
        })
    ).isRequired,
    isLoading: PropTypes.bool,
    onSelect: PropTypes.func.isRequired
};

UserList.defaultProps = {
    isLoading: false
};

Props Patterns

// Render props pattern
function DataFetcher({ url, render }) {
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchData();
    }, [url]);

    async function fetchData() {
        try {
            setLoading(true);
            const response = await fetch(url);
            const json = await response.json();
            setData(json);
        } catch (err) {
            setError(err.message);
        } finally {
            setLoading(false);
        }
    }

    return render({ data, loading, error });
}

// Using render props
function UserList() {
    return (
        <DataFetcher
            url="/api/users"
            render={({ data, loading, error }) => {
                if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
                if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;

                return (
                    <ul>
                        {data.map(user => (
                            <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
                        ))}
                    </ul>
                );
            }}
        />
    );
}

// Higher-Order Component (HOC) pattern
function withLoading(WrappedComponent) {
    return function WithLoadingComponent({ isLoading, ...props }) {
        if (isLoading) {
            return <div>Loading...</div>;
        }
        return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;
    };
}

// Using HOC
const UserListWithLoading = withLoading(UserList);

function Users() {
    const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchUsers();
    }, []);

    async function fetchUsers() {
        const response = await fetch('/api/users');
        const data = await response.json();
        setUsers(data);
        setLoading(false);
    }

    return <UserListWithLoading isLoading={loading} users={users} />;
}

5.5 State

Simple Explanation

State is the memory of a component. It's data that can change over time and when it changes, React automatically re-renders the component to show the updated information. Unlike props (which come from a parent), state is internal to the component and can be changed by the component itself.

Think of state as the current state of a toggled light switch - it can be on or off, and the component responds to changes by displaying the appropriate UI.

Technical Explanation

State is mutable data that a component maintains over its lifetime. When state changes, React schedules a re-render to update the UI. State is local and private to the component that creates it.

Key characteristics: - Mutable: Can be changed using setState or useState - Local: Belongs to the component that defines it - Asynchronous: State updates are batched and asynchronous - Triggers re-render: State changes cause component to re-render - Hook-based: Managed with useState or useReducer hooks

Professional Explanation

State management is central to React applications. Understanding state helps create predictable, performant applications.

State management strategies: - Local State: useState for component-specific data - Reducer State: useReducer for complex state logic - Global State: Context API or state management libraries - Server State: React Query for server data synchronization - URL State: Routing parameters and query strings

State Examples

// useState hook
function Counter() {
    // Declare state variable
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Count: {count}</p>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Increment</button>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count - 1)}>Decrement</button>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(0)}>Reset</button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Multiple state variables
function UserForm() {
    const [name, setName] = useState('');
    const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
    const [age, setAge] = useState('');
    const [isSubmitting, setIsSubmitting] = useState(false);
    const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

    const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        setIsSubmitting(true);

        // Validate form
        const validationErrors = {};
        if (!name) validationErrors.name = 'Name is required';
        if (!email) validationErrors.email = 'Email is required';
        if (!email.includes('@')) validationErrors.email = 'Invalid email';

        if (Object.keys(validationErrors).length > 0) {
            setErrors(validationErrors);
            setIsSubmitting(false);
            return;
        }

        try {
            // Submit form
            await submitUser({ name, email, age });
            // Success logic
        } catch (error) {
            setErrors({ submit: error.message });
        } finally {
            setIsSubmitting(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <div>
                <label>Name:</label>
                <input
                    value={name}
                    onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}
                    className={errors.name ? 'error' : ''}
                />
                {errors.name && <span>{errors.name}</span>}
            </div>
            <div>
                <label>Email:</label>
                <input
                    value={email}
                    onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)}
                    className={errors.email ? 'error' : ''}
                />
                {errors.email && <span>{errors.email}</span>}
            </div>
            <div>
                <label>Age:</label>
                <input
                    type="number"
                    value={age}
                    onChange={e => setAge(e.target.value)}
                />
            </div>
            {errors.submit && <div>{errors.submit}</div>}
            <button type="submit" disabled={isSubmitting}>
                {isSubmitting ? 'Submitting...' : 'Submit'}
            </button>
        </form>
    );
}

// Object state with useState
function SettingsPanel() {
    const [settings, setSettings] = useState({
        theme: 'light',
        notifications: true,
        language: 'en',
        privacy: {
            profileVisibility: 'public',
            emailVisibility: 'private'
        }
    });

    const updateSetting = (key, value) => {
        setSettings(prev => ({
            ...prev,
            [key]: value
        }));
    };

    const updateNestedSetting = (key1, key2, value) => {
        setSettings(prev => ({
            ...prev,
            [key1]: {
                ...prev[key1],
                [key2]: value
            }
        }));
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <label>
                <input
                    type="checkbox"
                    checked={settings.notifications}
                    onChange={e => updateSetting('notifications', e.target.checked)}
                />
                Enable notifications
            </label>

            <select
                value={settings.theme}
                onChange={e => updateSetting('theme', e.target.value)}
            >
                <option value="light">Light</option>
                <option value="dark">Dark</option>
                <option value="system">System</option>
            </select>

            <select
                value={settings.privacy.profileVisibility}
                onChange={e => updateNestedSetting('privacy', 'profileVisibility', e.target.value)}
            >
                <option value="public">Public</option>
                <option value="friends">Friends</option>
                <option value="private">Private</option>
            </select>
        </div>
    );
}

// Functional state updates
function CounterFunctional() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    // Using functional updates for dependent state
    const increment = () => {
        setCount(prev => prev + 1);
    };

    const incrementByTwo = () => {
        // Multiple updates are batched
        setCount(prev => prev + 1);
        setCount(prev => prev + 1);
    };

    const asyncIncrement = () => {
        setTimeout(() => {
            setCount(prev => prev + 1);
        }, 1000);
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Count: {count}</p>
            <button onClick={increment}>+1</button>
            <button onClick={incrementByTwo}>+2</button>
            <button onClick={asyncIncrement}>Async +1</button>
        </div>
    );
}

useReducer Hook

// useReducer for complex state logic
const initialState = {
    count: 0,
    history: [],
    isLoading: false,
    error: null
};

const reducer = (state, action) => {
    switch (action.type) {
        case 'INCREMENT':
            return {
                ...state,
                count: state.count + 1,
                history: [...state.history, { type: 'INCREMENT', value: state.count + 1 }]
            };

        case 'DECREMENT':
            return {
                ...state,
                count: state.count - 1,
                history: [...state.history, { type: 'DECREMENT', value: state.count - 1 }]
            };

        case 'RESET':
            return {
                ...state,
                count: 0,
                history: []
            };

        case 'SET_LOADING':
            return {
                ...state,
                isLoading: action.payload
            };

        case 'SET_ERROR':
            return {
                ...state,
                error: action.payload
            };

        default:
            return state;
    }
};

function CounterWithReducer() {
    const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

    const incrementAsync = async () => {
        dispatch({ type: 'SET_LOADING', payload: true });
        dispatch({ type: 'SET_ERROR', payload: null });

        try {
            await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
            dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT' });
        } catch (error) {
            dispatch({ type: 'SET_ERROR', payload: error.message });
        } finally {
            dispatch({ type: 'SET_LOADING', payload: false });
        }
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {state.count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT' })}>+</button>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'DECREMENT' })}>-</button>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'RESET' })}>Reset</button>
            <button onClick={incrementAsync} disabled={state.isLoading}>
                {state.isLoading ? 'Loading...' : 'Async +1'}
            </button>

            {state.error && <div className="error">{state.error}</div>}

            <h3>History</h3>
            <ul>
                {state.history.map((item, index) => (
                    <li key={index}>
                        {item.type}: {item.value}
                    </li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

5.6 Component Lifecycle

Simple Explanation

The component lifecycle is the journey a component goes through from being created to being destroyed. React provides hooks (for functional components) and methods (for class components) that let you run code at specific points in this journey.

Think of it like the life of a person: - Birth: The component is created (mounted) - Growth: The component changes (updates) - Death: The component is removed (unmounted)

Technical Explanation

The lifecycle consists of three main phases: 1. Mounting: Component is created and inserted into the DOM 2. Updating: Component re-renders due to state or prop changes 3. Unmounting: Component is removed from the DOM

For functional components, these are managed with useEffect and other hooks. For class components, these are managed with lifecycle methods.

Professional Explanation

Understanding the lifecycle is crucial for: - Data Fetching: When to fetch data (mounting) - DOM Manipulation: When to interact with the DOM - Resource Management: When to set up and clean up resources - Performance: When to optimize rendering - Debugging: Understanding component execution order

Functional Component Lifecycle with Hooks

// useEffect for lifecycle management
function LifecycleExample() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);
    const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState(true);

    // 1. ComponentDidMount - runs once when component mounts
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Component mounted');

        // Set up subscriptions
        const subscription = subscribeToData();

        // Cleanup on unmount (ComponentWillUnmount)
        return () => {
            console.log('Component unmounting');
            subscription.unsubscribe();
        };
    }, []); // Empty dependency array

    // 2. ComponentDidUpdate - runs when dependencies change
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Count changed to:', count);
    }, [count]); // Runs when count changes

    // 3. ComponentDidUpdate with multiple dependencies
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Count or data changed');
        // Both count and data cause this effect
    }, [count, data]);

    // 4. ComponentDidUpdate without dependencies - runs on every render
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Component rendered');
        // This runs on every render
    });

    // 5. ComponentDidMount - data fetching
    useEffect(() => {
        const fetchData = async () => {
            try {
                const response = await fetch('/api/data');
                const json = await response.json();
                setData(json);
            } catch (error) {
                console.error('Error fetching data:', error);
            }
        };

        fetchData();
    }, []); // Empty array for once

    // 6. Layout effect - runs before paint (synchronous)
    useLayoutEffect(() => {
        console.log('Layout effect - runs before paint');
        // For DOM measurements
        const element = document.getElementById('element');
        if (element) {
            const rect = element.getBoundingClientRect();
            console.log('Element position:', rect);
        }
    }, []);

    return (
        <div>
            {isVisible && (
                <div id="element">
                    <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
                    <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Increment</button>
                    <button onClick={() => setIsVisible(false)}>Unmount</button>
                    {data && <pre>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</pre>}
                </div>
            )}
        </div>
    );
}

Class Component Lifecycle (Legacy)

class LifecycleClass extends React.Component {
    constructor(props) {
        super(props);
        console.log('1. Constructor');
        this.state = {
            count: 0,
            data: null,
            loading: true
        };
    }

    // Mounting phase - before DOM
    static getDerivedStateFromProps(props, state) {
        console.log('2. getDerivedStateFromProps');
        // Return updated state based on props
        if (props.resetCount) {
            return { count: 0 };
        }
        return null;
    }

    // Mounting phase - after DOM
    componentDidMount() {
        console.log('4. componentDidMount');
        this.fetchData();
        this.subscription = subscribeToData();
    }

    // Updating phase - before DOM
    shouldComponentUpdate(nextProps, nextState) {
        console.log('5. shouldComponentUpdate');
        // Return false to prevent re-render
        return true;
    }

    // Updating phase - before DOM
    getSnapshotBeforeUpdate(prevProps, prevState) {
        console.log('6. getSnapshotBeforeUpdate');
        // Capture DOM state before update
        return { scrollHeight: document.body.scrollHeight };
    }

    // Updating phase - after DOM
    componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState, snapshot) {
        console.log('7. componentDidUpdate');
        console.log('Snapshot:', snapshot);

        if (prevState.count !== this.state.count) {
            console.log('Count changed');
        }
    }

    // Unmounting phase
    componentWillUnmount() {
        console.log('8. componentWillUnmount');
        this.subscription.unsubscribe();
    }

    // Error handling
    componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo) {
        console.log('Error caught:', error, errorInfo);
        this.setState({ error: error.message });
    }

    async fetchData() {
        try {
            const response = await fetch('/api/data');
            const json = await response.json();
            this.setState({ data: json, loading: false });
        } catch (error) {
            this.setState({ error: error.message });
        }
    }

    render() {
        console.log('3. render');

        if (this.state.error) {
            return <div>Error: {this.state.error}</div>;
        }

        if (this.state.loading) {
            return <div>Loading...</div>;
        }

        return (
            <div>
                <h2>Count: {this.state.count}</h2>
                <button onClick={() => this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 })}>
                    Increment
                </button>
                <pre>{JSON.stringify(this.state.data, null, 2)}</pre>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

5.7 Rendering

Simple Explanation

Rendering is the process of converting React components into actual HTML that appears on the screen. When a component's state or props change, React "re-renders" the component to reflect the new data.

Think of rendering like a magic whiteboard - you write something, and React makes it appear on the actual page. When you change what's written, React updates only the changed parts.

Technical Explanation

Rendering in React involves: 1. Initial Render: The first time a component is rendered 2. Re-renders: When state or props change 3. Reconciliation: Comparing new and old virtual DOM 4. Commit Phase: Applying changes to the real DOM 5. Batching: Grouping multiple updates

Professional Explanation

Rendering performance is crucial for user experience. React's rendering system is designed for efficiency but requires understanding for optimization.

Rendering concepts: - Rendering Phases: Render and Commit phases - Reconciliation: Virtual DOM diffing algorithm - Batching: Automatic batching of state updates - Scheduling: Prioritizing different render tasks - Concurrent Mode: Interruptible rendering

Rendering Examples

// Basic rendering
function BasicRender() {
    return <div>Hello, World!</div>;
}

// Conditional rendering
function ConditionalRender({ isLoggedIn }) {
    if (isLoggedIn) {
        return <div>Welcome back!</div>;
    }
    return <div>Please log in</div>;
}

// Multiple conditional rendering patterns
function MultipleConditionals({ user, isAdmin, isLoading }) {
    // 1. Early return
    if (isLoading) {
        return <div>Loading...</div>;
    }

    if (!user) {
        return <div>No user found</div>;
    }

    // 2. Ternary operator
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            {isAdmin ? (
                <div>
                    <p>Admin access granted</p>
                    <AdminPanel />
                </div>
            ) : (
                <div>
                    <p>Regular user access</p>
                    <UserPanel />
                </div>
            )}

            {/* 3. Logical && operator */}
            {user.isActive && (
                <div className="active-badge">Active</div>
            )}

            {/* 4. Switch statement */}
            {(() => {
                switch(user.role) {
                    case 'admin':
                        return <AdminDashboard />;
                    case 'manager':
                        return <ManagerDashboard />;
                    case 'user':
                        return <UserDashboard />;
                    default:
                        return <DefaultDashboard />;
                }
            })()}
        </div>
    );
}

// List rendering with keys
function ListRendering({ items }) {
    // Always use key prop for list items
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map(item => (
                <li key={item.id}>
                    {item.name}
                    {item.subItems && (
                        <ul>
                            {item.subItems.map(sub => (
                                <li key={sub.id}>{sub.name}</li>
                            ))}
                        </ul>
                    )}
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// Conditional rendering with children
function ConditionalWrapper({ condition, wrapper, children }) {
    if (condition) {
        return wrapper(children);
    }
    return children;
}

// Usage
function App() {
    return (
        <ConditionalWrapper
            condition={user.isAdmin}
            wrapper={(children) => (
                <div className="admin-wrapper">
                    <div className="admin-badge">Admin</div>
                    {children}
                </div>
            )}
        >
            <UserProfile user={user} />
        </ConditionalWrapper>
    );
}

// Preventing re-renders with React.memo
const MemoizedComponent = React.memo(({ name }) => {
    console.log('Rendering MemoizedComponent');
    return <div>Hello, {name}!</div>;
});

function Parent() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    const [name, setName] = useState('John');

    return (
        <div>
            <MemoizedComponent name={name} />
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Count: {count}</button>
            <button onClick={() => setName('Jane')}>Change Name</button>
        </div>
    );
}

5.8 Conditional Rendering

Simple Explanation

Conditional rendering is showing different UI based on different conditions. Just like you show different content to logged-in users vs guests, conditional rendering lets you show different components based on your application's state.

Think of it like a choose-your-own-adventure book - based on the user's status, permissions, or data, React shows different pages or content.

Technical Explanation

Conditional rendering allows components to render different outputs based on certain conditions. This is achieved using JavaScript operators and expressions.

Methods for conditional rendering: 1. if statements: For complex logic 2. Ternary operators: For simple conditions 3. Logical && operators: For single elements 4. Switch statements: For multiple conditions 5. Immediately Invoked Function Expressions (IIFE): For complex logic 6. Element variables: Storing JSX in variables

Professional Explanation

Conditional rendering is a fundamental pattern in React that affects component composition, reusability, and performance.

Best practices: - Keep conditionals simple: Prefer ternary over if statements - Avoid too many conditionals: Consider component extraction - Use early returns: For loading and error states - Test all branches: Ensure all conditions are handled - Consider performance: Avoid expensive computations in conditionals

Conditional Rendering Examples

// 1. if statement
function IfStatement({ isLoggedIn, user }) {
    if (isLoggedIn) {
        return <Dashboard user={user} />;
    } else {
        return <LoginPage />;
    }
}

// 2. Early return
function EarlyReturn({ isLoading, error, data }) {
    if (isLoading) {
        return <LoadingSpinner />;
    }

    if (error) {
        return <ErrorMessage error={error} />;
    }

    if (!data) {
        return <EmptyState />;
    }

    return <DataDisplay data={data} />;
}

// 3. Ternary operator
function TernaryOperator({ isLoggedIn }) {
    return (
        <div>
            {isLoggedIn ? (
                <button>Logout</button>
            ) : (
                <button>Login</button>
            )}
        </div>
    );
}

// 4. Logical && operator (for single elements)
function LogicalAnd({ isAdmin, notifications }) {
    return (
        <div>
            {isAdmin && <AdminPanel />}
            {notifications.length > 0 && (
                <div className="notification-badge">
                    {notifications.length}
                </div>
            )}
        </div>
    );
}

// 5. Element variables
function ElementVariables({ user }) {
    let userContent;

    if (user.role === 'admin') {
        userContent = <AdminDashboard />;
    } else if (user.role === 'manager') {
        userContent = <ManagerDashboard />;
    } else {
        userContent = <UserDashboard />;
    }

    return (
        <div>
            <Header />
            {userContent}
            <Footer />
        </div>
    );
}

// 6. Switch statement with IIFE
function SwitchStatement({ status }) {
    return (
        <div>
            {(() => {
                switch(status) {
                    case 'success':
                        return <SuccessMessage />;
                    case 'error':
                        return <ErrorMessage />;
                    case 'loading':
                        return <LoadingSpinner />;
                    default:
                        return <DefaultState />;
                }
            })()}
        </div>
    );
}

// 7. Conditional with props
function ConditionalProps({ user }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Welcome, {user.name}</h2>
            <UserMenu 
                showAdminLink={user.isAdmin}
                showSettings={user.isAuthenticated}
                showProfile={user.isAuthenticated}
            />
        </div>
    );
}

// 8. Conditional component composition
function ConditionalComposition({ user }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <Header>
                {user.isAdmin && <AdminNav />}
                {user.isAuthenticated && <UserNav />}
                {!user.isAuthenticated && <PublicNav />}
            </Header>
            <Content>
                {user.isAuthenticated ? (
                    <AuthenticatedContent user={user} />
                ) : (
                    <PublicContent />
                )}
            </Content>
            <Footer>
                {user.isAdmin && <AdminFooter />}
            </Footer>
        </div>
    );
}

5.9 Lists and Keys

Simple Explanation

Lists are used to render collections of data, like a list of users, products, or messages. Keys are special props that help React identify which items have changed, been added, or been removed.

Think of keys like name tags at a party - they help React keep track of each item so it knows exactly what to update when the list changes.

Technical Explanation

When rendering lists with .map(), each item needs a unique key prop. Keys help React with reconciliation - identifying which items have changed, been added, or removed.

Key characteristics: - Unique: Keys must be unique among siblings - Stable: Keys should not change over time - Predictable: Keys should be predictable and consistent - String or number: Keys must be strings or numbers - Index as fallback: Use index only if no stable IDs exist

Professional Explanation

Proper key usage is crucial for performance and preventing bugs.

Best practices for keys: - Use stable IDs: Database IDs or unique identifiers - Avoid using index: Can cause issues with reordering - Keep keys consistent: Same item should always have same key - Don't use random values: Causes unnecessary re-renders - Use key for top-level elements: Apply to the outermost element

List and Key Examples

// Basic list rendering
function BasicList({ items }) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map(item => (
                <li key={item.id}>
                    {item.name}
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// List with complex data
function ComplexList({ users }) {
    return (
        <div className="users-grid">
            {users.map(user => (
                <div key={user.id} className="user-card">
                    <Avatar src={user.avatar} alt={user.name} />
                    <h3>{user.name}</h3>
                    <p>{user.email}</p>
                    <div className="user-actions">
                        <button onClick={() => handleEdit(user)}>Edit</button>
                        <button onClick={() => handleDelete(user.id)}>Delete</button>
                    </div>
                </div>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

// List with inline styles
function StyledList({ todos }) {
    return (
        <div className="todo-list">
            {todos.map(todo => (
                <div 
                    key={todo.id}
                    className="todo-item"
                    style={{
                        textDecoration: todo.completed ? 'line-through' : 'none',
                        opacity: todo.completed ? 0.6 : 1,
                        background: todo.priority === 'high' ? '#fee' : '#fff'
                    }}
                >
                    <input 
                        type="checkbox" 
                        checked={todo.completed}
                        onChange={() => toggleTodo(todo.id)}
                    />
                    <span>{todo.text}</span>
                    <button onClick={() => deleteTodo(todo.id)}>×</button>
                </div>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

// List with conditional rendering
function FilteredList({ items, filter }) {
    const filteredItems = items.filter(item => {
        if (filter === 'active') return item.active;
        if (filter === 'inactive') return !item.active;
        return true;
    });

    return (
        <ul>
            {filteredItems.length === 0 ? (
                <li>No items found</li>
            ) : (
                filteredItems.map(item => (
                    <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>
                ))
            )}
        </ul>
    );
}

// Nested lists
function NestedList({ data }) {
    return (
        <div>
            {data.map(section => (
                <div key={section.id} className="section">
                    <h2>{section.title}</h2>
                    <ul>
                        {section.items.map(item => (
                            <li key={item.id}>
                                {item.name}
                                {item.subItems && (
                                    <ul>
                                        {item.subItems.map(sub => (
                                            <li key={sub.id}>{sub.name}</li>
                                        ))}
                                    </ul>
                                )}
                            </li>
                        ))}
                    </ul>
                </div>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

// List with proper key usage
function KeyExamples({ items }) {
    // ✅ Good: Using unique ID
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map(item => (
                <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );

    // ✅ Good: Using unique combination
    // return (
    //     <ul>
    //         {items.map(item => (
    //             <li key={`${item.type}-${item.id}`}>{item.name}</li>
    //         ))}
    //     </ul>
    // );

    // ✅ Acceptable: Using index (only for static lists)
    // return (
    //     <ul>
    //         {items.map((item, index) => (
    //             <li key={index}>{item.name}</li>
    //         ))}
    //     </ul>
    // );

    // ❌ Bad: Using random values
    // return (
    //     <ul>
    //         {items.map(item => (
    //             <li key={Math.random()}>{item.name}</li>
    //         ))}
    //     </ul>
    // );
}

// List with reordering
function ReorderableList({ items, onReorder }) {
    const [list, setList] = useState(items);

    const moveItem = (fromIndex, toIndex) => {
        const newList = [...list];
        const [removed] = newList.splice(fromIndex, 1);
        newList.splice(toIndex, 0, removed);
        setList(newList);
        onReorder(newList);
    };

    return (
        <ul>
            {list.map((item, index) => (
                <li key={item.id}>
                    {item.name}
                    <div className="move-buttons">
                        <button 
                            onClick={() => moveItem(index, index - 1)}
                            disabled={index === 0}
                        >
                            ↑
                        </button>
                        <button 
                            onClick={() => moveItem(index, index + 1)}
                            disabled={index === list.length - 1}
                        >
                            ↓
                        </button>
                    </div>
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

5.10 Children and Composition

Simple Explanation

props.children is a special prop that allows you to pass components or elements as children to other components. This enables component composition - building complex components from simpler ones.

Think of children like compartments in a container - you can put any content inside a component, and the component decides how to arrange that content.

Technical Explanation

Children are the content between opening and closing tags of a component. The children prop allows components to be composed and nested, enabling flexible and reusable layouts.

Key concepts: - Child content: Anything between the opening and closing tags - Render prop: A function as a child for controlling rendering - Nested components: Components inside other components - Composition over inheritance: Building components from smaller ones

Professional Explanation

Children and composition are fundamental patterns in React that enable flexible component design.

Composition patterns: - Slot pattern: Named slots for multiple content areas - Render props: Dynamic content generation - Context composition: Accessing context within children - HOC composition: Wrapping components for enhanced functionality

Children Examples

// Basic children usage
function Container({ children }) {
    return (
        <div className="container">
            {children}
        </div>
    );
}

// Using Container
function App() {
    return (
        <Container>
            <h1>Hello World</h1>
            <p>This is inside the container</p>
        </Container>
    );
}

// Multiple children
function Card({ title, children }) {
    return (
        <div className="card">
            {title && <div className="card-title">{title}</div>}
            <div className="card-body">{children}</div>
        </div>
    );
}

// Nested children
function Layout({ header, sidebar, main, footer }) {
    return (
        <div className="layout">
            <div className="header">{header}</div>
            <div className="content">
                <div className="sidebar">{sidebar}</div>
                <div className="main">{main}</div>
            </div>
            <div className="footer">{footer}</div>
        </div>
    );
}

// Using Layout
function HomePage() {
    return (
        <Layout
            header={<Header />}
            sidebar={<Sidebar />}
            main={<MainContent />}
            footer={<Footer />}
        />
    );
}

// Children with props manipulation
function WithWrapper({ children, className }) {
    // Children is an array, we can manipulate it
    const enhancedChildren = React.Children.map(children, child => {
        if (React.isValidElement(child)) {
            return React.cloneElement(child, {
                className: `${child.props.className || ''} wrapped`
            });
        }
        return child;
    });

    return <div className={className}>{enhancedChildren}</div>;
}

// Render props pattern
function DataProvider({ render, url }) {
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchData();
    }, [url]);

    async function fetchData() {
        const response = await fetch(url);
        const json = await response.json();
        setData(json);
        setLoading(false);
    }

    return render({ data, loading });
}

// Using render props
function UserList() {
    return (
        <DataProvider
            url="/api/users"
            render={({ data, loading }) => {
                if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
                return (
                    <ul>
                        {data.map(user => (
                            <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
                        ))}
                    </ul>
                );
            }}
        />
    );
}

// Function as child
function Toggle({ children }) {
    const [isOn, setIsOn] = useState(false);

    return children({
        isOn,
        toggle: () => setIsOn(!isOn),
        turnOn: () => setIsOn(true),
        turnOff: () => setIsOn(false)
    });
}

// Using function as child
function ToggleExample() {
    return (
        <Toggle>
            {({ isOn, toggle }) => (
                <div>
                    <button onClick={toggle}>
                        {isOn ? 'ON' : 'OFF'}
                    </button>
                    {isOn && <div>The toggle is on!</div>}
                </div>
            )}
        </Toggle>
    );
}

// Multiple children with props
function Modal({
    isOpen,
    onClose,
    title,
    children,
    footer
}) {
    if (!isOpen) return null;

    return (
        <div className="modal-overlay" onClick={onClose}>
            <div className="modal" onClick={e => e.stopPropagation()}>
                {title && (
                    <div className="modal-header">
                        <h2>{title}</h2>
                        <button className="close-btn" onClick={onClose}>×</button>
                    </div>
                )}
                <div className="modal-body">{children}</div>
                {footer && (
                    <div className="modal-footer">{footer}</div>
                )}
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}

// Using Modal with children and footer
function ConfirmDialog({ isOpen, onConfirm, onCancel, message }) {
    return (
        <Modal
            isOpen={isOpen}
            onClose={onCancel}
            title="Confirm Action"
            footer={
                <>
                    <button onClick={onConfirm} className="primary">Confirm</button>
                    <button onClick={onCancel} className="secondary">Cancel</button>
                </>
            }
        >
            <p>{message}</p>
            <div className="warning-icon">⚠️</div>
        </Modal>
    );
}

5.11 Common Mistakes and Best Practices

5.11.1 Common Mistakes

// ❌ Mutating state directly
function BadState() {
    const [items, setItems] = useState([]);

    const addItem = (item) => {
        items.push(item); // Direct mutation
        setItems(items); // No re-render
    };
}

// ✅ Using immutability
function GoodState() {
    const [items, setItems] = useState([]);

    const addItem = (item) => {
        setItems([...items, item]); // New array
    };
}

// ❌ Missing key in list
function BadList({ items }) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map(item => (
                <li>{item}</li> // No key
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// ✅ Using key
function GoodList({ items }) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map(item => (
                <li key={item.id}>{item}</li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// ❌ Using index as key with dynamic lists
function BadKey({ items }) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map((item, index) => (
                <li key={index}>{item}</li> // Index as key
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// ✅ Using unique ID
function GoodKey({ items }) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map(item => (
                <li key={item.id}>{item}</li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// ❌ Calling hooks conditionally
function BadHooks({ condition }) {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // ✅

    if (condition) {
        const [data, setData] = useState(null); // ❌ Conditional hook
    }
}

// ✅ Calling hooks at top level
function GoodHooks({ condition }) {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        if (condition) {
            // Use condition inside effect
        }
    }, [condition]);
}

5.11.2 Best Practices

// ✅ Component organization
function Component({ prop1, prop2 }) {
    // 1. Hooks
    const [state, setState] = useState();
    const dispatch = useDispatch();

    // 2. Memoized values
    const computedValue = useMemo(() => {
        return expensiveCalculation(prop1);
    }, [prop1]);

    // 3. Callbacks
    const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
        // Handle click
    }, []);

    // 4. Effects
    useEffect(() => {
        // Side effects
    }, []);

    // 5. Early returns
    if (!prop1) return <EmptyState />;

    // 6. Render
    return (
        <div>
            {/* JSX */}
        </div>
    );
}

// ✅ Destructuring props
function GoodProps({ user, onUpdate, onDelete }) {
    // Use destructured props
    return <div>{user.name}</div>;
}

// ❌ Anti-pattern
function BadProps(props) {
    // Accessing props with dot notation
    return <div>{props.user.name}</div>;
}

// ✅ Proper event handlers
function GoodHandlers() {
    const [input, setInput] = useState('');

    const handleChange = (e) => {
        setInput(e.target.value);
    };

    return <input value={input} onChange={handleChange} />;
}

// ✅ Component composition
function App() {
    return (
        <ErrorBoundary>
            <ThemeProvider>
                <Router>
                    <Layout>
                        <Routes>
                            <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                        </Routes>
                    </Layout>
                </Router>
            </ThemeProvider>
        </ErrorBoundary>
    );
}

5.12 Interview Questions

Junior Level Questions

Q: What is JSX and why use it?

Answer: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that allows writing HTML-like code in React. Benefits include: - Visual representation of UI - Error handling and debugging - Performance optimization - Type checking support

// JSX
const element = <h1 className="title">Hello</h1>;

// Transpiled to
const element = React.createElement('h1', { className: 'title' }, 'Hello');

Q: What's the difference between props and state?

Answer: - Props: Read-only, passed from parent, immutable - State: Read/write, internal to component, mutable

function Component({ prop }) {
    const [state, setState] = useState(0);
    // Props come from parent
    // State is managed internally
}

Mid Level Questions

Q: Explain the component lifecycle and how it's handled in functional components.

Answer: The lifecycle consists of: 1. Mounting: Component creation with useEffect([]) 2. Updating: Component updates with useEffect([dependencies]) 3. Unmounting: Cleanup with useEffect return function

function Component() {
    // Mounting and unmounting
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Mounted');
        return () => console.log('Unmounted');
    }, []);

    // Updating
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Count changed');
    }, [count]);
}

Q: When should you use useMemo vs useCallback?

Answer: - useMemo: Memoizes values/computations - useCallback: Memoizes functions

function Component({ data }) {
    // Memoize computed value
    const processed = useMemo(() => {
        return heavyComputation(data);
    }, [data]);

    // Memoize callback function
    const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
        console.log('Clicked');
    }, []);

    return <div>{processed}</div>;
}

Senior Level Questions

Q: Explain the reconciliation process and how keys affect it.

Answer: Reconciliation is React's algorithm for updating the DOM efficiently. It compares the new virtual DOM with the previous one and determines what changes to make.

Keys help React identify which items have changed: 1. Unique keys: Help React track items across re-renders 2. Stable keys: Same item always has same key 3. Avoid index keys: Can cause issues with reordering

// Good - unique ID
<li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>

// Bad - index (causes issues with reordering)
<li key={index}>{user.name}</li>

Q: How do you optimize React component performance?

Answer: 1. React.memo: Prevent unnecessary re-renders 2. useMemo: Cache expensive computations 3. useCallback: Memoize callback functions 4. Code splitting: Lazy loading with React.lazy 5. Virtualization: For large lists 6. Debouncing: For frequent updates

const MemoizedComponent = React.memo(({ data }) => {
    const processed = useMemo(() => {
        return processData(data);
    }, [data]);

    const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
        // Handle click
    }, []);

    return <div onClick={handleClick}>{processed}</div>;
});

5.13 Summary

Key React Fundamentals

Concept Description Example
JSX HTML-like syntax in JavaScript <div>Hello</div>
Components Reusable UI building blocks function App() {}
Props Read-only data from parent <Child name="John" />
State Mutable component data const [state, setState] = useState()

Conditional Rendering Showing UI based on conditions {condition && <Component />}

Best Practices Summary

  1. Use functional components with hooks
  2. Keep components focused (Single Responsibility)
  3. Use proper key props in lists
  4. Avoid direct state mutation
  5. Memoize expensive computations with useMemo
  6. Memoize callbacks with useCallback
  7. Clean up effects with return function
  8. Use composition over inheritance
  9. Use proper prop types or TypeScript
  10. Write tests for components

Common Pitfalls to Avoid

  1. ❌ Mutating state directly
  2. ❌ Missing keys in lists
  3. ❌ Using index as key
  4. ❌ Calling hooks conditionally
  5. ❌ Infinite loops in useEffect
  6. ❌ Prop drilling
  7. ❌ Ignoring cleanup functions
  8. ❌ Inline functions in render
