07

State Management in React

7.1 Introduction to State Management

Simple Explanation

State management is how you handle and share data across your React application. As applications grow, managing state becomes increasingly complex. You need to decide where to store data, how to update it, and how to share it between components.

Think of state management like a library system: - Local State: Books on your personal shelf (component-specific) - Shared State: Books in a shared reading room (multiple components) - Global State: The main library catalog (entire application)

Technical Explanation

State management encompasses all the patterns, tools, and practices for handling data in React applications. It includes:

  1. Local State: Component-specific state using useState/useReducer
  2. Shared State: State shared between components via props drilling
  3. Global State: Application-wide state using Context or libraries
  4. Server State: Data fetched from APIs (React Query, SWR)
  5. URL State: Routing and query parameters
  6. Persisted State: localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB

Professional Explanation

In enterprise React applications, state management is critical for:

  • Data Consistency: Ensuring all components show the same data
  • Performance: Optimizing re-renders and updates
  • Maintainability: Clear patterns for data flow
  • Scalability: Handling complex application state
  • Debugging: Tools and patterns for tracking state changes
  • Testing: Predictable state for testing

7.2 Local State Management

Simple Explanation

Local state is data that belongs to a single component. It's managed using useState or useReducer hooks. This is the simplest form of state management and should be your default choice.

Think of local state like the memory of a single employee - they remember their own tasks, preferences, and current status without needing to share it with everyone else.

Technical Explanation

Local state is component-specific state that doesn't need to be shared with other components. It's managed using React's built-in hooks and is the most straightforward approach to state management.

Key characteristics: - Component-specific: Only relevant to one component - Simple: Easy to understand and implement - Encapsulated: Not accessible to other components - Reactive: Updates trigger re-renders

Professional Explanation

Local state is the foundation of React state management. Always start with local state and lift state up only when needed.

When to use local state: - UI state: Toggle states, form inputs, loading states - Component-specific data: Data only needed by one component - Temporary data: Data that doesn't persist beyond the component - Simple state: State that doesn't need complex logic

Local State Examples

// Simple local state with useState
function ToggleButton() {
    const [isOn, setIsOn] = useState(false);

    return (
        <button onClick={() => setIsOn(!isOn)}>
            {isOn ? 'ON' : 'OFF'}
        </button>
    );
}

// Multiple local states
function LoginForm() {
    const [username, setUsername] = useState('');
    const [password, setPassword] = useState('');
    const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);
    const [error, setError] = useState(null);

    const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        setIsLoading(true);
        setError(null);

        try {
            await login(username, password);
            // Handle success
        } catch (err) {
            setError(err.message);
        } finally {
            setIsLoading(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <input
                value={username}
                onChange={(e) => setUsername(e.target.value)}
                disabled={isLoading}
            />
            <input
                type="password"
                value={password}
                onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)}
                disabled={isLoading}
            />
            {error && <div className="error">{error}</div>}
            <button type="submit" disabled={isLoading}>
                {isLoading ? 'Loading...' : 'Login'}
            </button>
        </form>
    );
}

// Local state with useReducer for complex logic
function ShoppingCart() {
    const [cart, dispatch] = useReducer(cartReducer, []);

    const addItem = (item) => {
        dispatch({ type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: item });
    };

    const removeItem = (itemId) => {
        dispatch({ type: 'REMOVE_ITEM', payload: itemId });
    };

    const updateQuantity = (itemId, quantity) => {
        dispatch({ type: 'UPDATE_QUANTITY', payload: { itemId, quantity } });
    };

    const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity, 0);

    return (
        <div>
            <ProductList onAdd={addItem} />
            <CartItems 
                items={cart} 
                onRemove={removeItem}
                onUpdateQuantity={updateQuantity}
            />
            <div>Total: ${total}</div>
        </div>
    );
}

7.3 Lifting State Up

Simple Explanation

Lifting state up means moving state from a child component to a parent component so multiple children can share it. This is a fundamental pattern for sharing state between components without external libraries.

Think of it like a family meeting - instead of each child making their own decision, the parent makes the decision and tells all the children what to do.

Technical Explanation

Lifting state up is the practice of moving state to the lowest common ancestor of components that need to share it. The parent component manages the state and passes it down via props, along with callbacks for updating it.

Key characteristics: - Single source of truth: State is managed in one place - Controlled components: Parent controls child behavior - Unidirectional data flow: Data flows down, events flow up - Simple sharing: No external libraries needed

Professional Explanation

Lifting state up is the most basic and often the most appropriate solution for sharing state between a few related components.

When to lift state up: - Sibling components: Two or more siblings need the same data - Controlled inputs: Parent needs to control child inputs - Form validation: Multiple fields need validation together - Data synchronization: Keeping multiple components in sync

Lifting State Up Examples

// Parent manages shared state
function TemperatureConverter() {
    const [temperature, setTemperature] = useState('');
    const [scale, setScale] = useState('c');

    const handleCelsiusChange = (value) => {
        setTemperature(value);
        setScale('c');
    };

    const handleFahrenheitChange = (value) => {
        setTemperature(value);
        setScale('f');
    };

    const celsius = scale === 'c' ? temperature : convertToCelsius(temperature);
    const fahrenheit = scale === 'f' ? temperature : convertToFahrenheit(temperature);

    return (
        <div>
            <TemperatureInput
                scale="c"
                temperature={celsius}
                onTemperatureChange={handleCelsiusChange}
            />
            <TemperatureInput
                scale="f"
                temperature={fahrenheit}
                onTemperatureChange={handleFahrenheitChange}
            />
        </div>
    );
}

// Child component receives state from parent
function TemperatureInput({ scale, temperature, onTemperatureChange }) {
    const handleChange = (e) => {
        onTemperatureChange(e.target.value);
    };

    return (
        <fieldset>
            <legend>Enter temperature in {scale === 'c' ? 'Celsius' : 'Fahrenheit'}:</legend>
            <input
                type="text"
                value={temperature}
                onChange={handleChange}
            />
        </fieldset>
    );
}

// Shopping cart with lifted state
function ShoppingApp() {
    const [cartItems, setCartItems] = useState([]);
    const [total, setTotal] = useState(0);

    const addToCart = (product) => {
        setCartItems(prev => {
            const existing = prev.find(item => item.id === product.id);
            if (existing) {
                return prev.map(item =>
                    item.id === product.id
                        ? { ...item, quantity: item.quantity + 1 }
                        : item
                );
            }
            return [...prev, { ...product, quantity: 1 }];
        });
    };

    const removeFromCart = (productId) => {
        setCartItems(prev => prev.filter(item => item.id !== productId));
    };

    const updateQuantity = (productId, quantity) => {
        setCartItems(prev =>
            prev.map(item =>
                item.id === productId
                    ? { ...item, quantity: Math.max(0, quantity) }
                    : item
            )
        );
    };

    useEffect(() => {
        const newTotal = cartItems.reduce(
            (sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity,
            0
        );
        setTotal(newTotal);
    }, [cartItems]);

    return (
        <div>
            <ProductCatalog onAddToCart={addToCart} />
            <ShoppingCart
                items={cartItems}
                onRemove={removeFromCart}
                onUpdateQuantity={updateQuantity}
                total={total}
            />
        </div>
    );
}

7.4 Context API

Simple Explanation

The Context API provides a way to share data across the component tree without passing props down manually at every level. It's built into React and doesn't require any external libraries.

Think of Context like a bulletin board in an office building - anyone can post information there, and anyone else can read it without having to go through intermediaries.

Technical Explanation

Context provides a way to share values like themes, user authentication, or preferences across the component tree. It creates a provider-consumer pattern where components can access data without prop drilling.

Key characteristics: - Avoids prop drilling: Data reaches deep components directly - Built-in: No external dependencies - Provider pattern: Wrap components with context providers - Dynamic updates: Context changes trigger re-renders - Multiple contexts: Use multiple contexts for different concerns

Professional Explanation

Context API is suitable for: - Themes: Light/dark mode, branding - Authentication: User session and permissions - Language/Locale: Internationalization - Feature flags: A/B testing and feature toggles - Configuration: Application settings

However, Context has limitations: - Performance: All consumers re-render on context changes - Complexity: Not ideal for complex state logic - Testing: Need to wrap components in providers

Context API Examples

// Creating a context
const ThemeContext = React.createContext('light');

// Using context with Provider
function App() {
    const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');

    const toggleTheme = () => {
        setTheme(prev => prev === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light');
    };

    return (
        <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, toggleTheme }}>
            <Header />
            <MainContent />
            <Footer />
        </ThemeContext.Provider>
    );
}

// Consuming context with useContext
function Header() {
    const { theme, toggleTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext);

    return (
        <header className={`header-${theme}`}>
            <h1>My App</h1>
            <button onClick={toggleTheme}>
                Switch to {theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light'} mode
            </button>
        </header>
    );
}

// Complex context with reducer
const AuthContext = React.createContext(null);

function AuthProvider({ children }) {
    const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(authReducer, {
        user: null,
        loading: false,
        error: null
    });

    const login = async (email, password) => {
        dispatch({ type: 'LOGIN_START' });

        try {
            const response = await fetch('/api/login', {
                method: 'POST',
                body: JSON.stringify({ email, password })
            });
            const user = await response.json();
            dispatch({ type: 'LOGIN_SUCCESS', payload: user });
            return user;
        } catch (error) {
            dispatch({ type: 'LOGIN_ERROR', payload: error.message });
            throw error;
        }
    };

    const logout = () => {
        dispatch({ type: 'LOGOUT' });
    };

    const value = {
        ...state,
        login,
        logout,
        isAuthenticated: !!state.user
    };

    return (
        <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>
            {children}
        </AuthContext.Provider>
    );
}

// Using Auth context
function ProfilePage() {
    const { user, loading, isAuthenticated } = useContext(AuthContext);

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (!isAuthenticated) return <LoginForm />;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Multiple contexts
const SettingsContext = React.createContext(null);
const UserContext = React.createContext(null);

function AppWithMultipleContexts() {
    const [settings, setSettings] = useState({
        language: 'en',
        notifications: true,
        privacy: 'public'
    });

    const [user] = useState({
        id: 1,
        name: 'John Doe',
        role: 'admin'
    });

    return (
        <SettingsContext.Provider value={{ settings, setSettings }}>
            <UserContext.Provider value={user}>
                <Dashboard />
            </UserContext.Provider>
        </SettingsContext.Provider>
    );
}

function Dashboard() {
    const { settings } = useContext(SettingsContext);
    const user = useContext(UserContext);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Welcome, {user.name}</h2>
            <p>Language: {settings.language}</p>
            <p>Notifications: {settings.notifications ? 'On' : 'Off'}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

7.5 Redux Toolkit (RTK)

Simple Explanation

Redux Toolkit is the official, recommended way to write Redux logic. It simplifies the Redux workflow by providing utilities to configure the store, create reducers, and write immutable updates. It's like Redux with training wheels, making it easier to use and maintain.

Think of Redux Toolkit like a well-organized filing system - everything has its place, and it's easy to find what you need and update records.

Technical Explanation

Redux Toolkit (RTK) is a set of tools and best practices for efficient Redux development. It includes utilities for: - Store Configuration: configureStore with good defaults - Slice Creation: createSlice for reducers and actions - Async Logic: createAsyncThunk for async actions - DevTools Integration: Redux DevTools out of the box - Immer Integration: Write mutable code that produces immutable updates

Professional Explanation

Redux Toolkit is the standard for Redux in enterprise applications.

Benefits: - Less Boilerplate: Less code than traditional Redux - Immutability: Built-in Immer for immutable updates - RTK Query: Powerful data fetching and caching - TypeScript: Excellent TypeScript support - DevTools: Redux DevTools integration

When to use Redux Toolkit: - Large applications: Complex state needs - Multiple features: Shared state across features - Team development: Predictable patterns - Enterprise apps: Robust state management

Redux Toolkit Examples

// Store Configuration
// store/index.js
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import counterReducer from './counterSlice';
import userReducer from './userSlice';
import productReducer from './productSlice';

export const store = configureStore({
    reducer: {
        counter: counterReducer,
        user: userReducer,
        products: productReducer
    },
    // Middleware can be added here
    middleware: (getDefaultMiddleware) =>
        getDefaultMiddleware({
            serializableCheck: false
        })
});

// Counter Slice
// store/counterSlice.js
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const counterSlice = createSlice({
    name: 'counter',
    initialState: {
        value: 0,
        history: []
    },
    reducers: {
        increment: (state) => {
            state.value += 1;
            state.history.push({ type: 'increment', value: state.value });
        },
        decrement: (state) => {
            state.value -= 1;
            state.history.push({ type: 'decrement', value: state.value });
        },
        incrementByAmount: (state, action) => {
            state.value += action.payload;
            state.history.push({ type: 'incrementByAmount', value: state.value });
        },
        reset: (state) => {
            state.value = 0;
            state.history = [];
        }
    }
});

export const { increment, decrement, incrementByAmount, reset } = counterSlice.actions;
export default counterSlice.reducer;

// Using counter in component
function Counter() {
    const count = useSelector((state) => state.counter.value);
    const history = useSelector((state) => state.counter.history);
    const dispatch = useDispatch();

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch(increment())}>+</button>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch(decrement())}>-</button>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch(incrementByAmount(5))}>+5</button>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch(reset())}>Reset</button>
            <ul>
                {history.map((item, index) => (
                    <li key={index}>{item.type}: {item.value}</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

// Async Actions with createAsyncThunk
// store/userSlice.js
import { createSlice, createAsyncThunk } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import { fetchUserApi, updateUserApi } from '../api/userApi';

// Async thunk
export const fetchUser = createAsyncThunk(
    'user/fetchUser',
    async (userId, { rejectWithValue }) => {
        try {
            const response = await fetchUserApi(userId);
            return response.data;
        } catch (error) {
            return rejectWithValue(error.message);
        }
    }
);

export const updateUser = createAsyncThunk(
    'user/updateUser',
    async (userData, { rejectWithValue }) => {
        try {
            const response = await updateUserApi(userData);
            return response.data;
        } catch (error) {
            return rejectWithValue(error.message);
        }
    }
);

const userSlice = createSlice({
    name: 'user',
    initialState: {
        data: null,
        loading: false,
        error: null,
        isUpdating: false
    },
    reducers: {
        clearUser: (state) => {
            state.data = null;
            state.error = null;
        }
    },
    extraReducers: (builder) => {
        builder
            // Fetch user
            .addCase(fetchUser.pending, (state) => {
                state.loading = true;
                state.error = null;
            })
            .addCase(fetchUser.fulfilled, (state, action) => {
                state.loading = false;
                state.data = action.payload;
            })
            .addCase(fetchUser.rejected, (state, action) => {
                state.loading = false;
                state.error = action.payload;
            })
            // Update user
            .addCase(updateUser.pending, (state) => {
                state.isUpdating = true;
                state.error = null;
            })
            .addCase(updateUser.fulfilled, (state, action) => {
                state.isUpdating = false;
                state.data = action.payload;
            })
            .addCase(updateUser.rejected, (state, action) => {
                state.isUpdating = false;
                state.error = action.payload;
            });
    }
});

export const { clearUser } = userSlice.actions;
export default userSlice.reducer;

// Using async actions in component
function UserProfile({ userId }) {
    const dispatch = useDispatch();
    const { data: user, loading, error, isUpdating } = useSelector((state) => state.user);

    useEffect(() => {
        dispatch(fetchUser(userId));
    }, [dispatch, userId]);

    const handleUpdate = async (userData) => {
        await dispatch(updateUser(userData));
    };

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;
    if (!user) return <div>User not found</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p>
            <button 
                onClick={() => handleUpdate({ ...user, name: 'Updated Name' })}
                disabled={isUpdating}
            >
                {isUpdating ? 'Updating...' : 'Update Name'}
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

// RTK Query - Data fetching and caching
// store/api.js
import { createApi, fetchBaseQuery } from '@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react';

export const api = createApi({
    reducerPath: 'api',
    baseQuery: fetchBaseQuery({
        baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com',
        prepareHeaders: (headers, { getState }) => {
            const token = getState().auth.token;
            if (token) {
                headers.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`);
            }
            return headers;
        }
    }),
    tagTypes: ['User', 'Post', 'Comment'],
    endpoints: (builder) => ({
        // Queries
        getUser: builder.query({
            query: (id) => `/users/${id}`,
            providesTags: (result, error, id) => [{ type: 'User', id }]
        }),
        getPosts: builder.query({
            query: (userId) => `/users/${userId}/posts`,
            providesTags: (result) =>
                result
                    ? [...result.map(({ id }) => ({ type: 'Post', id })), 'Post']
                    : ['Post']
        }),
        // Mutations
        updateUser: builder.mutation({
            query: ({ id, ...patch }) => ({
                url: `/users/${id}`,
                method: 'PATCH',
                body: patch
            }),
            invalidatesTags: (result, error, { id }) => [{ type: 'User', id }]
        }),
        createPost: builder.mutation({
            query: (post) => ({
                url: '/posts',
                method: 'POST',
                body: post
            }),
            invalidatesTags: ['Post']
        })
    })
});

// Using RTK Query in components
function UserWithPosts({ userId }) {
    const { data: user, isLoading: userLoading } = api.useGetUserQuery(userId);
    const { data: posts, isLoading: postsLoading } = api.useGetPostsQuery(userId);
    const [updateUser, { isLoading: isUpdating }] = api.useUpdateUserMutation();
    const [createPost, { isLoading: isCreating }] = api.useCreatePostMutation();

    if (userLoading || postsLoading) return <div>Loading...</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <button 
                onClick={() => updateUser({ id: userId, name: 'New Name' })}
                disabled={isUpdating}
            >
                Update Name
            </button>
            <div>
                <h3>Posts</h3>
                {posts.map(post => (
                    <div key={post.id}>
                        <h4>{post.title}</h4>
                        <p>{post.body}</p>
                    </div>
                ))}
            </div>
            <button 
                onClick={() => createPost({ userId, title: 'New Post', body: 'Content' })}
                disabled={isCreating}
            >
                Create Post
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

7.6 Zustand

Simple Explanation

Zustand is a small, fast, and scalable state management library. It's simpler than Redux but more powerful than Context. It uses a simple API where you create a store and use it directly in components.

Think of Zustand like a personal assistant - you can access it anywhere, it's always available, and it handles your state with minimal ceremony.

Technical Explanation

Zustand is a minimal state management library that uses hooks for accessing store state. It doesn't require providers or complex setup.

Key characteristics: - Simple API: Create stores with create - No Providers: Directly import and use stores - Selectors: Use selectors to prevent unnecessary re-renders - Immutability: Built-in Immer for immutable updates - Middleware: Support for devtools, persistence, etc.

Professional Explanation

Zustand is ideal for: - Small to medium applications: Less complexity - Gradual adoption: Can be added incrementally - Simple state needs: No complex boilerplate - Performance: Minimal overhead - TypeScript: Excellent TypeScript support

When to use Zustand: - Startup projects: Quick development - Simple state: No complex logic - Performance: Minimal overhead - Developer experience: Simple API

Zustand Examples

// Basic Zustand store
import { create } from 'zustand';

const useCounterStore = create((set) => ({
    count: 0,
    history: [],
    increment: () =>
        set((state) => ({
            count: state.count + 1,
            history: [...state.history, { type: 'increment', value: state.count + 1 }]
        })),
    decrement: () =>
        set((state) => ({
            count: state.count - 1,
            history: [...state.history, { type: 'decrement', value: state.count - 1 }]
        })),
    reset: () =>
        set({ count: 0, history: [] })
}));

// Using the store
function Counter() {
    const { count, history, increment, decrement, reset } = useCounterStore();

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
            <button onClick={increment}>+</button>
            <button onClick={decrement}>-</button>
            <button onClick={reset}>Reset</button>
            <ul>
                {history.map((item, index) => (
                    <li key={index}>{item.type}: {item.value}</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

// Complex store with async actions
const useUserStore = create((set, get) => ({
    users: [],
    loading: false,
    error: null,
    fetchUsers: async () => {
        set({ loading: true, error: null });
        try {
            const response = await fetch('/api/users');
            const data = await response.json();
            set({ users: data, loading: false });
        } catch (error) {
            set({ error: error.message, loading: false });
        }
    },
    addUser: (user) =>
        set((state) => ({
            users: [...state.users, { ...user, id: Date.now() }]
        })),
    deleteUser: (userId) =>
        set((state) => ({
            users: state.users.filter(user => user.id !== userId)
        })),
    updateUser: (userId, updates) =>
        set((state) => ({
            users: state.users.map(user =>
                user.id === userId ? { ...user, ...updates } : user
            )
        }))
}));

// Using the user store
function UserManagement() {
    const { users, loading, error, fetchUsers, addUser, deleteUser, updateUser } = useUserStore();
    const [newUserName, setNewUserName] = useState('');

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchUsers();
    }, []);

    const handleAddUser = () => {
        if (newUserName.trim()) {
            addUser({ name: newUserName, email: `${newUserName}@example.com` });
            setNewUserName('');
        }
    };

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <div>
                <input
                    value={newUserName}
                    onChange={(e) => setNewUserName(e.target.value)}
                    placeholder="New user name"
                />
                <button onClick={handleAddUser}>Add User</button>
            </div>
            <ul>
                {users.map(user => (
                    <li key={user.id}>
                        {user.name} ({user.email})
                        <button onClick={() => updateUser(user.id, { name: 'Updated' })}>
                            Update
                        </button>
                        <button onClick={() => deleteUser(user.id)}>
                            Delete
                        </button>
                    </li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

// Zustand with selectors for performance
const useProductStore = create((set, get) => ({
    products: [],
    filter: 'all',
    searchTerm: '',
    setFilter: (filter) => set({ filter }),
    setSearchTerm: (term) => set({ searchTerm: term }),
    filteredProducts: () => {
        const { products, filter, searchTerm } = get();
        return products
            .filter(p => filter === 'all' || p.category === filter)
            .filter(p => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(searchTerm.toLowerCase()));
    }
}));

// Using selectors
function ProductList() {
    const products = useProductStore((state) => state.filteredProducts());
    const setFilter = useProductStore((state) => state.setFilter);
    const setSearchTerm = useProductStore((state) => state.setSearchTerm);

    // Only re-renders when filtered products change
    return (
        <div>
            <input
                onChange={(e) => setSearchTerm(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Search..."
            />
            <select onChange={(e) => setFilter(e.target.value)}>
                <option value="all">All</option>
                <option value="electronics">Electronics</option>
                <option value="clothing">Clothing</option>
            </select>
            <ul>
                {products.map(product => (
                    <li key={product.id}>{product.name}</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

// Zustand with middleware
import { persist, createJSONStorage } from 'zustand/middleware';

const usePersistedStore = create(
    persist(
        (set) => ({
            theme: 'light',
            language: 'en',
            preferences: {
                notifications: true,
                sound: false
            },
            setTheme: (theme) => set({ theme }),
            setLanguage: (language) => set({ language }),
            toggleNotifications: () =>
                set((state) => ({
                    preferences: {
                        ...state.preferences,
                        notifications: !state.preferences.notifications
                    }
                }))
        }),
        {
            name: 'user-preferences',
            storage: createJSONStorage(() => localStorage)
        }
    )
);

7.7 Jotai

Simple Explanation

Jotai is a state management library that takes an atomic approach. Instead of having a single global store, you create small, independent atoms that can be composed together. Think of atoms like LEGO pieces - you can build complex state by combining simple atoms.

Think of Jotai like a toolbox full of small, specialized tools. Each atom does one thing well, and you can combine them to create complex behavior.

Technical Explanation

Jotai is a primitive and flexible state management library inspired by Recoil. It uses atoms as units of state that can be combined and derived.

Key characteristics: - Atomic: Each piece of state is an atom - No Providers: Atoms work without context providers - Derived atoms: Create computed state from other atoms - Async atoms: Handle async state natively - TypeScript: Excellent TypeScript support

Professional Explanation

Jotai is suitable for: - Micro-frontends: Independent state pieces - Complex derivations: Computed state - Lazy loading: Atoms can be loaded on demand - Testing: Isolated atoms are easy to test - Performance: Fine-grained re-renders

When to use Jotai: - Complex state logic: Derived and computed state - Small to medium applications: Quick development - Modular architecture: Independent state pieces - Performance: Fine-grained updates

Jotai Examples

// Basic Jotai setup
import { atom, useAtom } from 'jotai';

// Create atoms
const countAtom = atom(0);
const textAtom = atom('Hello');

// Using atoms
function Counter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useAtom(countAtom);
    const [text, setText] = useAtom(textAtom);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>+</button>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c - 1)}>-</button>
            <input
                value={text}
                onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)}
            />
            <p>Text: {text}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Derived atoms
const doubleCountAtom = atom((get) => get(countAtom) * 2);
const evenOddAtom = atom((get) => {
    const count = get(countAtom);
    return count % 2 === 0 ? 'Even' : 'Odd';
});

function DerivedValues() {
    const [doubleCount] = useAtom(doubleCountAtom);
    const [parity] = useAtom(evenOddAtom);

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Double: {doubleCount}</p>
            <p>{parity}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Async atoms
const fetchUserAtom = atom(async () => {
    const response = await fetch('/api/user');
    return response.json();
});

function AsyncUser() {
    const [user] = useAtom(fetchUserAtom);
    return <div>{user?.name}</div>;
}

// Atom with side effects
const todoListAtom = atom([]);
const filteredTodosAtom = atom(
    (get) => {
        const todos = get(todoListAtom);
        const filter = get(filterAtom);
        return todos.filter(todo => {
            if (filter === 'active') return !todo.completed;
            if (filter === 'completed') return todo.completed;
            return true;
        });
    },
    (get, set, newTodo) => {
        const todos = get(todoListAtom);
        set(todoListAtom, [...todos, { id: Date.now(), text: newTodo, completed: false }]);
    }
);

function TodoApp() {
    const [todos, setTodos] = useAtom(todoListAtom);
    const [filter, setFilter] = useAtom(filterAtom);
    const [filteredTodos] = useAtom(filteredTodosAtom);
    const [input, setInput] = useState('');

    const addTodo = () => {
        if (input.trim()) {
            setTodos(prev => [...prev, {
                id: Date.now(),
                text: input,
                completed: false
            }]);
            setInput('');
        }
    };

    const toggleTodo = (id) => {
        setTodos(prev =>
            prev.map(todo =>
                todo.id === id ? { ...todo, completed: !todo.completed } : todo
            )
        );
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <div>
                <input
                    value={input}
                    onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)}
                    placeholder="Add todo..."
                />
                <button onClick={addTodo}>Add</button>
            </div>
            <div>
                <button onClick={() => setFilter('all')}>All</button>
                <button onClick={() => setFilter('active')}>Active</button>
                <button onClick={() => setFilter('completed')}>Completed</button>
            </div>
            <ul>
                {filteredTodos.map(todo => (
                    <li key={todo.id}>
                        <input
                            type="checkbox"
                            checked={todo.completed}
                            onChange={() => toggleTodo(todo.id)}
                        />
                        <span style={{ textDecoration: todo.completed ? 'line-through' : 'none' }}>
                            {todo.text}
                        </span>
                    </li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

// Atoms with dependencies
const priceAtom = atom(10);
const quantityAtom = atom(1);
const totalAtom = atom(
    (get) => get(priceAtom) * get(quantityAtom),
    (get, set, newPrice) => {
        set(priceAtom, newPrice);
    }
);

function ShoppingCart() {
    const [price] = useAtom(priceAtom);
    const [quantity, setQuantity] = useAtom(quantityAtom);
    const [total] = useAtom(totalAtom);

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Price: ${price}</p>
            <button onClick={() => setPrice(price + 1)}>+</button>
            <p>Quantity: {quantity}</p>
            <button onClick={() => setQuantity(q => q + 1)}>+</button>
            <p>Total: ${total}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

7.8 Recoil

Simple Explanation

Recoil is a state management library developed by Facebook. It provides a React-like approach to state management with atoms and selectors. It's designed to be simple, powerful, and works seamlessly with React's concurrent features.

Think of Recoil like a graph database - each piece of state (atom) is a node, and selectors create relationships between nodes to derive new state.

Technical Explanation

Recoil provides a way to manage state using atoms and selectors. It's built with React in mind and supports concurrent rendering.

Key characteristics: - Atoms: Units of state - Selectors: Derived state from atoms or other selectors - RecoilRoot: Provider for state - Concurrent Mode: Supports React's concurrent features - TypeScript: Good TypeScript support

Professional Explanation

Recoil is suitable for: - Large applications: Complex state graphs - Performance: Fine-grained subscriptions - Derived state: Complex computed state - TypeScript: Good TypeScript support - React integration: Works well with React features

When to use Recoil: - Complex applications: Multiple state dependencies - Performance: Fine-grained updates - Derived state: Complex computed state - Facebook scale: Proven at large scale

Recoil Examples

// Basic Recoil setup
import { RecoilRoot, atom, selector, useRecoilState, useRecoilValue, useSetRecoilState } from 'recoil';

// Atoms
const countState = atom({
    key: 'countState',
    default: 0
});

const textState = atom({
    key: 'textState',
    default: 'Hello'
});

// Selectors
const doubleCountState = selector({
    key: 'doubleCountState',
    get: ({ get }) => {
        const count = get(countState);
        return count * 2;
    }
});

const evenOddState = selector({
    key: 'evenOddState',
    get: ({ get }) => {
        const count = get(countState);
        return count % 2 === 0 ? 'Even' : 'Odd';
    }
});

// Using Recoil
function RecoilCounter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useRecoilState(countState);
    const doubleCount = useRecoilValue(doubleCountState);
    const parity = useRecoilValue(evenOddState);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
            <p>Double: {doubleCount}</p>
            <p>Parity: {parity}</p>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>+</button>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c - 1)}>-</button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Async selectors
const userQuery = selector({
    key: 'userQuery',
    get: async () => {
        const response = await fetch('/api/user');
        return response.json();
    }
});

function AsyncUser() {
    const user = useRecoilValue(userQuery);
    return <div>{user.name}</div>;
}

// Complex state with family
const todoListState = atom({
    key: 'todoListState',
    default: []
});

const todoItemState = atomFamily({
    key: 'todoItemState',
    default: (id) => ({ id, text: '', completed: false })
});

function TodoItem({ id }) {
    const [todo, setTodo] = useRecoilState(todoItemState(id));

    const toggleCompleted = () => {
        setTodo({ ...todo, completed: !todo.completed });
    };

    const updateText = (text) => {
        setTodo({ ...todo, text });
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <input
                type="checkbox"
                checked={todo.completed}
                onChange={toggleCompleted}
            />
            <input
                value={todo.text}
                onChange={(e) => updateText(e.target.value)}
            />
        </div>
    );
}

// Todo list using atom family
function TodoList() {
    const [todos, setTodos] = useRecoilState(todoListState);
    const [input, setInput] = useState('');

    const addTodo = () => {
        if (input.trim()) {
            const id = Date.now();
            setTodos([...todos, id]);
            setInput('');
        }
    };

    const removeTodo = (id) => {
        setTodos(todos.filter(t => t !== id));
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <div>
                <input
                    value={input}
                    onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)}
                    placeholder="Add todo..."
                />
                <button onClick={addTodo}>Add</button>
            </div>
            {todos.map(id => (
                <div key={id}>
                    <TodoItem id={id} />
                    <button onClick={() => removeTodo(id)}>×</button>
                </div>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

// Selectors with dependencies
const filteredTodosState = selector({
    key: 'filteredTodosState',
    get: ({ get }) => {
        const todos = get(todoListState);
        const filter = get(filterState);
        const todoItems = todos.map(id => get(todoItemState(id)));

        return todoItems.filter(todo => {
            if (filter === 'active') return !todo.completed;
            if (filter === 'completed') return todo.completed;
            return true;
        });
    }
});

function FilteredTodoList() {
    const filteredTodos = useRecoilValue(filteredTodosState);
    const [filter, setFilter] = useRecoilState(filterState);

    return (
        <div>
            <div>
                <button onClick={() => setFilter('all')}>All</button>
                <button onClick={() => setFilter('active')}>Active</button>
                <button onClick={() => setFilter('completed')}>Completed</button>
            </div>
            {filteredTodos.map(todo => (
                <div key={todo.id}>
                    <input
                        type="checkbox"
                        checked={todo.completed}
                        readOnly
                    />
                    <span style={{ textDecoration: todo.completed ? 'line-through' : 'none' }}>
                        {todo.text}
                    </span>
                </div>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

7.9 React Query

Simple Explanation

React Query is a library for fetching, caching, and updating server data. It's not a state management library per se, but it handles server state better than traditional state management. It handles loading states, error states, caching, pagination, and more.

Think of React Query like a smart librarian - it fetches books (data) when needed, keeps track of what's available, and automatically updates when new books arrive.

Technical Explanation

React Query provides hooks for fetching, caching, and updating asynchronous data. It manages server state with features like caching, background updates, and stale-while-revalidate.

Key characteristics: - Data Fetching: Simple hooks for fetching data - Caching: Automatic caching of data - Background Updates: Re-fetch on focus, reconnect - Stale-While-Revalidate: Show stale data while updating - Pagination: Built-in pagination support - Infinite Queries: Infinite scrolling support - Optimistic Updates: Update UI before server confirms

Professional Explanation

React Query is the recommended approach for server state in React applications.

Benefits: - Reduced Complexity: No need to manage loading/error states - Performance: Automatic caching and deduplication - UX Improvements: Background updates and optimistic updates - Developer Experience: Simple API with powerful features - Integration: Works with any state management solution

When to use React Query: - Server state: Data from APIs - Real-time data: Needs frequent updates - Complex caching: Multiple data dependencies - User experience: Smooth, responsive interfaces

React Query Examples

// Basic React Query setup
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider, useQuery, useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

const queryClient = new QueryClient();

function App() {
    return (
        <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
            <UserList />
        </QueryClientProvider>
    );
}

// Fetching data with useQuery
function UserList() {
    const { data, isLoading, error, refetch } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['users'],
        queryFn: async () => {
            const response = await fetch('/api/users');
            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error('Failed to fetch users');
            }
            return response.json();
        },
        staleTime: 5000, // 5 seconds
        cacheTime: 10000, // 10 seconds
        refetchOnWindowFocus: true,
        refetchOnReconnect: true,
        retry: 3
    });

    if (isLoading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error.message}</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <button onClick={refetch}>Refetch</button>
            <ul>
                {data.map(user => (
                    <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

// Mutations with useMutation
function AddUser() {
    const queryClient = useQueryClient();
    const [name, setName] = useState('');

    const mutation = useMutation({
        mutationFn: async (newUser) => {
            const response = await fetch('/api/users', {
                method: 'POST',
                headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
                body: JSON.stringify(newUser)
            });
            return response.json();
        },
        onSuccess: (data) => {
            // Invalidate and refetch users
            queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['users'] });
            setName('');
        },
        onError: (error) => {
            console.error('Error adding user:', error);
        }
    });

    const handleSubmit = (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        mutation.mutate({ name });
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <input
                value={name}
                onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Enter user name"
            />
            <button type="submit" disabled={mutation.isPending}>
                {mutation.isPending ? 'Adding...' : 'Add User'}
            </button>
            {mutation.isError && <div>Error: {mutation.error.message}</div>}
            {mutation.isSuccess && <div>User added successfully!</div>}
        </form>
    );
}

// Pagination with React Query
function PaginatedUsers() {
    const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
    const { data, isLoading, error } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['users', page],
        queryFn: async () => {
            const response = await fetch(`/api/users?page=${page}&limit=10`);
            return response.json();
        },
        keepPreviousData: true
    });

    if (isLoading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error.message}</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <ul>
                {data.users.map(user => (
                    <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
            <button 
                onClick={() => setPage(p => Math.max(1, p - 1))}
                disabled={page === 1}
            >
                Previous
            </button>
            <span>Page {page}</span>
            <button 
                onClick={() => setPage(p => p + 1)}
                disabled={!data.hasMore}
            >
                Next
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Infinite queries
function InfiniteScrollUsers() {
    const { data, fetchNextPage, hasNextPage, isFetchingNextPage, status } = useInfiniteQuery({
        queryKey: ['users-infinite'],
        queryFn: async ({ pageParam = 1 }) => {
            const response = await fetch(`/api/users?page=${pageParam}&limit=10`);
            return response.json();
        },
        getNextPageParam: (lastPage, pages) => {
            if (lastPage.hasMore) {
                return pages.length + 1;
            }
            return undefined;
        }
    });

    if (status === 'pending') return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (status === 'error') return <div>Error</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            {data.pages.map((page, i) => (
                <div key={i}>
                    {page.users.map(user => (
                        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
                    ))}
                </div>
            ))}
            <button
                onClick={() => fetchNextPage()}
                disabled={!hasNextPage || isFetchingNextPage}
            >
                {isFetchingNextPage ? 'Loading more...' : 'Load More'}
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Optimistic updates
function TodoOptimistic() {
    const queryClient = useQueryClient();
    const [input, setInput] = useState('');

    const { data: todos } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['todos'],
        queryFn: fetchTodos
    });

    const mutation = useMutation({
        mutationFn: addTodo,
        onMutate: async (newTodo) => {
            // Cancel outgoing refetches
            await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] });

            // Snapshot previous value
            const previousTodos = queryClient.getQueryData(['todos']);

            // Optimistically update
            queryClient.setQueryData(['todos'], (old) => [
                ...old,
                { id: Date.now(), text: newTodo, completed: false }
            ]);

            return { previousTodos };
        },
        onError: (error, newTodo, context) => {
            // Rollback on error
            queryClient.setQueryData(['todos'], context.previousTodos);
        },
        onSettled: () => {
            // Always refetch after error or success
            queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] });
        }
    });

    const handleSubmit = (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        if (input.trim()) {
            mutation.mutate(input);
            setInput('');
        }
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
                <input
                    value={input}
                    onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)}
                    placeholder="Add todo..."
                />
                <button type="submit">Add</button>
            </form>
            <ul>
                {todos?.map(todo => (
                    <li key={todo.id}>
                        <input
                            type="checkbox"
                            checked={todo.completed}
                        />
                        {todo.text}
                    </li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

7.10 When to Use Each Approach

Decision Matrix

Approach Best For Complexity Learning Curve Performance Bundle Size
Local State Simple UI state, component-specific Low Minimal Excellent 0 (built-in)
Lifting State Up Sharing between few components Low Minimal Excellent 0 (built-in)
Context API Themes, auth, settings Low Low Good 0 (built-in)
Redux Toolkit Large apps, complex state Medium Medium Good ~100KB
Zustand Simple to medium apps Low Low Excellent ~5KB
Jotai Complex state with derivations Medium Medium Excellent ~5KB
Recoil Complex apps, Facebook scale Medium Medium Good ~20KB
React Query Server state, data fetching Low Low Excellent ~20KB

Decision Guide

// When to use each approach:

// 1. Local State - Use this by default
function SimpleComponent() {
    const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);
    const [value, setValue] = useState('');
    // Good for: UI state, form inputs, toggles
}

// 2. Lifting State Up - For sibling communication
function Parent() {
    const [sharedState, setSharedState] = useState('');
    return (
        <>
            <ChildA state={sharedState} setState={setSharedState} />
            <ChildB state={sharedState} setState={setSharedState} />
        </>
    );
}

// 3. Context API - For themes, auth, settings
const ThemeContext = createContext();
function App() {
    return (
        <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">
            <DeepComponent />
        </ThemeContext.Provider>
    );
}

// 4. Zustand - For simple global state
const useStore = create((set) => ({
    count: 0,
    increment: () => set((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 }))
}));

// 5. Redux Toolkit - For large apps with complex state
const counterSlice = createSlice({
    name: 'counter',
    initialState: { value: 0 },
    reducers: {
        increment: (state) => { state.value += 1; }
    }
});

// 6. React Query - For server state
function Users() {
    const { data } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['users'],
        queryFn: fetchUsers
    });
}

// 7. Jotai/Recoil - For complex state with dependencies
const countAtom = atom(0);
const doubleCountAtom = atom((get) => get(countAtom) * 2);

Combined Approaches

// Combining approaches for optimal results
function CombinedApproach() {
    // 1. Local state for UI
    const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);
    const [searchTerm, setSearchTerm] = useState('');

    // 2. React Query for server state
    const { data: products } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['products', searchTerm],
        queryFn: () => fetchProducts(searchTerm)
    });

    // 3. Zustand for global UI state
    const { theme, toggleTheme } = useThemeStore();

    // 4. Context for user authentication
    const { user } = useContext(AuthContext);

    return (
        <div className={`app-${theme}`}>
            <Header user={user} />
            <SearchBar
                value={searchTerm}
                onChange={setSearchTerm}
                isLoading={isLoading}
            />
            <ProductList products={products} />
        </div>
    );
}

7.11 Common Mistakes and Best Practices

7.11.1 Common Mistakes

// ❌ Using Context for frequently changing state
const UserContext = createContext(null);
function App() {
    const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
    // This will re-render all consumers on every change
    return (
        <UserContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>
            <DeepComponent />
        </UserContext.Provider>
    );
}

// ✅ Use Context for stable values or combine with selectors
function App() {
    const [user] = useState(null);
    const [setUser] = useState(() => () => {});
    return (
        <UserContext.Provider value={user}>
            <DeepComponent />
        </UserContext.Provider>
    );
}

// ❌ Overusing Redux for everything
const uiSlice = createSlice({
    name: 'ui',
    initialState: { isOpen: false },
    reducers: { toggle: (state) => { state.isOpen = !state.isOpen; } }
});

// ✅ Use local state for simple UI
function Component() {
    const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);
    return <div>...</div>;
}

// ❌ Not handling loading states in React Query
function BadQuery() {
    const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['data'], queryFn: fetchData });
    return <div>{data}</div>; // ❌ data might be undefined
}

// ✅ Always handle loading and error states
function GoodQuery() {
    const { data, isLoading, error } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['data'],
        queryFn: fetchData
    });

    if (isLoading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error.message}</div>;
    return <div>{data}</div>;
}

7.11.2 Best Practices

// ✅ Keep state as local as possible
function Component() {
    // Start with local state
    const [value, setValue] = useState('');

    // Lift state only when needed
    // Use context only when necessary
    // Use state management libraries only when appropriate
}

// ✅ Use selectors for derived state
function SelectorExample() {
    const users = useSelector(state => state.users);
    const activeUsers = useSelector(state => 
        state.users.filter(user => user.active)
    );
    // Prevents unnecessary re-renders
}

// ✅ Use React Query for server state
function ServerState() {
    const { data } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['data'],
        queryFn: fetchData,
        staleTime: 5000,
        cacheTime: 10000
    });
    // Automatic caching, revalidation, and background updates
}

// ✅ Use optimistic updates for better UX
function OptimisticUpdate() {
    const queryClient = useQueryClient();
    const mutation = useMutation({
        mutationFn: updateData,
        onMutate: async (newData) => {
            await queryClient.cancelQueries(['data']);
            const previous = queryClient.getQueryData(['data']);
            queryClient.setQueryData(['data'], newData);
            return { previous };
        },
        onError: (err, newData, context) => {
            queryClient.setQueryData(['data'], context.previous);
        }
    });
}

// ✅ Use atom families for dynamic data
function DynamicAtoms() {
    const todoState = atomFamily({
        key: 'todoState',
        default: (id) => ({ id, text: '', completed: false })
    });
    // Each todo gets its own atom
}

7.12 Interview Questions

Junior Level Questions

Q: What is the difference between props and state?

Answer: - Props: Read-only, passed from parent, immutable - State: Read/write, managed within component, mutable

function Child({ prop }) {
    const [state, setState] = useState(0);
    // prop comes from parent, state is local
}

Q: When would you lift state up?

Answer: When multiple components need to share and synchronize the same state. The state is moved to their common parent, which manages it and passes it down via props.

Mid Level Questions

Q: Compare Context API vs Redux.

Answer: - Context API: Built-in, simpler, good for small apps, can cause unnecessary re-renders - Redux: External library, more powerful, better for large apps, predictable state

// Context: Simple
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

// Redux: More powerful
const counterSlice = createSlice({
    name: 'counter',
    initialState: { value: 0 },
    reducers: { increment: (state) => { state.value += 1; } }
});

Q: When would you use Zustand over Redux?

Answer: Zustand is simpler and lighter than Redux. Use Zustand for: - Smaller applications - Simple state needs - Faster development - When you want less boilerplate

Senior Level Questions

Q: How do you handle server state in React applications?

Answer: Use React Query or SWR for: 1. Automatic caching 2. Background updates 3. Stale-while-revalidate 4. Pagination and infinite scrolling 5. Optimistic updates 6. Error handling and retries

function ServerStateExample() {
    const { data, isLoading } = useQuery({
        queryKey: ['data'],
        queryFn: fetchData,
        staleTime: 5000,
        cacheTime: 10000
    });
}

Q: How do you choose between different state management solutions?

Answer: Consider: 1. Application size: Small → useState/Context, Large → Redux/Zustand 2. State complexity: Simple → useState, Complex → Redux/Jotai 3. Team size: Small → Zustand, Large → Redux 4. Performance needs: Fine-grained → Jotai/Recoil, Standard → Redux 5. Server state: Always use React Query regardless of other choices

7.13 Summary

State Management Hierarchy

Local State (useState/useReducer)
    ↓ (Lift up when needed)
Lifted State (Shared between siblings)
    ↓ (When props drilling becomes excessive)
Context API (Theme, Auth, Settings)
    ↓ (When state becomes complex)
State Management Libraries
    ├── Zustand (Simple, lightweight)
    ├── Redux Toolkit (Complex, scalable)
    ├── Jotai (Atomic, derived state)
    ├── Recoil (Facebook, React-first)
    └── React Query (Server state)

Decision Flowchart

graph TD
    A[Start] --> B{Is it server data?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use React Query]
    B -->|No| D{Is it component-specific?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Use useState/useReducer]
    D -->|No| F{Is it shared with few components?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Lift state up]
    F -->|No| H{Is it app-wide?}
    H -->|Yes| I{Complex state?}
    I -->|No| J[Use Context API]
    I -->|Yes| K{Team preference?}
    K -->|Simple| L[Use Zustand]
    K -->|Complex| M[Use Redux Toolkit]
    K -->|Atomic| N[Use Jotai or Recoil]

Best Practices Summary

  1. Start with local state - Use useState/useReducer first
  2. Lift state up - When multiple components need it
  3. Use Context sparingly - For themes, auth, settings
  4. Choose appropriate library - Based on application needs
  5. Use React Query for server state - Always
  6. Keep state normalized - Avoid duplication
  7. Use selectors - For derived and filtered data
  8. Implement optimistic updates - For better UX
  9. Handle loading and error states - Always
  10. Test state logic - In isolation

Key Takeaways

  • Local state is always the best starting point
  • Lift state up when needed for sharing
  • Context API is built-in and sufficient for many cases
  • State management libraries provide additional features for complex needs
  • React Query is the standard for server state
  • Choose based on your needs, not on trends
  • Combine approaches for optimal results
