08

Routing in React

8.1 Introduction to Routing

Simple Explanation

Routing is how you navigate between different pages or views in a React application. Just like a website has different pages (Home, About, Contact), a React app needs to show different components based on the URL. React Router is the most popular library for handling routing in React applications.

Think of routing like a GPS navigation system - the URL is your current location, and React Router helps you determine which "screen" (component) to show based on that location.

Technical Explanation

Routing in React involves mapping URLs to components. When a user navigates to a specific URL, the router renders the corresponding component. React Router provides declarative routing for React applications.

Key concepts: - Routes: Mapping between URLs and components - Navigation: Programmatic and declarative navigation - Nested Routes: Routes within routes - Protected Routes: Routes that require authentication - Dynamic Routes: Routes with parameters - Lazy Loading: Loading routes only when needed

Professional Explanation

In enterprise React applications, routing is crucial for: - User Experience: Smooth navigation between views - State Management: Preserving state during navigation - Code Splitting: Loading code on demand - Deep Linking: Sharing specific application states - SEO: Server-side rendering for search engines - Analytics: Tracking user navigation patterns

8.2 React Router Setup

Simple Explanation

React Router is the standard routing library for React. Setting it up involves installing the package and wrapping your app with a router component. Then you define routes using Route components.

Think of React Router like a traffic controller - you tell it which URL patterns should show which components, and it handles all the routing logic for you.

Technical Explanation

React Router v6 is the latest version with significant improvements over previous versions. It provides a declarative API for routing.

Core components: - BrowserRouter: The router implementation for web - Routes: Container for Route components - Route: Defines a mapping between URL and component - Link: Declarative navigation component - useNavigate: Hook for programmatic navigation

Professional Explanation

React Router setup varies based on application needs: - BrowserRouter: Standard web applications - HashRouter: Static file hosting - StaticRouter: Server-side rendering - MemoryRouter: Testing environment

React Router Setup Examples

// Installation
// npm install react-router-dom

// Basic setup
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link } from 'react-router-dom';

function App() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <nav>
                <Link to="/">Home</Link>
                <Link to="/about">About</Link>
                <Link to="/contact">Contact</Link>
            </nav>

            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

function Home() {
    return <h1>Home Page</h1>;
}

function About() {
    return <h1>About Page</h1>;
}

function Contact() {
    return <h1>Contact Page</h1>;
}

// Setup with navigation component
function Navigation() {
    return (
        <nav>
            <ul>
                <li><Link to="/">Home</Link></li>
                <li><Link to="/about">About</Link></li>
                <li><Link to="/contact">Contact</Link></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    );
}

// App with custom navigation
function AppWithNavigation() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Navigation />
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

8.3 Basic Routes

Simple Explanation

Routes are the building blocks of routing. Each Route component defines a path and the component to render when that path matches the current URL. The Routes component contains all the routes and decides which one to render.

Think of Routes like a switch statement - it checks each route from top to bottom and renders the first one that matches the current URL.

Technical Explanation

A Route component matches a path pattern and renders a component when the URL matches. The Routes component selects the best match among its children.

Route types: - Exact routes: Match exactly (default in v6) - Nested routes: Routes within routes - Dynamic routes: Routes with parameters - Index routes: Default routes for parent paths - Fallback routes: Catch-all for unmatched paths

Professional Explanation

Route matching in React Router v6: - Routes are matched by the best match, not by order - Nested routes are matched relative to their parent - Index routes render at parent paths - Wildcards for catch-all routes

Basic Routes Examples

// Simple routes
function App() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
                <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Routes with layout
function AppWithLayout() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route element={<Layout />}>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                    <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

function Layout() {
    return (
        <div>
            <header>
                <nav>
                    <Link to="/">Home</Link>
                    <Link to="/about">About</Link>
                    <Link to="/contact">Contact</Link>
                </nav>
            </header>
            <main>
                <Outlet />
            </main>
            <footer>
                <p>&copy; 2024 My App</p>
            </footer>
        </div>
    );
}

// Routes with index route
function AppWithIndex() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Dashboard />}>
                    <Route index element={<Home />} />
                    <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
                    <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

function Dashboard() {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Dashboard</h2>
            <nav>
                <Link to="/">Home</Link>
                <Link to="/settings">Settings</Link>
                <Link to="/profile">Profile</Link>
            </nav>
            <Outlet />
        </div>
    );
}

// Routes with multiple layouts
function AppWithMultipleLayouts() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route element={<PublicLayout />}>
                    <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />
                    <Route path="/register" element={<Register />} />
                </Route>
                <Route element={<PrivateLayout />}>
                    <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
                    <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} />
                    <Route path="/profile" element={<Profile />} />
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

8.4 Dynamic Routes

Simple Explanation

Dynamic routes allow you to capture URL parameters and use them in your components. This is useful for user profiles, blog posts, product pages, and other pages where the content depends on an ID or slug.

Think of dynamic routes like templates - the route pattern defines the structure, and the actual value in the URL determines what content to show.

Technical Explanation

Dynamic routes use parameters that are captured from the URL. These parameters can be accessed using the useParams hook or the useMatches hook.

Features: - Path parameters: URL segments like /users/:id - Optional parameters: Optional segments - Wildcards: Catch-all routes - Nested routes: Routes with dynamic segments

Professional Explanation

Dynamic routes are essential for: - CRUD Operations: Managing resources - User Profiles: Displaying user-specific content - Blog/Content: Showing articles - E-commerce: Product pages - SEO: Clean, descriptive URLs

Dynamic Routes Examples

// Basic dynamic route
function App() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserProfile />} />
                <Route path="/posts/:postId/comments/:commentId" element={<CommentDetail />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Using useParams
function UserProfile() {
    const { id } = useParams();
    const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

    useEffect(() => {
        const fetchUser = async () => {
            try {
                const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
                const data = await response.json();
                setUser(data);
            } catch (error) {
                console.error('Error fetching user:', error);
            } finally {
                setLoading(false);
            }
        };

        fetchUser();
    }, [id]);

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (!user) return <div>User not found</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p>
            <p>{user.bio}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Nested dynamic routes
function AppWithNestedDynamic() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/users/:userId" element={<UserLayout />}>
                    <Route index element={<UserProfile />} />
                    <Route path="posts" element={<UserPosts />} />
                    <Route path="posts/:postId" element={<UserPostDetail />} />
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

function UserLayout() {
    const { userId } = useParams();
    const [user, setUser] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchUser(userId).then(setUser);
    }, [userId]);

    if (!user) return <div>Loading...</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <nav>
                <Link to={`/users/${userId}`}>Profile</Link>
                <Link to={`/users/${userId}/posts`}>Posts</Link>
            </nav>
            <Outlet />
        </div>
    );
}

// Multiple parameters
function CommentDetail() {
    const { postId, commentId } = useParams();
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchComment(postId, commentId).then(setData);
    }, [postId, commentId]);

    return (
        <div>
            <h3>Post: {postId}</h3>
            <h4>Comment: {commentId}</h4>
            <p>{data?.text}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Optional parameters
function ProductPage() {
    const { category, productId } = useParams();

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Products</h1>
            {category && <p>Category: {category}</p>}
            {productId && <p>Product ID: {productId}</p>}
            {!category && <p>Showing all products</p>}
        </div>
    );
}

8.5 Nested Routes

Simple Explanation

Nested routes are routes within other routes. They allow you to create complex layouts where different parts of the page change independently. The Outlet component is used to render nested routes.

Think of nested routes like nesting dolls - each route can contain other routes, and the Outlet component marks where the nested routes should appear.

Technical Explanation

Nested routes allow you to compose UI layouts and keep related routes together. The Outlet component is a placeholder that renders the matched child route.

Key concepts: - Outlet: Renders the matched child route - Relative routes: Routes inherit parent path - Layout routes: Routes that provide a layout - Index routes: Default child routes - Nested routing: Routes can be nested infinitely

Professional Explanation

Nested routes are powerful for: - Complex layouts: Different sections with their own routing - Feature modules: Self-contained routing - Code organization: Keeping routes close to components - State preservation: Maintaining state in parent layouts - User experience: Smooth transitions between sections

Nested Routes Examples

// Basic nested routes
function AppWithNestedRoutes() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />}>
                    <Route index element={<DashboardHome />} />
                    <Route path="analytics" element={<Analytics />} />
                    <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
                    <Route path="settings/:tab" element={<SettingsTab />} />
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Dashboard component with Outlet
function Dashboard() {
    return (
        <div className="dashboard">
            <aside className="sidebar">
                <nav>
                    <Link to="/dashboard">Home</Link>
                    <Link to="/dashboard/analytics">Analytics</Link>
                    <Link to="/dashboard/settings">Settings</Link>
                </nav>
            </aside>
            <main className="content">
                <Outlet />
            </main>
        </div>
    );
}

// Nested routes with layout
function AppWithLayoutAndNested() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route element={<RootLayout />}>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />

                    <Route path="/products" element={<ProductsLayout />}>
                        <Route index element={<ProductsList />} />
                        <Route path=":productId" element={<ProductDetail />}>
                            <Route index element={<ProductOverview />} />
                            <Route path="reviews" element={<ProductReviews />} />
                            <Route path="specs" element={<ProductSpecs />} />
                        </Route>
                        <Route path="category/:categoryId" element={<CategoryProducts />} />
                    </Route>
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// ProductsLayout with nested routes
function ProductsLayout() {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Products</h2>
            <div className="products-layout">
                <aside className="filters">
                    <Link to="/products">All Products</Link>
                    <Link to="/products/category/electronics">Electronics</Link>
                    <Link to="/products/category/clothing">Clothing</Link>
                </aside>
                <div className="products-content">
                    <Outlet />
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}

// ProductDetail with nested routes
function ProductDetail() {
    const { productId } = useParams();
    const [product, setProduct] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchProduct(productId).then(setProduct);
    }, [productId]);

    if (!product) return <div>Loading...</div>;

    return (
        <div className="product-detail">
            <h3>{product.name}</h3>
            <p>{product.description}</p>
            <p>Price: ${product.price}</p>

            <nav className="product-nav">
                <Link to={`/products/${productId}`}>Overview</Link>
                <Link to={`/products/${productId}/reviews`}>Reviews</Link>
                <Link to={`/products/${productId}/specs`}>Specifications</Link>
            </nav>

            <div className="product-content">
                <Outlet />
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}

// Deeply nested routes
function AppWithDeepNesting() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<AppLayout />}>
                    <Route path="admin" element={<AdminLayout />}>
                        <Route path="users" element={<UserManagement />}>
                            <Route index element={<UserList />} />
                            <Route path=":userId" element={<UserDetail />}>
                                <Route index element={<UserProfile />} />
                                <Route path="orders" element={<UserOrders />} />
                                <Route path="settings" element={<UserSettings />} />
                            </Route>
                        </Route>
                        <Route path="settings" element={<AdminSettings />} />
                    </Route>
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

8.6 Protected Routes

Simple Explanation

Protected routes are routes that require the user to be authenticated before accessing them. If the user is not authenticated, they are redirected to the login page. This is essential for applications with private content.

Think of protected routes like a VIP section at a club - only authorized people (authenticated users) can enter. If you're not on the list, you're redirected to the entrance (login page).

Technical Explanation

Protected routes are implemented by checking authentication status before rendering the route. If the user is not authenticated, they are redirected to the login page or shown an unauthorized message.

Implementation approaches: - Layout wrapper: Wrap protected routes in a layout that checks auth - Route guard: Create a component that checks auth before rendering - Conditional rendering: Show different content based on auth status - Redirect component: Redirect to login if not authenticated

Professional Explanation

Protected routes are essential for: - User authentication: Restricting access to logged-in users - Authorization: Different access levels for different users - Security: Protecting sensitive data - User experience: Guiding users through authentication flow - Analytics: Tracking authenticated user behavior

Protected Routes Examples

// Protected route component
function ProtectedRoute({ children }) {
    const { user, loading } = useContext(AuthContext);
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!loading && !user) {
            navigate('/login', { replace: true });
        }
    }, [user, loading, navigate]);

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (!user) return null;

    return children;
}

// Using ProtectedRoute
function AppWithProtectedRoutes() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />
                <Route path="/register" element={<Register />} />
                <Route element={<ProtectedRoute />}>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Dashboard />}>
                        <Route index element={<Home />} />
                        <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
                        <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
                    </Route>
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Role-based access control
function RoleProtectedRoute({ children, allowedRoles }) {
    const { user, loading } = useContext(AuthContext);
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!loading) {
            if (!user) {
                navigate('/login', { replace: true });
            } else if (!allowedRoles.includes(user.role)) {
                navigate('/unauthorized', { replace: true });
            }
        }
    }, [user, loading, navigate, allowedRoles]);

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (!user) return null;
    if (!allowedRoles.includes(user.role)) return null;

    return children;
}

// App with role-based routes
function AppWithRoles() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />
                <Route path="/unauthorized" element={<Unauthorized />} />

                <Route element={<ProtectedRoute />}>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Dashboard />}>
                        <Route index element={<Home />} />

                        <Route element={<RoleProtectedRoute allowedRoles={['admin']} />}>
                            <Route path="admin" element={<AdminPanel />}>
                                <Route index element={<AdminHome />} />
                                <Route path="users" element={<UserManagement />} />
                                <Route path="settings" element={<SystemSettings />} />
                            </Route>
                        </Route>

                        <Route element={<RoleProtectedRoute allowedRoles={['admin', 'manager']} />}>
                            <Route path="reports" element={<Reports />} />
                            <Route path="analytics" element={<Analytics />} />
                        </Route>

                        <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
                        <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
                    </Route>
                </Route>
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Custom auth hook with redirect
function useAuthRedirect() {
    const { user, loading } = useContext(AuthContext);
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!loading && user) {
            navigate('/dashboard');
        }
    }, [user, loading, navigate]);
}

function LoginPage() {
    const { login, error } = useContext(AuthContext);
    const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
    const [password, setPassword] = useState('');
    const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);

    // Redirect if already authenticated
    useAuthRedirect();

    const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        setIsLoading(true);
        try {
            await login(email, password);
        } catch (error) {
            console.error('Login failed:', error);
        } finally {
            setIsLoading(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <input
                type="email"
                value={email}
                onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Email"
                disabled={isLoading}
            />
            <input
                type="password"
                value={password}
                onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Password"
                disabled={isLoading}
            />
            {error && <div className="error">{error}</div>}
            <button type="submit" disabled={isLoading}>
                {isLoading ? 'Logging in...' : 'Login'}
            </button>
        </form>
    );
}

// Auth provider setup
function AuthProvider({ children }) {
    const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        // Check for existing session
        const token = localStorage.getItem('authToken');
        if (token) {
            validateToken(token)
                .then(setUser)
                .catch(() => {
                    localStorage.removeItem('authToken');
                })
                .finally(() => setLoading(false));
        } else {
            setLoading(false);
        }
    }, []);

    const login = async (email, password) => {
        setError(null);
        try {
            const response = await fetch('/api/login', {
                method: 'POST',
                body: JSON.stringify({ email, password })
            });
            const data = await response.json();

            if (data.token) {
                localStorage.setItem('authToken', data.token);
                setUser(data.user);
            } else {
                throw new Error('Invalid credentials');
            }
        } catch (err) {
            setError(err.message);
            throw err;
        }
    };

    const logout = () => {
        localStorage.removeItem('authToken');
        setUser(null);
    };

    const value = {
        user,
        loading,
        error,
        login,
        logout,
        isAuthenticated: !!user
    };

    return (
        <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>
            {children}
        </AuthContext.Provider>
    );
}

8.7 Lazy Loading and Code Splitting

Simple Explanation

Lazy loading means loading components only when they're needed, rather than loading everything upfront. This makes your application load faster initially. React.lazy and Suspense make this easy.

Think of lazy loading like a buffet - instead of putting all the food out at once, you put out the main dishes first and bring out specialty items when someone asks for them.

Technical Explanation

Lazy loading allows you to split your code into chunks that are loaded on demand. React.lazy is a function that lets you load components dynamically. Suspense is a component that shows a fallback while loading.

Key concepts: - React.lazy: Dynamic import for components - Suspense: Fallback UI while loading - Code splitting: Breaking bundle into smaller chunks - Chunk loading: Loading chunks on demand - Route-based splitting: Splitting by routes

Professional Explanation

Lazy loading is essential for: - Performance: Faster initial load times - User experience: Progressive loading - Bandwidth: Less data transferred initially - SEO: Better Core Web Vitals - Maintainability: Smaller, focused bundles

Lazy Loading Examples

// Basic lazy loading
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const Home = lazy(() => import('./pages/Home'));
const About = lazy(() => import('./pages/About'));
const Contact = lazy(() => import('./pages/Contact'));
const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));

function App() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
                <Routes>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                    <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
                    <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
                </Routes>
            </Suspense>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Lazy loading with fallback component
const LoadingFallback = () => (
    <div className="loading-container">
        <div className="spinner"></div>
        <p>Loading page...</p>
    </div>
);

function AppWithCustomFallback() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Suspense fallback={<LoadingFallback />}>
                <Routes>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                    <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
                </Routes>
            </Suspense>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Lazy loading with nested routes
const DashboardLayout = lazy(() => import('./layouts/DashboardLayout'));
const Analytics = lazy(() => import('./pages/Analytics'));
const Settings = lazy(() => import('./pages/Settings'));
const Profile = lazy(() => import('./pages/Profile'));

function AppWithNestedLazy() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
                <Routes>
                    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                    <Route element={<DashboardLayout />}>
                        <Route path="/analytics" element={<Analytics />} />
                        <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} />
                        <Route path="/profile" element={<Profile />} />
                    </Route>
                </Routes>
            </Suspense>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Prefetching lazy components
function PrefetchComponent() {
    const [isPrefetching, setIsPrefetching] = useState(false);
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    const prefetchDashboard = () => {
        setIsPrefetching(true);
        // Prefetch the component
        import('./pages/Dashboard').then(() => {
            setIsPrefetching(false);
            navigate('/dashboard');
        });
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <button 
                onClick={prefetchDashboard}
                disabled={isPrefetching}
            >
                {isPrefetching ? 'Loading...' : 'Go to Dashboard'}
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Error handling in lazy loading
function AppWithErrorHandling() {
    return (
        <ErrorBoundary fallback={<div>Something went wrong loading the page.</div>}>
            <BrowserRouter>
                <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
                    <Routes>
                        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                        <Route path="/dashboard" element={
                            <ErrorBoundary fallback={<div>Failed to load dashboard.</div>}>
                                <Dashboard />
                            </ErrorBoundary>
                        } />
                    </Routes>
                </Suspense>
            </BrowserRouter>
        </ErrorBoundary>
    );
}

// Component-level lazy loading
const HeavyComponent = lazy(() => import('./components/HeavyComponent'));
const ExpensiveChart = lazy(() => import('./components/ExpensiveChart'));

function FeaturePage() {
    const [showChart, setShowChart] = useState(false);

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Feature Page</h1>
            <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading heavy component...</div>}>
                <HeavyComponent />
            </Suspense>

            <button onClick={() => setShowChart(!showChart)}>
                {showChart ? 'Hide' : 'Show'} Chart
            </button>

            {showChart && (
                <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading chart...</div>}>
                    <ExpensiveChart />
                </Suspense>
            )}
        </div>
    );
}

8.8 Navigation

Simple Explanation

Navigation in React Router can be done in two ways: declaratively (with the Link component) or programmatically (with the useNavigate hook). Links are like regular HTML links but they handle routing without page reloads.

Think of Link like a navigation button that changes the URL without refreshing the page. useNavigate is like a remote control that lets you navigate programmatically.

Technical Explanation

Navigation in React Router is handled through: - Link: Declarative navigation component - NavLink: Enhanced link with active state - useNavigate: Programmatic navigation hook - useLocation: Access current location - useHistory: Navigate in history (legacy)

Professional Explanation

Navigation patterns: - Declarative: Using Link and NavLink - Programmatic: Using useNavigate - Redirects: Redirecting after actions - History: Navigating backward/forward - State: Passing state during navigation

Navigation Examples

// Basic navigation with Link
function Navigation() {
    return (
        <nav>
            <Link to="/">Home</Link>
            <Link to="/about">About</Link>
            <Link to="/contact">Contact</Link>
            <Link to="/products">Products</Link>
        </nav>
    );
}

// NavLink with active states
function ActiveNavigation() {
    return (
        <nav>
            <NavLink 
                to="/" 
                className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? 'active-link' : 'link'}
            >
                Home
            </NavLink>
            <NavLink 
                to="/about"
                style={({ isActive }) => ({
                    fontWeight: isActive ? 'bold' : 'normal',
                    color: isActive ? 'blue' : 'black'
                })}
            >
                About
            </NavLink>
            <NavLink 
                to="/products"
                end
                className={({ isActive }) => `nav-link ${isActive ? 'active' : ''}`}
            >
                Products
            </NavLink>
        </nav>
    );
}

// Programmatic navigation with useNavigate
function LoginForm() {
    const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
    const [password, setPassword] = useState('');
    const navigate = useNavigate();
    const location = useLocation();
    const from = location.state?.from?.pathname || '/';

    const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        try {
            await login(email, password);
            navigate(from, { replace: true });
        } catch (error) {
            console.error('Login failed:', error);
        }
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <input
                type="email"
                value={email}
                onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Email"
            />
            <input
                type="password"
                value={password}
                onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Password"
            />
            <button type="submit">Login</button>
        </form>
    );
}

// Navigation with state
function ProductCard({ product }) {
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    const handleClick = () => {
        navigate(`/products/${product.id}`, {
            state: {
                from: 'product-list',
                product: product
            }
        });
    };

    return (
        <div className="product-card" onClick={handleClick}>
            <h3>{product.name}</h3>
            <p>${product.price}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Accessing location state
function ProductDetail() {
    const location = useLocation();
    const { state } = location;
    const [product, setProduct] = useState(state?.product || null);
    const { id } = useParams();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!product) {
            fetchProduct(id).then(setProduct);
        }
    }, [id, product]);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{product?.name}</h2>
            <p>{product?.description}</p>
            <p>From: {state?.from || 'unknown'}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Navigation with query parameters
function SearchPage() {
    const [searchParams, setSearchParams] = useSearchParams();
    const query = searchParams.get('q') || '';
    const [results, setResults] = useState([]);

    const handleSearch = (value) => {
        setSearchParams({ q: value });
    };

    useEffect(() => {
        if (query) {
            searchItems(query).then(setResults);
        }
    }, [query]);

    return (
        <div>
            <input
                value={query}
                onChange={(e) => handleSearch(e.target.value)}
                placeholder="Search..."
            />
            <div>
                {results.map(result => (
                    <div key={result.id}>{result.title}</div>
                ))}
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}

// Navigation with confirm
function UnsavedChangesGuard({ isDirty }) {
    const navigate = useNavigate();
    const location = useLocation();
    const [showConfirm, setShowConfirm] = useState(false);
    const [nextLocation, setNextLocation] = useState(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        if (isDirty && location.pathname !== nextLocation?.pathname) {
            if (window.confirm('You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?')) {
                navigate(nextLocation);
            }
        }
    }, [isDirty, location, navigate, nextLocation]);

    const handleNavigate = (to) => {
        if (isDirty) {
            setNextLocation(to);
            setShowConfirm(true);
        } else {
            navigate(to);
        }
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <button onClick={() => handleNavigate('/')}>Home</button>
            <button onClick={() => handleNavigate('/about')}>About</button>
        </div>
    );
}

8.9 Scroll Management

Simple Explanation

Scroll management controls where the page scrolls to when navigating between routes. By default, React Router doesn't automatically scroll to the top when navigating, which can be confusing for users.

Think of scroll management like bookmarks - when you change pages, you want to start at the top of the new page, not where you were on the previous page.

Technical Explanation

Scroll management involves controlling the scroll position during navigation. React Router v6 provides a ScrollRestoration component for this, or you can implement custom scroll management.

Key concepts: - Scroll restoration: Remembering scroll position when going back - Scroll to top: Scrolling to top on navigation - Hash scrolling: Scrolling to elements with IDs - Custom scroll: Implementing custom scroll behavior

Professional Explanation

Scroll management is important for: - User experience: Consistent navigation behavior - Accessibility: Keyboard navigation - Single-page apps: Handling scroll like traditional pages - Hash links: Navigating to specific content - History: Maintaining scroll position in history

Scroll Management Examples

// Basic scroll to top with useEffect
function ScrollToTop() {
    const { pathname } = useLocation();

    useEffect(() => {
        window.scrollTo(0, 0);
    }, [pathname]);

    return null;
}

// Using in app
function AppWithScrollToTop() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <ScrollToTop />
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// React Router v6 ScrollRestoration
function AppWithScrollRestoration() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <ScrollRestoration />
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                <Route path="/products" element={<Products />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Custom scroll management
function CustomScrollManager() {
    const { pathname } = useLocation();
    const location = useLocation();

    useEffect(() => {
        // Smooth scroll to top
        window.scrollTo({
            top: 0,
            behavior: 'smooth'
        });
    }, [pathname]);

    // Handle hash scrolling
    useEffect(() => {
        if (location.hash) {
            const element = document.getElementById(location.hash.slice(1));
            if (element) {
                element.scrollIntoView({
                    behavior: 'smooth',
                    block: 'start'
                });
            }
        }
    }, [location]);

    return null;
}

// Scroll to top with exceptions
function ScrollToTopWithExceptions({ excludePaths = [] }) {
    const { pathname } = useLocation();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!excludePaths.includes(pathname)) {
            window.scrollTo(0, 0);
        }
    }, [pathname, excludePaths]);

    return null;
}

// App with scroll exceptions
function AppWithScrollExceptions() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <ScrollToTopWithExceptions 
                excludePaths={['/products', '/search']}
            />
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/products" element={<ProductList />} />
                <Route path="/search" element={<SearchResults />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// Scroll restoration with hash
function ArticlePage() {
    const location = useLocation();
    const [scrollY, setScrollY] = useState(0);

    useEffect(() => {
        const handleScroll = () => {
            setScrollY(window.scrollY);
        };

        window.addEventListener('scroll', handleScroll);
        return () => window.removeEventListener('scroll', handleScroll);
    }, []);

    useEffect(() => {
        if (location.hash) {
            const element = document.getElementById(location.hash.slice(1));
            if (element) {
                element.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' });
            }
        } else if (scrollY > 0) {
            window.scrollTo(0, scrollY);
        }
    }, [location, scrollY]);

    return <div>{/* Article content */}</div>;
}

8.10 Common Mistakes and Best Practices

8.10.1 Common Mistakes

// ❌ Not wrapping app with Router
function BadApp() {
    return (
        <Routes>
            <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        </Routes>
    );
}

// ✅ Wrap with Router
function GoodApp() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// ❌ Incorrect route ordering
function BadRoutes() {
    return (
        <Routes>
            <Route path="/products/:id" element={<ProductDetail />} />
            <Route path="/products" element={<ProductList />} />
        </Routes>
    );
}

// ✅ Correct route ordering (specific before general)
function GoodRoutes() {
    return (
        <Routes>
            <Route path="/products" element={<ProductList />} />
            <Route path="/products/:id" element={<ProductDetail />} />
        </Routes>
    );
}

// ❌ Missing key in route list
function BadRouteList({ routes }) {
    return (
        <Routes>
            {routes.map(route => (
                <Route path={route.path} element={route.component} />
            ))}
        </Routes>
    );
}

// ✅ Adding key
function GoodRouteList({ routes }) {
    return (
        <Routes>
            {routes.map((route, index) => (
                <Route key={index} path={route.path} element={route.component} />
            ))}
        </Routes>
    );
}

// ❌ Not handling 404
function BadAppWith404() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// ✅ Always include a catch-all route
function GoodAppWith404() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
                <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
                <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

8.10.2 Best Practices

// ✅ Organize routes in a separate file
// routes.js
import { lazy } from 'react';

const Home = lazy(() => import('./pages/Home'));
const About = lazy(() => import('./pages/About'));
const Contact = lazy(() => import('./pages/Contact'));

export const routes = [
    { path: '/', element: <Home />, exact: true },
    { path: '/about', element: <About /> },
    { path: '/contact', element: <Contact /> }
];

// ✅ Use route configuration
function AppWithRouteConfig() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Routes>
                {routes.map(route => (
                    <Route
                        key={route.path}
                        path={route.path}
                        element={route.element}
                        exact={route.exact}
                    />
                ))}
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

// ✅ Use constants for route paths
// constants/routes.js
export const ROUTES = {
    HOME: '/',
    ABOUT: '/about',
    CONTACT: '/contact',
    PRODUCTS: '/products',
    PRODUCT_DETAIL: '/products/:id',
    DASHBOARD: '/dashboard',
    SETTINGS: '/dashboard/settings'
};

// ✅ Use route constants
function NavigationWithConstants() {
    return (
        <nav>
            <Link to={ROUTES.HOME}>Home</Link>
            <Link to={ROUTES.ABOUT}>About</Link>
            <Link to={ROUTES.CONTACT}>Contact</Link>
            <Link to={ROUTES.PRODUCTS}>Products</Link>
        </nav>
    );
}

// ✅ Lazy load routes
function AppWithLazyRoutes() {
    const routes = [
        { path: '/', element: lazy(() => import('./pages/Home')) },
        { path: '/about', element: lazy(() => import('./pages/About')) },
        { path: '/contact', element: lazy(() => import('./pages/Contact')) }
    ];

    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
                <Routes>
                    {routes.map(route => (
                        <Route
                            key={route.path}
                            path={route.path}
                            element={<route.element />}
                        />
                    ))}
                </Routes>
            </Suspense>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

8.11 Interview Questions

Junior Level Questions

Q: What is React Router and why use it?

Answer: React Router is the standard routing library for React. It enables navigation between different views/components in a React application. Benefits include: - Declarative routing - Nested routes - Dynamic routes - URL parameters - Programmatic navigation - Lazy loading support

// Basic React Router setup
<BrowserRouter>
    <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
    </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

Q: What is the difference between Link and NavLink?

Answer: - Link: Basic navigation component - NavLink: Enhanced Link with active state styling

<Link to="/about">About</Link>
<NavLink 
    to="/about"
    className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? 'active' : ''}
>
    About
</NavLink>

Mid Level Questions

Q: How do you handle protected routes in React Router?

Answer: Protected routes are implemented by checking authentication status before rendering the route. If not authenticated, redirect to login.

function ProtectedRoute({ children }) {
    const { user } = useAuth();
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!user) {
            navigate('/login', { replace: true });
        }
    }, [user, navigate]);

    return user ? children : null;
}

Q: What are nested routes and when would you use them?

Answer: Nested routes allow you to have routes within routes, creating complex layouts where different parts of the page change independently.

<Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />}>
    <Route index element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
    <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
</Route>

Senior Level Questions

Q: How do you implement lazy loading with React Router?

Answer: Use React.lazy with dynamic imports and wrap with Suspense.

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));

function App() {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
            </Routes>
        </Suspense>
    );
}

Q: How do you handle scroll restoration in React Router?

Answer: React Router v6 provides ScrollRestoration, or you can implement custom scroll management.

import { ScrollRestoration } from 'react-router-dom';

function App() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <ScrollRestoration />
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
            </Routes>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}
