TypeScript in React

10.1 Introduction to TypeScript

Simple Explanation

TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static typing. It helps you catch errors early, write more predictable code, and get better editor support. Think of it as JavaScript with superpowers - you write JavaScript, but with type annotations that help prevent bugs.

Think of TypeScript like a spell-checker for your code. Just as a spell-checker catches spelling errors before you send an email, TypeScript catches type errors before you run your code.

Technical Explanation

TypeScript is a strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript. It adds optional static types, classes, interfaces, and other features to JavaScript. TypeScript code is transpiled to plain JavaScript that runs anywhere JavaScript runs.

Key characteristics: - Static Typing: Catch errors at compile time - Type Inference: TypeScript can infer types automatically - Structural Typing: Types are checked by their structure - Generics: Write reusable, type-safe code - ES Features: Support for latest ECMAScript features - Tooling: Excellent IDE support with autocomplete and refactoring

Professional Explanation

In enterprise React development, TypeScript is essential for: - Code Quality: Catch type errors before runtime - Maintainability: Types serve as documentation - Refactoring: Safe refactoring with type checking - Collaboration: Clear contracts between components - IDE Support: Better autocomplete and error detection - Scalability: Types help manage growing codebases

10.2 TypeScript Setup with React

Simple Explanation

Setting up TypeScript with React involves creating a project with TypeScript support. The easiest way is using Create React App with the TypeScript template, or Vite with TypeScript support.

Technical Explanation

TypeScript can be added to React projects in several ways: 1. Create React App: npx create-react-app my-app --template typescript 2. Vite: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts 3. Manual Setup: Install TypeScript and configure tsconfig.json

Key files: - tsconfig.json: TypeScript configuration - .tsx: TypeScript file with JSX - .ts: TypeScript file without JSX - types/: Directory for type declarations

Professional Explanation

Enterprise TypeScript setup includes: - Strict Mode: Enable strict type checking - Path Aliases: Cleaner imports - Declaration Files: Types for third-party libraries - Build Configuration: Production-ready build setup - Linting: ESLint with TypeScript rules - Formatting: Prettier for consistent formatting

TypeScript Setup Examples

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2020",
    "useDefineForClassFields": true,
    "lib": ["ES2020", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
    "module": "ESNext",
    "skipLibCheck": true,

    /* Bundler mode */
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "jsx": "react-jsx",

    /* Linting */
    "strict": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,

    /* Path Aliases */
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": {
      "@/*": ["src/*"],
      "@components/*": ["src/components/*"],
      "@hooks/*": ["src/hooks/*"],
      "@utils/*": ["src/utils/*"],
      "@types/*": ["src/types/*"],
      "@api/*": ["src/api/*"]
    }
  },
  "include": ["src"],
  "references": [{ "path": "./tsconfig.node.json" }]
}

// Vite configuration with TypeScript
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import path from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  resolve: {
    alias: {
      '@': path.resolve(__dirname, './src'),
      '@components': path.resolve(__dirname, './src/components'),
      '@hooks': path.resolve(__dirname, './src/hooks'),
      '@utils': path.resolve(__dirname, './src/utils'),
      '@types': path.resolve(__dirname, './src/types'),
      '@api': path.resolve(__dirname, './src/api')
    }
  }
});

// Type declaration file
// src/vite-env.d.ts
/// <reference types="vite/client" />

interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly VITE_API_URL: string;
  readonly VITE_APP_TITLE: string;
}

interface ImportMeta {
  readonly env: ImportMetaEnv;
}

10.3 Basic Types

Simple Explanation

Basic types in TypeScript are the building blocks of type annotations. They include primitive types like string, number, boolean, and more complex types like arrays and objects.

Technical Explanation

TypeScript has several basic types: - Primitive Types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint - Any: Disables type checking (avoid using) - Void: No return value - Never: Function that never returns - Unknown: Type-safe alternative to any - Arrays: type[] or Array<type> - Tuples: Fixed-length arrays - Enums: Named constants

Professional Explanation

In React TypeScript, basic types are used for: - Props: Define component prop types - State: Type state variables - Functions: Type parameters and return values - API Responses: Type API data - Event Handlers: Type event objects

Basic Types Examples

// Primitive types
let name: string = "John Doe";
let age: number = 30;
let isActive: boolean = true;
let value: null = null;
let data: undefined = undefined;

// Any (use sparingly)
let anything: any = "Hello";
anything = 42;
anything = { key: "value" };

// Unknown (safe alternative to any)
let unknownValue: unknown = "Hello";
if (typeof unknownValue === "string") {
    console.log(unknownValue.toUpperCase());
}

// Void (no return value)
function logMessage(message: string): void {
    console.log(message);
    // No return value
}

// Never (function never returns)
function throwError(message: string): never {
    throw new Error(message);
}

function infiniteLoop(): never {
    while (true) {
        // Infinite loop
    }
}

// Arrays
let numbers: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let strings: Array<string> = ["Hello", "World"];
let mixed: (string | number)[] = ["Hello", 42];

// Tuples (fixed-length arrays)
let user: [number, string, boolean] = [1, "John", true];
const [userId, userName, isAdmin] = user;

// Enums
enum UserRole {
    Admin = "admin",
    User = "user",
    Guest = "guest"
}

enum Status {
    Pending = 0,
    Approved = 1,
    Rejected = 2
}

function getRole(role: UserRole): string {
    return `User role: ${role}`;
}

// React component with types
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
    age?: number; // Optional property
    role: UserRole;
    tags: string[];
    address: {
        street: string;
        city: string;
        country: string;
    };
}

function UserProfile({ user }: { user: User }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>Email: {user.email}</p>
            {user.age && <p>Age: {user.age}</p>}
            <p>Role: {user.role}</p>
            <p>Address: {user.address.street}, {user.address.city}</p>
            <ul>
                {user.tags.map(tag => (
                    <li key={tag}>{tag}</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </div>
    );
}

10.4 Interfaces and Type Aliases

Simple Explanation

Interfaces and type aliases are ways to define custom types. They describe the shape of an object or the structure of a type. Interfaces are more commonly used for object types, while type aliases can be used for any type.

Think of interfaces like contracts that define what properties and methods an object must have.

Technical Explanation

Interfaces: Define contracts for object structures - Can be extended - Can be implemented by classes - Can be merged (declaration merging) - Better for object types

Type Aliases: Create new names for types - Can represent any type (primitives, unions, intersections) - Cannot be extended - No declaration merging - More flexible for complex types

Professional Explanation

Best practices: - Use interfaces for public API definitions - Use type aliases for union types, tuple types, and type aliases - Use interfaces when you need inheritance - Use type aliases for function signatures - Document interfaces with JSDoc

Interfaces and Type Aliases Examples

// Interface definition
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
    age?: number; // Optional property
    readonly createdAt: Date; // Readonly property
}

// Interface with methods
interface UserService {
    getUser(id: number): Promise<User>;
    createUser(user: Omit<User, 'id'>): Promise<User>;
    updateUser(id: number, user: Partial<User>): Promise<User>;
    deleteUser(id: number): Promise<void>;
}

// Interface extension
interface Admin extends User {
    permissions: string[];
    role: 'admin' | 'superadmin';
}

interface PremiumUser extends User {
    subscription: {
        tier: 'basic' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';
        expiresAt: Date;
    };
}

// Interface with index signature
interface Dictionary<T> {
    [key: string]: T;
}

interface StringDictionary {
    [key: string]: string;
}

// Type alias
type UserRole = 'admin' | 'user' | 'guest';
type UserStatus = 'active' | 'inactive' | 'suspended';

// Type alias for union type
type UserType = User | Admin | PremiumUser;

// Type alias for function
type UserCallback = (user: User) => void;
type AsyncUserCallback = (user: User) => Promise<void>;

// Type alias with generic
type ApiResponse<T> = {
    data: T;
    status: number;
    message: string;
};

type UserResponse = ApiResponse<User>;
type UsersResponse = ApiResponse<User[]>;

// Type alias for tuple
type Coordinates = [number, number];
type UserTuple = [number, string, boolean];

// Type alias with conditional type
type IsArray<T> = T extends any[] ? true : false;
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

// Using interfaces in React
interface ButtonProps {
    variant: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger';
    size: 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';
    disabled?: boolean;
    onClick?: (event: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void;
    children: React.ReactNode;
}

function Button({ variant, size, disabled, onClick, children }: ButtonProps) {
    const className = `btn btn-${variant} btn-${size}`;
    return (
        <button
            className={className}
            disabled={disabled}
            onClick={onClick}
        >
            {children}
        </button>
    );
}

// Type alias for props
type InputProps = {
    value: string;
    onChange: (value: string) => void;
    placeholder?: string;
    error?: string;
    disabled?: boolean;
    type?: 'text' | 'email' | 'password' | 'number';
};

// Generic interface
interface Repository<T> {
    find(id: string): Promise<T | null>;
    findAll(): Promise<T[]>;
    create(data: Omit<T, 'id'>): Promise<T>;
    update(id: string, data: Partial<T>): Promise<T>;
    delete(id: string): Promise<void>;
}

// Implementing an interface
class UserRepository implements Repository<User> {
    async find(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
        // Implementation
        return null;
    }

    async findAll(): Promise<User[]> {
        // Implementation
        return [];
    }

    async create(data: Omit<User, 'id'>): Promise<User> {
        // Implementation
        return {} as User;
    }

    async update(id: string, data: Partial<User>): Promise<User> {
        // Implementation
        return {} as User;
    }

    async delete(id: string): Promise<void> {
        // Implementation
    }
}

10.5 Generics

Simple Explanation

Generics allow you to create reusable components and functions that work with multiple types. They're like type variables that you can specify when using the component or function.

Think of generics like a template for a stamp - you can use the same stamp with different colored ink (types) to stamp different designs.

Technical Explanation

Generics allow you to write code that works with a variety of types rather than a single one. The type is specified when the function or component is used.

Key concepts: - Type Parameters: Placeholders for types - Constraints: Restrict type parameters - Default Types: Default type if not specified - Generic Components: Reusable React components - Generic Hooks: Reusable hooks with generic types

Professional Explanation

Generics are essential for: - Data Structures: Reusable collections - API Clients: Type-safe API responses - Form Hooks: Type-safe form handling - Component Libraries: Flexible, type-safe components - Utility Functions: Reusable type-safe utilities

Generics Examples

// Basic generic function
function identity<T>(value: T): T {
    return value;
}

const num = identity<number>(42); // Type: number
const str = identity<string>("Hello"); // Type: string
const inferred = identity("Hello"); // Type inferred as string

// Generic with multiple type parameters
function pair<T, U>(first: T, second: U): [T, U] {
    return [first, second];
}

const result = pair("Hello", 42); // Type: [string, number]

// Generic with constraints
interface HasLength {
    length: number;
}

function logLength<T extends HasLength>(item: T): T {
    console.log(item.length);
    return item;
}

logLength("Hello"); // Works
logLength([1, 2, 3]); // Works
// logLength(42); // Error: number doesn't have length

// Generic interface
interface ApiResponse<T> {
    data: T;
    status: number;
    message: string;
}

function fetchApi<T>(url: string): Promise<ApiResponse<T>> {
    return fetch(url).then(res => res.json());
}

// Using generic interface
async function getUser(id: number): Promise<ApiResponse<User>> {
    return fetchApi<User>(`/api/users/${id}`);
}

// Generic class
class Box<T> {
    private value: T;

    constructor(value: T) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    getValue(): T {
        return this.value;
    }

    setValue(value: T): void {
        this.value = value;
    }
}

const numberBox = new Box(42);
const stringBox = new Box("Hello");

// Generic React component
interface ListProps<T> {
    items: T[];
    renderItem: (item: T, index: number) => React.ReactNode;
    keyExtractor?: (item: T) => string;
}

function List<T>({ items, renderItem, keyExtractor }: ListProps<T>) {
    return (
        <ul>
            {items.map((item, index) => (
                <li key={keyExtractor ? keyExtractor(item) : String(index)}>
                    {renderItem(item, index)}
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// Using generic component
interface Product {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    price: number;
}

function ProductList({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
    return (
        <List<Product>
            items={products}
            keyExtractor={(product) => String(product.id)}
            renderItem={(product) => (
                <div>
                    <h3>{product.name}</h3>
                    <p>${product.price}</p>
                </div>
            )}
        />
    );
}

// Generic custom hook
function useApi<T>(url: string) {
    const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        const fetchData = async () => {
            try {
                const response = await fetch(url);
                const json = await response.json();
                setData(json);
            } catch (err) {
                setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : 'An error occurred');
            } finally {
                setLoading(false);
            }
        };

        fetchData();
    }, [url]);

    return { data, loading, error };
}

// Using generic hook
function UserPage() {
    const { data: user, loading, error } = useApi<User>('/api/users/1');

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;
    if (!user) return <div>User not found</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Generic with default type
function createArray<T = string>(length: number, value: T): T[] {
    return Array(length).fill(value);
}

const strings = createArray(3, "Hello"); // Type: string[]
const numbers = createArray(3, 42); // Type: number[] (inferred)

// Generic with extends and keyof
function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
    return obj[key];
}

const user = { name: "John", age: 30, email: "john@example.com" };
const name = getProperty(user, "name"); // Type: string
const age = getProperty(user, "age"); // Type: number
// const invalid = getProperty(user, "invalid"); // Error: invalid key

10.6 Utility Types

Simple Explanation

Utility types are built-in TypeScript types that help you transform existing types. They allow you to create new types based on existing ones without rewriting them.

Think of utility types like tools in a workshop - each tool (utility type) helps you shape and transform your materials (types) in a specific way.

Technical Explanation

TypeScript provides several built-in utility types: - Partial: Makes all properties optional - Required: Makes all properties required - Readonly: Makes all properties readonly - Pick: Select specific properties - Omit: Remove specific properties - Exclude: Exclude types - Extract: Extract types - Record: Create object type with keys - ReturnType: Get function return type - Parameters: Get function parameters

Professional Examples

Utility types are essential for: - Form Handling: Partial for form values - API Clients: Pick for selecting fields - Type Safety: Readonly for immutable data - Data Transformation: Omit for sensitive data - Type Mapping: Record for dictionaries

Utility Types Examples

// Partial<T>
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
    age: number;
}

type PartialUser = Partial<User>;
// { id?: number; name?: string; email?: string; age?: number; }

function updateUser(id: number, updates: Partial<User>) {
    // updates can contain any subset of User properties
    console.log('Updating user:', id, updates);
}

// Required<T>
type RequiredUser = Required<PartialUser>;
// { id: number; name: string; email: string; age: number; }

// Readonly<T>
type ReadonlyUser = Readonly<User>;
// { readonly id: number; readonly name: string; readonly email: string; readonly age: number; }

const readonlyUser: ReadonlyUser = {
    id: 1,
    name: "John",
    email: "john@example.com",
    age: 30
};
// readonlyUser.name = "Jane"; // Error: Cannot assign to 'name' because it is a read-only property

// Pick<T, K>
type UserNameEmail = Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>;
// { name: string; email: string; }

function getUserBasicInfo(user: User): Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> {
    return {
        name: user.name,
        email: user.email
    };
}

// Omit<T, K>
type UserWithoutEmail = Omit<User, 'email'>;
// { id: number; name: string; age: number; }

function getUserProfile(user: User): Omit<User, 'email'> {
    const { email, ...profile } = user;
    return profile;
}

// Exclude<T, U>
type MyTypes = 'one' | 'two' | 'three' | 'four';
type ExcludeOne = Exclude<MyTypes, 'one'>;
// 'two' | 'three' | 'four'

// Extract<T, U>
type ExtractOne = Extract<MyTypes, 'one' | 'two'>;
// 'one' | 'two'

// NonNullable<T>
type NullableType = string | null | undefined;
type NonNullableType = NonNullable<NullableType>;
// string

// Record<K, T>
type UserRoles = 'admin' | 'user' | 'guest';
type RolePermissions = Record<UserRoles, string[]>;
// { admin: string[]; user: string[]; guest: string[]; }

const permissions: RolePermissions = {
    admin: ['read', 'write', 'delete'],
    user: ['read', 'write'],
    guest: ['read']
};

// ReturnType<T>
function getUser(): User {
    return {
        id: 1,
        name: "John",
        email: "john@example.com",
        age: 30
    };
}

type GetUserReturn = ReturnType<typeof getUser>;
// User

// Parameters<T>
function createUser(name: string, age: number): User {
    return {
        id: Date.now(),
        name,
        age,
        email: `${name}@example.com`
    };
}

type CreateUserParams = Parameters<typeof createUser>;
// [string, number]

// Custom utility type
type Nullable<T> = T | null;
type Optional<T> = T | undefined;
type Maybe<T> = T | null | undefined;

type UserData = {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    age: Maybe<number>;
};

// Combining utility types
type UserFormData = Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>;
// Partial of User without id

// React component with utility types
interface FormFieldProps {
    value: string;
    onChange: (value: string) => void;
    error?: string;
    label: string;
    type: 'text' | 'email' | 'password';
    required?: boolean;
}

function FormField({
    value,
    onChange,
    error,
    label,
    type,
    required
}: FormFieldProps) {
    return (
        <div className="form-group">
            <label>
                {label}
                {required && <span className="required">*</span>}
            </label>
            <input
                type={type}
                value={value}
                onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}
                className={error ? 'error' : ''}
            />
            {error && <span className="error-message">{error}</span>}
        </div>
    );
}

// Type-safe event handlers
type FormEvent = React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>;
type ChangeEvent = React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>;
type ClickEvent = React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>;

function LoginForm() {
    const [formData, setFormData] = useState<Pick<User, 'email'>>({
        email: ''
    });
    const [errors, setErrors] = useState<Partial<Record<keyof Pick<User, 'email'>, string>>>({});

    const handleChange = (e: ChangeEvent) => {
        const { name, value } = e.target;
        setFormData(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }));
    };

    const handleSubmit = (e: FormEvent) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        // Validation logic
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <FormField
                label="Email"
                type="email"
                value={formData.email}
                onChange={(value) => setFormData(prev => ({ ...prev, email: value }))}
                error={errors.email}
                required
            />
            <button type="submit">Login</button>
        </form>
    );
}

10.7 Type Narrowing and Type Guards

Simple Explanation

Type narrowing is the process of refining a variable's type from a broader type to a more specific one. Type guards are conditions that help TypeScript narrow down types.

Think of type narrowing like a detective investigation - you start with a suspect (unknown type) and gather clues (conditions) until you can identify exactly who they are (specific type).

Technical Explanation

Type narrowing helps TypeScript understand more specific types: - typeof: Check primitive types - instanceof: Check class instances - in: Check property existence - Equality: Check equality with specific values - User-defined: Custom type guard functions

Type guards are functions that return a type predicate, helping TypeScript narrow types.

Professional Explanation

Type narrowing is essential for: - API Responses: Handling different response shapes - Form Inputs: Validating user input - Error Handling: Different error types - Event Handling: Different event types - Polymorphism: Handling different types

Type Narrowing and Type Guards Examples

// typeof type guard
function processValue(value: string | number | boolean) {
    if (typeof value === 'string') {
        // value is string
        return value.toUpperCase();
    }

    if (typeof value === 'number') {
        // value is number
        return value.toFixed(2);
    }

    // value is boolean
    return value ? 'true' : 'false';
}

// instanceof type guard
class Dog {
    bark() {
        console.log('Woof!');
    }
}

class Cat {
    meow() {
        console.log('Meow!');
    }
}

function makeSound(animal: Dog | Cat) {
    if (animal instanceof Dog) {
        animal.bark(); // Dog
    } else {
        animal.meow(); // Cat
    }
}

// in operator type guard
interface Car {
    drive(): void;
    fuel: string;
}

interface Boat {
    sail(): void;
    fuel: string;
}

function operate(vehicle: Car | Boat) {
    if ('drive' in vehicle) {
        vehicle.drive(); // Car
    } else {
        vehicle.sail(); // Boat
    }
}

// Equality narrowing
function processStatus(status: 'success' | 'error' | 'loading') {
    if (status === 'success') {
        // Handle success
        return 'Operation completed successfully';
    }

    if (status === 'error') {
        // Handle error
        return 'Operation failed';
    }

    // status is 'loading'
    return 'Operation in progress...';
}

// User-defined type guard
interface AdminUser {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    role: 'admin';
    permissions: string[];
}

interface RegularUser {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    role: 'user';
    preferences: {
        theme: 'light' | 'dark';
        notifications: boolean;
    };
}

function isAdmin(user: AdminUser | RegularUser): user is AdminUser {
    return user.role === 'admin';
}

function isRegularUser(user: AdminUser | RegularUser): user is RegularUser {
    return user.role === 'user';
}

function getUserInfo(user: AdminUser | RegularUser) {
    if (isAdmin(user)) {
        // user is AdminUser
        return `Admin with permissions: ${user.permissions.join(', ')}`;
    }

    if (isRegularUser(user)) {
        // user is RegularUser
        return `User with theme: ${user.preferences.theme}`;
    }

    return 'Unknown user type';
}

// Type guard with discriminated union
type Shape =
    | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
    | { kind: 'rectangle'; width: number; height: number }
    | { kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number };

function getArea(shape: Shape): number {
    switch (shape.kind) {
        case 'circle':
            return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
        case 'rectangle':
            return shape.width * shape.height;
        case 'triangle':
            return (shape.base * shape.height) / 2;
        default:
            throw new Error('Unknown shape');
    }
}

// Type guard with null checks
function processString(value: string | null | undefined): string {
    if (value === null || value === undefined) {
        return 'No value provided';
    }

    // value is string
    return value.toUpperCase();
}

// Custom type guard with async
async function isUserValid(user: unknown): Promise<user is User> {
    if (!user || typeof user !== 'object') {
        return false;
    }

    const possibleUser = user as User;
    return typeof possibleUser.id === 'number' &&
           typeof possibleUser.name === 'string' &&
           typeof possibleUser.email === 'string';
}

// React component with type guards
interface ApiError {
    code: number;
    message: string;
}

interface ApiSuccess<T> {
    data: T;
    status: 'success';
}

function isApiError(response: unknown): response is ApiError {
    return (
        typeof response === 'object' &&
        response !== null &&
        'code' in response &&
        'message' in response
    );
}

function DataFetcher() {
    const [data, setData] = useState<unknown>(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetch('/api/data')
            .then(res => res.json())
            .then((response) => {
                if (isApiError(response)) {
                    setError(response.message);
                } else {
                    setData(response);
                }
            })
            .catch((err) => {
                setError(err.message);
            })
            .finally(() => {
                setLoading(false);
            });
    }, []);

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;

    return <div>{JSON.stringify(data)}</div>;
}

10.8 Advanced Types

Simple Explanation

Advanced types in TypeScript allow you to create complex, flexible type definitions. They include mapped types, conditional types, template literal types, and other powerful type-level programming features.

Think of advanced types like a swiss army knife - each tool allows you to solve a specific type problem in a precise way.

Technical Explanation

Advanced types include: - Mapped Types: Transform properties of a type - Conditional Types: Types based on conditions - Template Literal Types: String manipulation at type level - Infer: Extract types from complex types - Indexed Access Types: Access property types - Recursive Types: Self-referential types

Professional Explanation

Advanced types are useful for: - Type Libraries: Creating reusable type utilities - API Clients: Type-safe API responses - Form Libraries: Type-safe form handling - State Management: Type-safe state updates - Component Libraries: Flexible, type-safe components

Advanced Types Examples

// Mapped types
type Readonly<T> = {
    readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P];
};

type Partial<T> = {
    [P in keyof T]?: T[P];
};

type Nullable<T> = {
    [P in keyof T]: T[P] | null;
};

type MyUser = {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
    age: number;
};

type ReadonlyUser = Readonly<MyUser>;
type PartialUser = Partial<MyUser>;
type NullableUser = Nullable<MyUser>;

// Conditional types
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type IsNumber<T> = T extends number ? true : false;

type StringCheck = IsString<'hello'>; // true
type NumberCheck = IsNumber<'hello'>; // false

// Template literal types
type EventType = 'click' | 'hover' | 'focus';
type EventHandler = `on${Capitalize<EventType>}`;
// 'onClick' | 'onHover' | 'onFocus'

type Color = 'red' | 'blue' | 'green';
type Size = 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';
type ColorSize = `${Color}-${Size}`;
// 'red-small' | 'red-medium' | 'red-large' | 'blue-small' | ...

// Infer keyword
type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;

function greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

type GreetReturn = ReturnType<typeof greet>; // string

// Indexed access types
type UserName = MyUser['name']; // string
type UserAge = MyUser['age']; // number
type UserKeys = keyof MyUser; // 'id' | 'name' | 'email' | 'age'

// Recursive types
type JsonPrimitive = string | number | boolean | null;
type JsonValue = JsonPrimitive | JsonObject | JsonArray;
interface JsonObject {
    [key: string]: JsonValue;
}
interface JsonArray extends Array<JsonValue> {}

// Mapped type with modifiers
type Mutable<T> = {
    -readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P];
};

type Required<T> = {
    [P in keyof T]-?: T[P];
};

// Conditional mapped types
type ExtractProperty<T, U> = {
    [P in keyof T]: T[P] extends U ? P : never;
}[keyof T];

// Union transformation types
type UnionToIntersection<U> =
    (U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never) extends ((k: infer I) => void) ? I : never;

type Union = { a: number } | { b: string } | { c: boolean };
type Intersection = UnionToIntersection<Union>; // { a: number } & { b: string } & { c: boolean }

// Advanced React type definitions
type ComponentProps<T> = T extends React.ComponentType<infer P> ? P : never;

function withAuth<T extends React.ComponentType<any>>(
    Component: T
): React.ComponentType<Omit<ComponentProps<T>, 'user'>> {
    return function AuthenticatedComponent(props: Omit<ComponentProps<T>, 'user'>) {
        const user = useAuth();
        return <Component {...props as any} user={user} />;
    };
}

// Type-safe event system
type EventMap = {
    userCreated: { id: number; name: string };
    userDeleted: { id: number };
    userUpdated: { id: number; changes: Partial<User> };
};

type EventListener<T> = (data: T) => void;

class EventBus {
    private listeners: {
        [K in keyof EventMap]?: EventListener<EventMap[K]>[];
    } = {};

    emit<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, data: EventMap[K]) {
        const listeners = this.listeners[event] || [];
        listeners.forEach(listener => listener(data));
    }

    on<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, listener: EventListener<EventMap[K]>) {
        if (!this.listeners[event]) {
            this.listeners[event] = [];
        }
        this.listeners[event]!.push(listener);
        return () => this.off(event, listener);
    }

    off<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, listener: EventListener<EventMap[K]>) {
        const listeners = this.listeners[event];
        if (listeners) {
            this.listeners[event] = listeners.filter(l => l !== listener);
        }
    }
}

// Using the event system
const eventBus = new EventBus();

eventBus.on('userCreated', (data) => {
    console.log('User created:', data.id, data.name);
});

eventBus.emit('userCreated', { id: 1, name: 'John' });

10.9 TypeScript in React Components

Simple Explanation

TypeScript enhances React components by providing type safety for props, state, and events. This leads to fewer bugs, better IDE support, and self-documenting components.

Technical Explanation

TypeScript with React components involves: - Props: Define prop types - State: Type state variables - Events: Type event handlers - Hooks: Type useState, useReducer, etc. - Context: Type context values - Refs: Type refs - Higher-Order Components: Type HOCs

Professional Examples

TypeScript makes React components robust and maintainable by catching type errors at compile time.

TypeScript in React Components Examples

// Functional component with props
interface ButtonProps {
    variant: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger';
    size?: 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';
    disabled?: boolean;
    onClick?: (event: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void;
    children: React.ReactNode;
    className?: string;
}

const Button: React.FC<ButtonProps> = ({
    variant,
    size = 'medium',
    disabled = false,
    onClick,
    children,
    className
}) => {
    const baseClasses = 'btn';
    const variantClasses = {
        primary: 'btn-primary',
        secondary: 'btn-secondary',
        danger: 'btn-danger'
    };
    const sizeClasses = {
        small: 'btn-sm',
        medium: 'btn-md',
        large: 'btn-lg'
    };

    return (
        <button
            className={`${baseClasses} ${variantClasses[variant]} ${sizeClasses[size]} ${className || ''}`}
            disabled={disabled}
            onClick={onClick}
        >
            {children}
        </button>
    );
};

// Component with generic props
interface ListProps<T> {
    items: T[];
    renderItem: (item: T, index: number) => React.ReactNode;
    keyExtractor: (item: T) => string;
    emptyMessage?: string;
    className?: string;
}

function List<T>({
    items,
    renderItem,
    keyExtractor,
    emptyMessage,
    className
}: ListProps<T>) {
    if (items.length === 0) {
        return <div>{emptyMessage || 'No items to display'}</div>;
    }

    return (
        <ul className={className}>
            {items.map((item, index) => (
                <li key={keyExtractor(item)}>
                    {renderItem(item, index)}
                </li>
            ))}
        </ul>
    );
}

// Component with state
interface CounterState {
    count: number;
    lastUpdated: Date;
}

function Counter() {
    const [state, setState] = useState<CounterState>({
        count: 0,
        lastUpdated: new Date()
    });

    const increment = () => {
        setState(prev => ({
            count: prev.count + 1,
            lastUpdated: new Date()
        }));
    };

    const decrement = () => {
        setState(prev => ({
            count: prev.count - 1,
            lastUpdated: new Date()
        }));
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Count: {state.count}</p>
            <p>Last updated: {state.lastUpdated.toLocaleTimeString()}</p>
            <button onClick={increment}>+</button>
            <button onClick={decrement}>-</button>
        </div>
    );
}

// Component with refs
interface InputProps {
    value: string;
    onChange: (value: string) => void;
    placeholder?: string;
    error?: string;
}

const Input = React.forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, InputProps>(
    ({ value, onChange, placeholder, error }, ref) => {
        return (
            <div className="input-group">
                <input
                    ref={ref}
                    type="text"
                    value={value}
                    onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}
                    placeholder={placeholder}
                    className={error ? 'error' : ''}
                />
                {error && <span className="error-message">{error}</span>}
            </div>
        );
    }
);

// Component with context
interface ThemeContextValue {
    theme: 'light' | 'dark';
    toggleTheme: () => void;
}

const ThemeContext = React.createContext<ThemeContextValue | null>(null);

function ThemeProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
    const [theme, setTheme] = useState<'light' | 'dark'>('light');

    const toggleTheme = () => {
        setTheme(prev => prev === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light');
    };

    const value: ThemeContextValue = {
        theme,
        toggleTheme
    };

    return (
        <ThemeContext.Provider value={value}>
            {children}
        </ThemeContext.Provider>
    );
}

function useTheme() {
    const context = useContext(ThemeContext);
    if (!context) {
        throw new Error('useTheme must be used within a ThemeProvider');
    }
    return context;
}

function ThemedButton() {
    const { theme, toggleTheme } = useTheme();

    return (
        <button
            className={`btn-theme-${theme}`}
            onClick={toggleTheme}
        >
            Switch to {theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light'} mode
        </button>
    );
}

// Custom hook with types
function useFetch<T>(url: string): {
    data: T | null;
    loading: boolean;
    error: string | null;
    refetch: () => void;
} {
    const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

    const fetchData = useCallback(async () => {
        setLoading(true);
        setError(null);
        try {
            const response = await fetch(url);
            const json = await response.json();
            setData(json);
        } catch (err) {
            setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : 'An error occurred');
        } finally {
            setLoading(false);
        }
    }, [url]);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchData();
    }, [fetchData]);

    return { data, loading, error, refetch: fetchData };
}

// Component with custom hook
function UserProfile() {
    const { data: user, loading, error } = useFetch<User>('/api/users/1');

    if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
    if (error) return <div>Error: {error}</div>;
    if (!user) return <div>User not found</div>;

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p>
            {user.age && <p>Age: {user.age}</p>}
        </div>
    );
}

10.10 Common Mistakes and Best Practices

10.10.1 Common Mistakes

// ❌ Using any instead of proper types
function processData(data: any) {
    // Disables type checking
    return data.name;
}

// ✅ Use proper types
function processData(data: { name: string }) {
    return data.name;
}

// ❌ Not handling optional props
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email?: string;
}

function UserCard({ user }: { user: User }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email}</p> {/* ❌ email might be undefined */}
        </div>
    );
}

// ✅ Handle optional props
function UserCard({ user }: { user: User }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <p>{user.email || 'No email provided'}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// ❌ Type assertion abuse
const user = {} as User;
user.id = 1; // ❌ Not safe

// ✅ Use proper initialization
const user: User = {
    id: 1,
    name: 'John'
};

// ❌ Overly complex types
interface ComplexType {
    data: {
        items: {
            id: number;
            name: string;
            metadata: {
                created: string;
                updated: string;
                tags: string[];
            };
        }[];
        pagination: {
            page: number;
            limit: number;
            total: number;
        };
    };
}

// ✅ Break down complex types
interface Item {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    metadata: Metadata;
}

interface Metadata {
    created: string;
    updated: string;
    tags: string[];
}

interface Pagination {
    page: number;
    limit: number;
    total: number;
}

interface DataResponse {
    items: Item[];
    pagination: Pagination;
}

10.10.2 Best Practices

// ✅ Use interfaces for object types
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}

// ✅ Use type aliases for union types
type UserRole = 'admin' | 'user' | 'guest';

// ✅ Use proper event types
function handleClick(event: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) {
    // Type-safe event handling
}

// ✅ Use generic components
function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: ListProps<T>) {
    // Reusable type-safe list
}

// ✅ Use strict null checks
function getValue(value: string | null | undefined): string {
    return value ?? 'default';
}

// ✅ Document types with JSDoc
/**
 * User information interface
 * @property id - Unique user identifier
 * @property name - Full name of the user
 * @property email - Email address of the user
 */
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}

// ✅ Use utility types
type UserPreview = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>;
type UserUpdate = Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>;
type UserResponse = ApiResponse<User>;

// ✅ Use discriminated unions
type ApiState =
    | { status: 'idle' }
    | { status: 'loading' }
    | { status: 'success'; data: User }
    | { status: 'error'; error: string };

function handleState(state: ApiState) {
    switch (state.status) {
        case 'idle':
            return 'Ready';
        case 'loading':
            return 'Loading...';
        case 'success':
            return `User: ${state.data.name}`;
        case 'error':
            return `Error: ${state.error}`;
    }
}

10.11 Interview Questions

Junior Level Questions

Q: What is TypeScript and why use it with React?

Answer: TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript that adds static typing. Benefits with React: - Better IDE support and autocomplete - Catch errors at compile time - Self-documenting code - Easier refactoring

interface Props {
    name: string;
    age: number;
}

function Greeting({ name, age }: Props) {
    return <h1>Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.</h1>;
}

Q: What is the difference between interface and type?

Answer: - Interface: For object types, can be extended, declaration merging - Type: More flexible, supports union types, can be used for any type

// Interface
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
}

// Type
type User = {
    id: number;
    name: string;
};

type UserRole = 'admin' | 'user';

Mid Level Questions

Q: How do you use generics in React components?

Answer: Generics allow components to work with multiple types while maintaining type safety.

function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: ListProps<T>) {
    return items.map((item, index) => renderItem(item, index));
}

// Usage
<List<User>
    items={users}
    renderItem={(user) => <UserCard user={user} />}
/>

Q: What are utility types and when would you use them?

Answer: Utility types are built-in TypeScript types that transform existing types. Common ones: - Partial<T>: Make all properties optional - Pick<T, K>: Select specific properties - Omit<T, K>: Remove specific properties - Readonly<T>: Make all properties readonly

type UserUpdate = Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>;
function updateUser(id: number, updates: UserUpdate) {
    // updates can contain any subset of User properties
}

Senior Level Questions

Q: How do you create type-safe API clients with TypeScript?

Answer: Use generics, utility types, and conditional types to create type-safe API clients.

interface ApiClient {
    get<T>(url: string): Promise<ApiResponse<T>>;
    post<T>(url: string, data: unknown): Promise<ApiResponse<T>>;
    put<T>(url: string, data: unknown): Promise<ApiResponse<T>>;
    delete<T>(url: string): Promise<ApiResponse<T>>;
}

// Using the client
const user = await client.get<User>('/users/1');
const users = await client.get<User[]>('/users');

Q: How do you implement type-safe forms in React?

Answer: Use TypeScript with form libraries like React Hook Form for type-safe forms.

interface FormData {
    name: string;
    email: string;
    age: number;
}

function MyForm() {
    const { register, handleSubmit } = useForm<FormData>();

    const onSubmit = (data: FormData) => {
        console.log(data);
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
            <input {...register('name')} />
            <input {...register('email')} />
            <input {...register('age')} />
            <button type="submit">Submit</button>
        </form>
    );
}

10.12 Summary

TypeScript Concepts

Concept Description Example
Primitives Basic types string, number, boolean
Interfaces Object type definitions interface User { name: string }
Type Aliases Custom type names type UserRole = 'admin' \| 'user'
Generics Type parameters function<T>(value: T): T
Utility Types Type transformations Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>
Type Guards Type narrowing typeof, instanceof, user-defined

TypeScript in React

React Concept TypeScript Usage Example
Props Interface or type interface Props { name: string }
State Type annotation const [state, setState] = useState<Type>()
Events Event types (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => void
Hooks Type parameters useState<string>('')
Context Context types const ctx = createContext<Type | null>(null)
Refs Ref types const ref = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)

Best Practices Summary

  1. Use interfaces for object types
  2. Use type aliases for union types and complex types
  3. Use generics for reusable components
  4. Use utility types to transform existing types
  5. Use type guards for safe type narrowing
  6. Avoid any type
  7. Use strict mode in TypeScript
  8. Document types with JSDoc
  9. Use discriminated unions for state management
  10. Keep types organized and maintainable

11

Enterprise React Project Structure

Introduction

As React applications grow, organizing files becomes just as important as writing good code.

A small project with only a few pages can keep everything inside the src folder without any structure.

Example:

src
│
├── App.tsx
├── Login.tsx
├── Customer.tsx
├── Order.tsx
├── Employee.tsx
└── index.css

This works for very small applications.

However, an enterprise application may contain:

  • 100+ pages
  • 500+ React components
  • Hundreds of API endpoints
  • Multiple development teams
  • Thousands of files

Without a proper architecture, maintaining the project becomes nearly impossible.

For this reason, professional companies organize React applications into specialized folders where each folder has one responsibility.

Why Project Structure Matters

A good project structure provides:

  • Better maintainability
  • Easier onboarding for new developers
  • Better scalability
  • Less duplicated code
  • Easier debugging
  • Cleaner architecture
  • Separation of concerns
  • Reusable code

Every developer on the team immediately knows where each file belongs.

How Data Flows Through the Application

Before understanding the folders, you should understand how data travels inside a React application.

Imagine a user clicks the Create Customer button.

The request flows like this:

User → Customer Page → Customer Form Component → Customer Service → Customer API → Axios Instance → Spring Boot REST API → Controller → Service → Repository → Database

Database → Repository → Service → Controller → JSON Response → Axios → Customer API → Customer Service → React Query → React Component → User Interface

Understanding this flow makes understanding the folder structure much easier.

Root Project Structure

A typical enterprise React application may look like this:

src
│
├── api
├── assets
├── components
├── config
├── constants
├── context
├── hooks
├── layouts
├── pages
├── providers
├── routes
├── services
├── store
├── types
├── utils
├── validations
├── features
├── shared
│
├── App.tsx
├── main.tsx
├── index.css
└── vite-env.d.ts

Each folder has a single responsibility.

api/

Purpose

The api folder contains all communication with the backend.

Its responsibility is only sending HTTP requests.

It should never contain business logic.

Example:

api
│
├── api.ts
├── auth.api.ts
├── customer.api.ts
├── employee.api.ts
├── order.api.ts
├── payment.api.ts
└── report.api.ts

Example:

export function getCustomers() {
    return api.get("/customers");
}

Responsibilities:

  • GET requests
  • POST requests
  • PUT requests
  • DELETE requests
  • Upload requests
  • Download requests

Not responsible for:

  • Filtering data
  • Business rules
  • UI logic

assets/

Stores static resources.

Example:

assets
│
├── images
├── icons
├── fonts
├── videos
└── styles

Contains:

  • Logos
  • Images
  • Icons
  • Fonts
  • Global CSS
  • Animations

components/

Contains reusable UI components.

Instead of rewriting the same button 50 times:

<button>Create</button>

You create:

<Button />

Project:

components
│
├── common
├── forms
├── layout
└── ui

Examples:

  • Button
  • Card
  • Modal
  • Table
  • Loader
  • Input
  • Pagination

Reusable everywhere.

pages/

A page represents an entire screen.

Examples:

pages
│
├── Dashboard
├── Customers
├── Orders
├── Employees
├── Reports
└── Login

Usually every page corresponds to one route.

Example:

/customers

loads

CustomersPage.tsx

layouts/

Layouts define page structure.

Example:

  • Dashboard Layout
  • +--------------------------------+
  • Navbar
  • Sidebar | Main Content
  • Footer
  • +--------------------------------+

Instead of rewriting Navbar and Sidebar on every page, pages are wrapped inside layouts.

hooks/

Contains reusable custom hooks.

Example:

hooks
│
├── useAuth.ts
├── usePagination.ts
├── useApi.ts
├── useTheme.ts
└── useToast.ts

Hooks encapsulate reusable logic.

Example:

const { login } = useAuth();

services/

Contains business logic.

Services sit between Components and APIs.

Flow:

Component → Service → API

Example:

API returns:

100 customers

Service filters:

Only Active Customers

Components receive clean data.

routes/

Responsible for navigation.

Example:

routes
│
├── AppRouter.tsx
├── ProtectedRoute.tsx
├── PublicRoute.tsx
└── RouteGuard.tsx

Responsibilities:

  • Page navigation
  • Authentication protection
  • Authorization
  • Lazy loading

context/

Stores global application state.

Example:

AuthContext → Current User → Accessible by every component

Examples:

  • Authentication
  • Theme
  • Language

store/

Contains centralized state management.

Usually used with:

  • Redux Toolkit
  • Zustand
  • MobX

Stores application-wide data.

providers/

Wrap global providers around the application.

Example:

<QueryClientProvider>

<AuthProvider>

<ThemeProvider>

<App />

</ThemeProvider>

</AuthProvider>

</QueryClientProvider>

constants/

Stores values that rarely change.

Example:

  • API_URL
  • ADMIN_ROLE
  • CUSTOMER_ROLE
  • ORDER_PENDING
  • ORDER_COMPLETED
  • MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE

Instead of repeating strings throughout the project.

config/

Contains project configuration.

Examples:

  • Axios
  • React Query
  • Theme
  • Environment
  • Application Settings

utils/

General helper functions.

Examples:

  • formatDate()
  • formatCurrency()
  • downloadFile()
  • parseJwt()
  • generateUUID()
  • capitalize()

Pure functions.

No React code.

types/

Contains TypeScript definitions.

Example:

export interface Customer {

    id: number;

    name: string;

    phone: string;

}

Used everywhere.

validations/

Contains validation schemas.

Usually built using:

  • Zod
  • Yup

Example:

CustomerSchema

Rules:

  • Name required
  • Phone format
  • Email validation

features/

Some enterprise projects organize by feature.

Example:

features
│
├── auth
├── customer
├── employee
├── order
└── payment

Each feature contains:

customer
│
├── api
├── components
├── hooks
├── pages
├── services
├── types
└── validations

Everything related to Customers stays together.

shared/

Contains code shared across multiple features.

Example:

shared
│
├── components
├── hooks
├── utils
├── constants
└── types

Main Files

main.tsx

Application entry point.

Responsibilities:

  • Mount React
  • Create root
  • Register providers
  • Render App

App.tsx

Root application component.

Responsibilities:

  • Render layouts
  • Render router
  • Global application structure

index.css

Global CSS styles.

Typically imports:

  • Tailwind
  • Variables
  • Global styles
  • Fonts

vite-env.d.ts

TypeScript declarations generated for Vite.

Allows TypeScript to understand:

import.meta.env

File Extensions

.ts

TypeScript file.

Contains:

  • Functions
  • Classes
  • Utilities
  • Services
  • APIs
  • Hooks (without JSX)

Example:

customer.service.ts

.tsx

TypeScript + JSX.

Contains React Components.

Example:

CustomerTable.tsx

.css

Regular CSS file.

Global styles.

.module.css

Scoped CSS.

Styles only affect one component.

Example:

import styles from "./Button.module.css";

.scss

Sass stylesheet.

Supports:

  • Variables
  • Nesting
  • Mixins

.svg

Vector graphics.

Best for:

  • Icons
  • Logos

.png

Raster image.

Supports transparency.

.jpg

Compressed photograph.

Best for photos.

.json

Configuration or data.

Examples:

  • package.json
  • tsconfig.json
  • launch.json

.env

Environment variables.

Example:

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080

Never commit secrets.

.env.local

Local environment variables.

Ignored by Git.

.md

Markdown documentation.

Used for:

  • README
  • Documentation
  • Architecture
  • Tutorials

Summary

A well-designed React project structure is not about creating many folders—it is about assigning a clear responsibility to each part of the application.

When every folder has one purpose, developers can quickly locate files, understand data flow, collaborate efficiently, and scale the application without creating technical debt.

This architecture is the foundation of professional React applications used in enterprise environments.

12

Understanding Data Flow in React Applications

Introduction

One of the biggest challenges for new React developers is understanding how data moves through an application.

Many beginners understand Components, Hooks, or APIs individually, but they don't understand how everything connects together.

In enterprise applications, every button click follows a predictable journey.

Understanding this journey is the key to reading any React project.

This chapter explains that journey from the moment a user interacts with the application until the data reaches the database and returns back to the screen.

The Complete Data Flow

Imagine the following scenario.

A user opens the application and clicks:

Create Customer

The request travels through multiple layers.

User → React Page → React Component → Event Handler → Custom Hook (Optional) → Business Service → API Layer → Axios → Internet (HTTP Request) → Spring Boot Controller → Spring Boot Service → Repository → Database

Database → Repository → Service → Controller → JSON Response → Axios → API Layer → Service Layer → React Query → React Component → Browser UI

Every enterprise React application follows approximately this architecture.

Step 1 — The User

Everything starts with the user.

The user can:

  • Click a button
  • Fill a form
  • Type into an input
  • Select an item
  • Delete data
  • Update data
  • Navigate to another page

Example:

<Button>Create Customer</Button>

Nothing happens until the user performs an action.

Step 2 — React Page

The current page receives the interaction.

Example:

CustomersPage.tsx

Responsibilities:

  • Display data
  • Organize components
  • Connect UI with business logic

Example:

export default function CustomersPage() {

    return (

        <CustomerTable />

    );

}

Pages usually contain multiple components.

Step 3 — React Component

Components contain the actual UI.

Example:

CustomerForm.tsx

Responsibilities:

  • Render HTML
  • Receive Props
  • Display State
  • Handle Events

Example:

<Button onClick={handleSubmit}>

Create

</Button>

The component itself should remain as simple as possible.

Step 4 — Event Handler

When the button is clicked:

onClick={handleSubmit}

React executes:

function handleSubmit() {

    ...

}

This function becomes the starting point of the business process.

Step 5 — Reading State

Before sending anything to the server, React reads the current data.

Example:

const [customer, setCustomer] = useState(...)

Current values:

  • Name
  • Phone
  • Address
  • Email

These values become the request body.

Step 6 — Validation

Professional applications validate data before sending it.

Example:

  • Name required
  • Phone format
  • Email format
  • Password length

Libraries:

  • Zod
  • Yup
  • React Hook Form

If validation fails:

  • Stop
  • Show Error
  • Do NOT call API

Step 7 — Custom Hooks (Optional)

Many enterprise projects move logic into hooks.

Example:

  • useCustomer()
  • useOrders()
  • useEmployees()

Instead of writing everything inside the component.

Example:

const { createCustomer } = useCustomer();

Now the component becomes much cleaner.

Step 8 — Business Service

The Service Layer contains business rules.

Example:

customer.service.ts

Responsibilities:

  • Prepare data
  • Transform data
  • Filter data
  • Decide which API to call
  • Handle business logic

Example:

Component → Customer Service → Customer API

Services should not render UI.

Step 9 — API Layer

Now the request reaches:

customer.api.ts

Responsibilities:

  • Send HTTP Requests
  • Receive HTTP Responses

Example:

export function createCustomer(data){

    return api.post("/customers", data);

}

Notice:

No validation.

No filtering.

No UI.

Only communication.

Step 10 — Axios

Every API file usually uses one shared Axios instance.

Example:

const api = axios.create({

    baseURL: "http://localhost:8080"

});

Axios automatically:

  • Adds Base URL
  • Adds Authorization Token
  • Converts JSON
  • Handles Errors
  • Executes Interceptors

Step 11 — HTTP Request

Axios converts the JavaScript object into JSON.

Example:

{

"name":"John",

"phone":"123456"

}

Then sends:

  • POST
  • /customers

Through the Internet.

Step 12 — Spring Boot Controller

The request reaches:

CustomerController

Responsibilities:

  • Receive Request
  • Validate Request
  • Call Service

Example:

@PostMapping

public Customer create(...)

Controllers should remain thin.

Step 13 — Spring Service

Now business logic executes.

Example:

CustomerService

Responsibilities:

  • Validate business rules
  • Calculate values
  • Execute workflow
  • Call Repository

Step 14 — Repository

Repository communicates with the database.

Example:

CustomerRepository

Responsibilities:

  • Save
  • Update
  • Delete
  • Find

Example:

repository.save(customer);

Step 15 — Database

Finally data reaches:

  • MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • Oracle
  • SQL Server

The record is stored.

The Response Journey

Everything now returns backwards.

Database → Repository → Service → Controller → JSON → Axios → API → Service → React Query → Component → Screen

React Query

Most enterprise applications use React Query.

Responsibilities:

  • Cache Data
  • Loading State
  • Error State
  • Refetch
  • Synchronization

Instead of:

  • Loading...
  • Loading...
  • Loading...

React Query handles it automatically.

Updating the UI

React receives new data.

State changes.

React re-renders only affected components.

Example:

  • Old Table
  • 10 Customers
  • ↓
  • New Table
  • 11 Customers

Only the table updates.

The entire page is NOT reloaded.

Why React Re-renders

React compares:

Old Virtual DOM → New Virtual DOM → Diff Algorithm → Only Changed Nodes → Real DOM Update

This makes React very fast.

Complete Enterprise Example

Imagine the Laundry Management System.

Customer submits a new laundry order.

User → OrdersPage → CreateOrderForm → handleSubmit() → React Hook Form → Zod Validation → useOrder() → order.service.ts → order.api.ts → Axios → POST /orders → Spring Boot → OrderController → OrderService → OrderRepository → MySQL

MySQL → OrderRepository → OrderService → OrderController → 201 Created → Axios → React Query Cache Update → Order Table → Success Toast → UI Updated

This is exactly how enterprise React applications operate.

Error Flow

Suppose something fails.

Example:

Database Down

The flow becomes:

Database → Exception → Spring Boot → HTTP 500 → Axios → Interceptor → API Layer → Service Layer → React Query → Component → Toast → Error Message

The user sees:

  • Unable to create customer.
  • Please try again.

Instead of a broken application.

Authentication Flow

Login follows a slightly different path.

User → Login Form → Validation → auth.service.ts → auth.api.ts → POST /login → Spring Boot → JWT Token → Axios → Local Storage → Auth Context → Protected Routes → Dashboard

Every future request automatically includes:

  • Authorization:
  • Bearer

Axios Interceptors usually attach this token automatically.

File Upload Flow

Uploading files introduces another path.

User → Select File → File Object → FormData → Axios → Multipart Request → Spring Boot → Storage Service → Cloud / Local Disk → Database stores file path → Response → React → Image Preview

Data Flow Responsibilities

Layer Responsibility
User Starts the interaction
Page Organizes UI
Component Displays interface
Event Handler Responds to user actions
Hook Reusable logic
Validation Validate inputs
Service Business logic
API HTTP communication
Axios Network client
Spring Controller Receives request
Spring Service Business processing
Repository Database communication
Database Stores information
React Query Cache & synchronization
React Component Displays updated UI

Best Practices

✅ Keep Components focused on UI.

✅ Move business logic to Services.

✅ Keep API files responsible only for HTTP requests.

✅ Use React Query for server state.

✅ Validate before sending requests.

✅ Handle loading and error states.

✅ Use reusable hooks.

✅ Separate concerns between UI, logic, networking, and persistence.

Common Mistakes

❌ Calling Axios directly inside every component.

❌ Mixing UI code with business logic.

❌ Duplicating API calls.

❌ Keeping large amounts of state inside a single component.

❌ Ignoring loading and error states.

❌ Repeating validation logic in multiple places.

❌ Making components responsible for everything.

Chapter Summary

Understanding React data flow is more important than memorizing APIs or hooks.

Every enterprise React application is built around a layered architecture where each layer has one clear responsibility.

Enterprise React Architecture Case Study

Laundry Management System (React + TypeScript + Spring Boot)

Introduction

In the previous chapters, you learned:

  • React fundamentals
  • Enterprise folder structure
  • Data flow
  • Services
  • APIs
  • Components
  • Hooks

In this chapter, we will combine everything into one complete enterprise application.

Our case study is a Laundry Management System.

This chapter explains how every folder communicates with the others and how data flows through the application from the user interface to the database.

High-Level Architecture

                        Browser
                           │
                           ▼
                 React Application
                           │
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                 UI Layer                    │
 │ Pages → Layouts → Components               │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │             Application Layer               │
 │ Hooks → Context → Services                 │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │            Communication Layer              │
 │ API → Axios → HTTP                         │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │         Spring Boot Backend                 │
 │ Controller → Service → Repository          │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                      MySQL Database

Every layer has one responsibility.

Overall Folder Structure

src
│
├── api
├── assets
├── components
├── config
├── constants
├── context
├── hooks
├── layouts
├── pages
├── providers
├── routes
├── services
├── types
├── utils
├── validations
│
├── App.tsx
├── main.tsx
└── index.css

Now let's see how every folder communicates with the others.

Application Startup

When the application starts, React executes:

main.tsx → Render React → Load Providers → Load Router → Render App.tsx → Open Login Page or Dashboard

Example:

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(

<App />

)

Authentication Architecture

Login is usually the first workflow.

Login Page → Login Form → Validation → auth.service.ts → auth.api.ts → Axios → POST /login → Spring Boot → JWT Token → LocalStorage → AuthContext → Dashboard

Responsibilities

File Responsibility
LoginPage UI
LoginForm Form
Validation Validate email/password
auth.service.ts Business logic
auth.api.ts HTTP request
Axios Communication
AuthContext Store current user
ProtectedRoute Protect pages

Customer Module

Imagine the user clicks:

Customers

The application loads:

CustomersPage → CustomerTable → useCustomers() → customer.service.ts → customer.api.ts → GET /customers → Spring Boot → Database

Returned data:

Customers → React Query Cache → CustomerTable → Screen

Customer Folder Communication

CustomersPage
        │
        ▼
CustomerTable
        │
        ▼
CustomerForm
        │
        ▼
useCustomer()
        │
        ▼
customer.service.ts
        │
        ▼
customer.api.ts
        │
        ▼
Axios
        │
        ▼
Spring Boot

Notice that the UI never communicates directly with Spring Boot.

Everything goes through the Service and API layers.

Creating a Customer

User clicks:

Save

Flow:

Button → handleSubmit() → React Hook Form → Zod Validation → customer.service.create() → customer.api.create() → Axios POST → Spring Boot → Database → 201 Created → React Query Refetch → Customer Table Updated

Orders Module

Orders are more complicated.

Each order belongs to:

  • Customer
  • Laundry
  • Tailoring
  • Payment

Architecture:

OrdersPage → CreateOrderForm → Select Customer → Select Services → Calculate Total → order.service.ts → order.api.ts → POST /orders

Backend:

OrderController → OrderService → CustomerRepository → LaundryRepository → TailoringRepository → PaymentRepository → Database

Order Status Flow

Example:

Pending → Received → Washing → Drying → Ironing → Tailoring → Ready → Delivered

React updates the badge automatically after each backend response.

Laundry Module

Laundry employees open:

Laundry Dashboard

Flow:

LaundryPage → LaundryTable → laundry.service.ts → laundry.api.ts → GET /laundry/jobs → Backend → Database → LaundryTable

Updating status:

Click → Update Status → PATCH Request → Backend → Database → React Query → Updated Badge

Tailoring Module

The tailoring department works almost the same way.

Tailoring Page → Tailoring Queue → tailoring.service.ts → tailoring.api.ts → PATCH /tailoring → Backend → Database → Updated UI

Employee Module

Manager opens:

Employees

Architecture:

EmployeesPage → EmployeeTable → EmployeeModal → employee.service.ts → employee.api.ts → Spring Boot

CRUD Operations:

  • Create
  • Read
  • Update
  • Delete

Payment Module

Payment process:

Payment Page → Payment Form → Calculate Remaining Balance → payment.service.ts → payment.api.ts → Backend → Invoice → Receipt → Success Message

Reports Module

Reports usually generate PDFs or Excel files.

Flow:

Reports Page → Filter Form → report.service.ts → report.api.ts → Backend → Generate PDF → Download File → User

Dashboard Module

Dashboard loads multiple APIs simultaneously.

Dashboard → Total Orders → Revenue → Customers → Employees → Pending Jobs → Charts

Flow:

DashboardPage → dashboard.service.ts → dashboard.api.ts → Multiple REST APIs → React Query → Dashboard Cards

Components Communication

Example:

OrdersPage

Contains:

  • PageHeader
  • SearchBar
  • OrderFilters
  • OrderTable
  • Pagination
  • CreateOrderModal
  • DeleteDialog

Each component has only one responsibility.

Context Communication

Global Context is available everywhere.

Example:

App
│
├── Navbar
├── Sidebar
├── Dashboard
├── Orders
├── Customers
└── Footer

Every component can access:

const { user } = useAuth();

Without passing props through every level.

Hooks Communication

Custom hooks simplify components.

Instead of:

CustomersPage

↓

Axios

↓

State

↓

Loading

↓

Error

↓

Success

We simply write:

const {

customers,

loading,

createCustomer

} = useCustomers();

The hook hides all complexity.

Services Communication

Services are the application's brain.

Example:

Customer Page → Customer Service → Validate Data → Transform Data → Call API → Return Result

Services should never render UI.

API Communication

API files are responsible only for HTTP communication.

Example:

  • customer.api.ts
  • ↓
  • GET
  • POST
  • PUT
  • DELETE

Nothing else.

Axios Communication

Axios automatically:

Add Base URL → Attach JWT → Serialize JSON → Send Request → Receive Response → Handle Errors → Return Data

All API files reuse the same Axios instance.

React Query Communication

React Query sits between Components and APIs.

Component → React Query → Service → API → Axios

Responsibilities:

  • Cache
  • Refetch
  • Retry
  • Synchronization
  • Loading State
  • Error State

Example — Complete Customer Creation

User → Customers Page → Customer Form → Button Click → handleSubmit() → React Hook Form → Zod Validation → useCustomer() → customer.service.ts → customer.api.ts → Axios → POST /customers → Spring Boot → Controller → Service → Repository → Database

Database → Repository → Service → Controller → HTTP 201 → Axios → React Query → Customer Table Refresh → Success Toast → Updated UI

                          │
                          ▼
                     React Router
                          │
                          ▼
                       Pages
                          │

                    React Components

                  Custom Hooks (Optional)

                    Business Services

                     API Functions

                     Axios Client

                   Spring Boot API
                          │

                     Controllers

                          ▼
                       Services
                          │

                    Repositories

                    JSON Response
                          │
                          ▲
                     Axios Client

Responsibility Matrix

Layer Responsibility
Pages Represent screens
Components Build UI
Layouts Shared page structure
Hooks Reusable logic
Context Global state
Services Business rules
APIs HTTP communication
Axios Networking
React Query Server state management
Spring Controller Receive requests
Spring Service Business processing
Repository Database access
Database Persist data

Best Practices

  • Keep components focused on presentation.
  • Move business logic into services.
  • Keep API files limited to HTTP communication.
  • Reuse components whenever possible.
  • Use custom hooks to reduce duplication.
  • Use React Query for all server state.
  • Keep layouts independent from business logic.
  • Validate data before calling APIs.
  • Never mix UI logic with networking code.
  • Separate responsibilities between layers.

Common Mistakes

❌ Calling Axios directly inside every component.

❌ Placing business logic inside pages.

❌ Creating huge components with hundreds of lines.

❌ Duplicating API calls.

❌ Mixing authentication with UI code.

❌ Ignoring loading and error states.

❌ Passing props through many nested components instead of using Context when appropriate.

❌ Creating utility functions inside components instead of using the utils folder.

Chapter Summary

An enterprise React application is built using layers, where each layer has a single responsibility.

A user action flows from the UI through Components, Hooks, Services, APIs, Axios, and the Spring Boot backend before reaching the database. The response then travels back through the same layers until React updates only the necessary parts of the interface.

By understanding how these layers interact—and by respecting the separation of concerns—you can confidently read, maintain, and build large-scale React applications integrated with Spring Boot. Once you understand this journey—from the user's click to the database and back—you can confidently read, debug, extend, and build professional React applications integrated with Spring Boot or any modern backend.
