14

React Performance Optimization

Introduction

React is already fast by default.

However, fast does not always mean optimized.

As applications grow, unnecessary rendering, expensive calculations, large JavaScript bundles, and excessive API requests can significantly reduce performance.

Performance optimization is the process of making your application:

  • Faster
  • More responsive
  • More scalable
  • More memory efficient
  • Easier to maintain

Enterprise applications often serve thousands or millions of users simultaneously, making performance optimization a critical skill for every React developer.

Why Performance Matters

Imagine an application with:

  • 50 pages
  • 300 React components
  • 200 API endpoints
  • Thousands of records
  • Hundreds of users online

Without optimization:

  • Slow loading
  • UI freezes
  • Laggy scrolling
  • Excessive network requests
  • High memory usage
  • Poor user experience

A well-optimized React application feels smooth even when handling large amounts of data.

Understanding Rendering

Everything in React starts with rendering.

Rendering means:

React executes a component function and produces a new Virtual DOM representation.

Example:

function Welcome() {
    return <h1>Hello</h1>;
}

Every time React renders this component, the function executes again.

Rendering does not necessarily mean updating the browser.

React first compares the new Virtual DOM with the previous one.

Only actual differences are applied to the Real DOM.

The Rendering Process

State Changes
      │
      ▼
React Executes Component
      │
      ▼
New Virtual DOM
      │
      ▼
Compare With Previous Virtual DOM
      │
      ▼
Find Differences
      │
      ▼
Update Only Changed DOM Nodes

This comparison process is called Reconciliation.

What Causes a Component to Re-render?

A component renders again when:

  • State changes
  • Props change
  • Context changes
  • Parent component re-renders
  • Forced update

Example:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Calling:

setCount(count + 1);

causes React to render again.

Unnecessary Re-renders

Consider this example:

function Parent() {

    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <>
            <Child />
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Click
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

Every click causes:

Parent → Child

Even if Child never uses count.

This is called an unnecessary re-render.

React.memo()

Purpose

Prevent a component from re-rendering when its props have not changed.

Example:

const CustomerCard = React.memo(function CustomerCard(props) {

    return <div>{props.name}</div>;

});

Now React compares props before rendering.

If props remain the same:

Skip Rendering

Without React.memo()

Parent Render → Child Render → Child Render → Child Render → Child Render

With React.memo()

Parent Render → Compare Props → Props Same → Skip Rendering

When to Use React.memo()

Good candidates:

  • Tables
  • Cards
  • Lists
  • Dashboard widgets
  • Expensive components

Avoid wrapping every component.

React.memo also performs comparisons, which has its own cost.

useMemo()

Purpose

Memoize expensive calculations.

Without useMemo:

const total = calculateTotal(customers);

The calculation executes on every render.

With useMemo:

const total = useMemo(() => {

    return calculateTotal(customers);

}, [customers]);

Now React recalculates only when customers changes.

Real Example

Imagine:

10,000 Orders

Calculating totals:

  • Sum
  • Average
  • Revenue
  • Tax
  • Discount

These operations may become expensive.

Memoization prevents unnecessary recalculation.

When to Use useMemo()

Good for:

  • Sorting
  • Filtering
  • Searching
  • Large calculations
  • Statistics
  • Chart preparation

Not for simple arithmetic.

useCallback()

Functions are recreated every render.

Example:

const handleDelete = () => {

    ...

};

Every render:

New Function → New Reference

If passed to child components:

Props Changed → Child Re-renders

Solution

const handleDelete = useCallback(() => {

    ...

}, []);

React reuses the same function reference.

useMemo vs useCallback

useMemo useCallback
Memoizes values Memoizes functions
Returns value Returns function

Example:

const filtered = useMemo(...)

const handleClick = useCallback(...)

Lazy Loading

Large applications should not download everything immediately.

Instead of:

  • Dashboard
  • Customers
  • Orders
  • Reports
  • Employees
  • Invoices
  • Settings
  • Analytics
  • Admin

Loading all at startup...

Only load the page the user visits.

React.lazy()

Example:

const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import("./Dashboard"));

Dashboard is downloaded only when needed.

Suspense

Lazy components need a loading state.

Example:

<Suspense fallback={<Loader />}>

    <Dashboard />

</Suspense>

Flow:

User Opens Dashboard → Loading... → Download Component → Render Dashboard

Code Splitting

Instead of one huge JavaScript bundle:

  • app.js
  • 15 MB

React splits it into smaller files.

Example:

  • login.js
  • dashboard.js
  • orders.js
  • customers.js
  • reports.js

Browser downloads only what is necessary.

Route-Based Code Splitting

Example:

  • /
  • ↓
  • Login Bundle
  • /dashboard
  • ↓
  • Dashboard Bundle
  • /reports
  • ↓
  • Reports Bundle

This greatly improves startup performance.

Image Optimization

Large images slow applications.

Bad:

5000x5000 PNG

Good:

  • Compressed WebP
  • Responsive Images
  • Lazy Loading

Use:

<img loading="lazy">

when appropriate.

Virtualization

Suppose you have:

100,000 Customers

Rendering every row is expensive.

Instead:

Visible Rows Only

Libraries:

  • react-window
  • react-virtualized

Flow:

100,000 Records → 20 Visible → Render Only 20 → Scroll → Render Next 20

Huge performance improvement.

Pagination vs Virtualization

Pagination:

Page 1 → 20 Records

Virtualization:

100,000 Records → Only Visible Rows Render

Large enterprise dashboards often combine both.

Debouncing

User types:

  • A
  • AB
  • ABC
  • ABCD

Without debounce:

4 API Requests

With debounce:

Wait → One API Request

Useful for:

  • Search
  • Autocomplete
  • Filters

Throttling

Throttle limits how often a function executes.

Example:

Scrolling.

Without throttle:

1000 Events

With throttle:

20 Events

React Query Performance

React Query automatically improves performance.

Features:

  • Request caching
  • Background refetching
  • Request deduplication
  • Retry
  • Pagination support
  • Infinite scrolling

Without React Query:

Component → API → API → API → API

With React Query:

Component → Cache → Reuse Data

Memoizing Derived Data

Instead of:

customers.filter(...).sort(...)

on every render,

use:

useMemo(...)

Only recompute when data changes.

Optimizing Context

Large Context objects cause many re-renders.

Bad:

One Huge Context → Entire Application Re-renders

Better:

  • Auth Context
  • Theme Context
  • Language Context
  • Notification Context

Separate contexts reduce unnecessary updates.

Avoid Anonymous Functions in Large Lists

Bad:

<button onClick={() => deleteCustomer(id)}>

inside thousands of rows.

Prefer memoized handlers when performance becomes an issue.

Keys in Lists

Bad:

key={index}

Good:

key={customer.id}

Stable keys help React update efficiently.

Bundle Optimization

Large dependencies increase bundle size.

Instead of importing entire libraries unnecessarily:

import _ from "lodash";

Prefer importing only what you need when possible.

Remove unused dependencies regularly.

Measuring Performance

React provides the Profiler.

The Profiler shows:

  • Render duration
  • Number of renders
  • Slow components
  • Component hierarchy

It helps identify bottlenecks instead of guessing.

React Developer Tools

React DevTools provides:

  • Component tree
  • Props
  • State
  • Context
  • Hooks
  • Profiler

Every professional React developer should use it.

Common Performance Mistakes

❌ Wrapping everything in React.memo().

❌ Using useMemo() for trivial calculations.

❌ Using useCallback() everywhere.

❌ Fetching the same data multiple times.

❌ Rendering huge lists without virtualization.

❌ Loading all routes on startup.

❌ Ignoring bundle size.

❌ Passing new object literals as props every render.

❌ Creating very large Context objects.

❌ Using array indexes as keys.

Enterprise Performance Checklist

✅ Use React Query for server state.

✅ Split code by route.

✅ Lazy-load heavy pages.

✅ Memoize expensive calculations.

✅ Memoize callbacks only when beneficial.

✅ Use stable keys.

✅ Optimize images.

✅ Cache API responses.

✅ Virtualize large lists.

✅ Debounce search inputs.

✅ Profile before optimizing.

Performance Optimization Decision Flow

Application Feels Slow
        │
        ▼
Measure Performance
        │
        ▼
Identify Bottleneck
        │
        ├───────────────┐
        ▼               ▼
Rendering?          Network?
        │               │
        ▼               ▼
React.memo()      React Query
useMemo()         Cache
useCallback()     Pagination
        │
        ▼
Still Slow?
        │
        ▼
Virtualization
        │
        ▼
Code Splitting
        │
        ▼
Lazy Loading
        │
        ▼
Profile Again

Performance Optimization Summary

Technique Purpose
React.memo Prevent unnecessary component renders
useMemo Cache expensive computed values
useCallback Cache function references
React.lazy Load components on demand
Suspense Display fallback UI while loading
Code Splitting Reduce initial bundle size
React Query Cache and synchronize server data
Virtualization Render only visible list items
Debounce Reduce rapid API calls
Throttle Limit frequent event execution
Profiler Measure rendering performance

Chapter Summary

Performance optimization in React is about reducing unnecessary work, not applying every optimization technique everywhere.

A well-performing React application:

  • Renders only what is necessary.
  • Downloads only what the user needs.
  • Reuses previously computed values.
  • Avoids duplicate network requests.
  • Efficiently handles large datasets.
  • Measures performance before applying optimizations.

The best optimization is understanding why React is doing work and ensuring it only performs the work that truly matters.

← Previous chapter13 · Enterprise React Architecture Case StudyNext chapter →15 · Testing React Applications
15

Testing React Applications

Introduction

Writing code is only half of a software developer's job.

The other half is ensuring that the code works correctly.

This is where testing comes in.

Testing is the process of verifying that your application behaves as expected under different conditions.

Professional software companies invest heavily in automated testing because it:

  • Prevents bugs
  • Improves code quality
  • Makes refactoring safer
  • Increases developer confidence
  • Reduces production issues

Testing is especially important in enterprise React applications where multiple developers work on the same codebase.

What is Testing?

Testing means writing code that verifies other code.

Instead of manually checking whether a button works every time you make a change, you write an automated test that checks it for you.

Example:

User clicks Login → Login API called → Success response → Redirect to Dashboard → Test Passed

Why Testing Matters

Imagine a project with:

  • 100 React components
  • 500 API endpoints
  • 20 developers
  • Thousands of users

One small change could accidentally break another feature.

Without tests:

Developer Changes Code → Deploy → Production Bug → Customer Complaints

With tests:

Developer Changes Code → Run Tests → Bug Found → Fix Before Deployment

Types of Testing

React applications commonly use three levels of testing.

                 End-to-End Tests
              (Entire Application)

            Integration Tests
     (Multiple Components Together)

         Unit Tests
   (Single Function or Component)

Unit Testing

Unit tests verify a single unit of code.

A unit can be:

  • Function
  • Hook
  • Utility
  • Component

Example:

function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

Test:

  • Input:
  • 2 + 3
  • ↓
  • Expected:
  • 5

Only one function is tested.

Component Testing

React components are also units.

Example:

<Button>

Save

</Button>

Questions:

  • Does the button render?
  • Does it display the correct text?
  • Does clicking it call the function?

Integration Testing

Integration tests verify that multiple parts work together.

Example:

Login Form → Validation → API Call → Dashboard Redirect

Instead of testing one component, we test the interaction between components.

End-to-End Testing (E2E)

E2E tests simulate a real user.

Example:

Open Website → Login → Navigate → Create Customer → Update Customer → Delete Customer → Logout

Everything is tested from the user's perspective.

Popular tools:

  • Cypress
  • Playwright

Testing Pyramid

Professional applications usually follow the testing pyramid.

            E2E Tests
          Small Number

      Integration Tests
       Moderate Number

         Unit Tests
        Large Number

Why?

Unit tests are:

  • Fast
  • Cheap
  • Easy to maintain

E2E tests are:

  • Slow
  • Expensive
  • Harder to maintain

Testing Tools

Most React projects use:

  • Vitest
  • Jest
  • React Testing Library
  • Mock Service Worker (MSW)

Why Vitest?

Modern React projects created with Vite usually use Vitest.

Advantages:

  • Very fast
  • Native Vite integration
  • TypeScript support
  • Jest-compatible API
  • Easy configuration

Why Jest?

Jest has been the standard testing framework for React for many years.

Features:

  • Test Runner
  • Assertions
  • Mocking
  • Snapshots
  • Code Coverage

Many older enterprise projects still use Jest.

React Testing Library (RTL)

RTL focuses on testing applications the same way users interact with them.

Instead of testing implementation details, it tests behavior.

Example:

User sees button → Clicks button → Button performs action

This approach produces more reliable tests.

Testing Philosophy

Bad test:

Does Component use useState?

Good test:

Can the user successfully submit the form?

Always test behavior, not implementation.

Project Structure

Example:

src
│
├── components
│
│   ├── Button.tsx
│   └── Button.test.tsx
│
├── hooks
│
│   ├── useAuth.ts
│   └── useAuth.test.ts
│
├── services
│
│   ├── customer.service.ts
│   └── customer.service.test.ts

Every important module has its own tests.

Naming Convention

Examples:

  • Button.tsx
  • Button.test.tsx
  • CustomerTable.tsx
  • CustomerTable.test.tsx

Writing Your First Test

Component:

<Button>

Save

</Button>

Test:

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import Button from "./Button";

test("renders button text", () => {
    render(<Button>Save</Button>);
    expect(screen.getByText("Save")).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Explanation:

  • Render component
  • Search for text
  • Verify it exists

Testing User Interaction

Instead of checking HTML directly, simulate user behavior.

Example:

User Click → Button → Function Called → Success

This ensures your application behaves correctly.

Testing Forms

Example:

Enter Name → Enter Email → Click Submit → Validation → API Request

Things to test:

  • Required fields
  • Invalid input
  • Valid input
  • Error messages
  • Successful submission

Testing API Calls

Components often call APIs.

Instead of calling the real backend during tests, use mocking.

Example:

Real Backend → Replace with Fake Response → Component Receives Data → Test UI

This keeps tests:

  • Fast
  • Predictable
  • Independent

Mocking

Mocking replaces real dependencies with fake ones.

Instead of:

Real Server

Return:

[
    {
        "id":1,
        "name":"John"
    }
]

The component believes it received real data.

Mock Service Worker (MSW)

MSW intercepts HTTP requests.

Instead of:

Axios → Internet → Backend

MSW changes the flow to:

Axios → Mock Server → Fake Response

No real backend is required.

Testing React Query

When using React Query:

Component → Query → Cache → API

Tests usually provide a custom Query Client.

This isolates each test and prevents cache interference.

Testing Context

Applications often use:

  • AuthContext
  • ThemeContext
  • LanguageContext

Tests wrap components with the appropriate providers.

Example:

AuthProvider → Component → Test

Testing Custom Hooks

Hooks contain reusable logic.

Example:

usePagination() → Current Page → Next Page → Previous Page

Tests verify the hook's behavior without rendering an entire page.

Snapshot Testing

A snapshot stores the rendered output of a component.

Future tests compare the new output with the saved snapshot.

Useful for:

  • Static components
  • UI libraries

Not recommended for frequently changing components.

Code Coverage

Coverage measures how much of your application is tested.

Example:

Files → Functions → Branches → Lines

Example report:

  • Statements
  • 92%
  • Branches
  • 88%
  • Functions
  • 95%
  • Lines
  • 93%

Higher coverage generally means better confidence, but 100% coverage does not guarantee bug-free software.

Continuous Integration

Professional teams run tests automatically.

Workflow:

Developer Pushes Code → GitHub Actions → Install Dependencies → Run Tests → Tests Pass? → Yes → Build → No → Reject

Broken code never reaches production.

What Should You Test?

Always test:

  • Utility functions
  • Business logic
  • Form validation
  • Components
  • Custom hooks
  • API interactions
  • Authentication flow
  • Error handling

What Should You Avoid Testing?

Avoid testing:

  • Third-party libraries
  • React internals
  • Browser internals
  • Implementation details
  • Private component state

Focus on what users experience.

Common Testing Mistakes

❌ Testing implementation instead of behavior.

❌ Depending on a real backend.

❌ Writing fragile tests.

❌ Ignoring edge cases.

❌ Creating huge tests that verify too many things.

❌ Not cleaning up test data.

❌ Forgetting loading and error states.

Best Practices

✅ Test user behavior.

✅ Keep tests small.

✅ Test one feature per test.

✅ Mock external services.

✅ Use meaningful test names.

✅ Test success and failure cases.

✅ Test loading states.

✅ Test error states.

✅ Keep tests independent.

✅ Run tests in CI/CD pipelines.

Enterprise Testing Workflow

Developer Writes Feature
        │
        ▼
Write Unit Tests
        │
        ▼
Write Integration Tests
        │
        ▼
Run Tests Locally
        │
        ▼
Push to Git
        │
        ▼
GitHub Actions
        │
        ▼
Run All Tests
        │
        ▼
Tests Pass?
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   │         │
  Yes        No
   │         │
   ▼         ▼
Deploy     Fix Bugs

Testing Tools Comparison

Tool Purpose
Vitest Test runner for Vite projects
Jest General JavaScript testing framework
React Testing Library Test React components through user interactions
MSW Mock API requests
Cypress End-to-end testing
Playwright Cross-browser end-to-end testing

Choosing the Right Tool

Scenario Recommended Tool
Vite + React Vitest + RTL
Older React project Jest + RTL
Mock HTTP requests MSW
Browser automation Playwright or Cypress
Full application testing Playwright or Cypress

Chapter Summary

Testing is an essential part of professional React development.

Enterprise applications rely on multiple layers of testing:

  • Unit Tests verify individual functions, hooks, and components.
  • Integration Tests ensure multiple parts work together correctly.
  • End-to-End Tests simulate real user behavior across the entire application.

Modern React projects commonly use Vitest (or Jest) with React Testing Library for component testing, MSW for mocking API requests, and Playwright or Cypress for end-to-end testing.

A strong testing strategy catches bugs early, improves code quality, enables safe refactoring, and gives development teams confidence to evolve large applications without breaking existing functionality.

← Previous chapter14 · React Performance OptimizationNext chapter →16 · Deployment and DevOps for React Applications
16

Deployment and DevOps for React Applications

Introduction

Building a React application is only the first step.

A completed application must eventually be deployed so that users can access it over the Internet.

This chapter explains how professional React applications move from a developer's computer to production servers using modern deployment techniques.

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • Development vs Production
  • Vite Build Process
  • Environment Variables
  • Static Hosting
  • Reverse Proxy
  • Docker
  • Docker Compose
  • CI/CD
  • GitHub Actions
  • Nginx
  • Production Best Practices

What is Deployment?

Deployment is the process of making an application available to users.

Development Environment

Developer Computer → localhost:5173

Production Environment

Internet → https://mycompany.com

Instead of running on your computer, the application runs on a production server.

Development vs Production

Development

Characteristics:

  • Fast Refresh
  • Source Maps
  • Error Overlay
  • Debugging
  • Development Server

Command

npm run dev

Example

http://localhost:5173

Production

Characteristics

  • Minified JavaScript
  • Optimized CSS
  • Compressed Assets
  • Tree Shaking
  • Fast Loading

Command

npm run build

Result

dist/

The dist folder is the application that gets deployed.

How Vite Works

When you run:

npm run dev

Vite starts a development server.

Browser → Vite Dev Server → Source Files

No production build is created.

When you run:

npm run build

Flow:

TypeScript → Compile → Bundle → Optimize → Minify → Generate dist/

The Build Process

Example project

src/ → Vite → Rollup → Optimization → dist/

The output may look like:

dist
│
├── assets
├── index.html
├── logo.svg
└── favicon.ico

Everything inside dist is production-ready.

What Happens During Build?

Vite performs many optimizations.

Minification

Before

function calculatePrice(price) {

    return price * 0.16;

}

After

function a(b){return.16*b}

Smaller files download faster.

Tree Shaking

Unused code is removed.

Example

Imported:

100 Functions

Used:

5 Functions

Output:

Only 5 Functions

Code Splitting

Instead of

  • app.js
  • 15 MB

React generates

  • login.js
  • dashboard.js
  • customers.js
  • orders.js

Each page loads independently.

Asset Optimization

Images

Fonts

CSS

JavaScript

All optimized for production.

Environment Variables

Applications should never hardcode:

  • API URLs
  • Secrets
  • API Keys
  • Tokens

Instead use environment variables.

Example:

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080

Access inside React:

const url = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;

Common Environment Files

  • .env
  • .env.local
  • .env.development
  • .env.production

.env

Shared variables.

Example

VITE_APP_NAME=Laundry Management

.env.development

Development only.

Example

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080

.env.production

Production only.

Example

VITE_API_URL=https://api.company.com

.env.local

Personal settings.

Ignored by Git.

Useful for:

  • Local API URLs
  • Personal tokens
  • Developer-specific configuration

Never Store Secrets

Bad

DATABASE_PASSWORD=123456

React runs in the browser.

Users can inspect JavaScript.

Frontend secrets are not secret.

Only public values belong in React environment variables.

Static Hosting

React produces static files.

Meaning:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

These files can be served by:

  • Nginx
  • Apache
  • GitHub Pages
  • Netlify
  • Vercel
  • Firebase Hosting

Nginx

Nginx is a web server.

Architecture

Browser → Nginx → React Files

Nginx serves the generated dist folder.

Why Use Nginx?

Advantages

  • Very fast
  • Lightweight
  • HTTPS support
  • Compression
  • Reverse Proxy
  • Static file serving
  • Load balancing

Reverse Proxy

React

https://company.com

Backend

http://localhost:8080

Instead of exposing Spring Boot directly:

Browser → Nginx → Spring Boot

Benefits:

  • Security
  • SSL termination
  • Centralized routing
  • Better performance

Docker

Docker packages an application with everything it needs.

Without Docker

Works On My Machine

Problem:

Different computers

Different Node versions

Different operating systems

Different dependencies

With Docker

  • Application
  • +
  • Node
  • +
  • Dependencies
  • +
  • Configuration
  • =
  • Container

Runs the same everywhere.

Dockerfile

Example structure

Project
│
├── Dockerfile
├── package.json
└── src

Dockerfile defines:

  • Base image
  • Install dependencies
  • Build application
  • Serve production files

Multi-Stage Docker Build

Professional projects use multiple stages.

Flow

Node Image → Install Packages → Build React → Generate dist/ → Copy dist → Nginx Image → Production Container

Smaller and faster images.

Docker Compose

Applications often have multiple services.

Example

  • React
  • Spring Boot
  • MySQL
  • Redis
  • Nginx

Docker Compose starts them together.

Architecture

Docker Compose
│
├── frontend
├── backend
├── mysql
├── redis
└── nginx

One command starts everything.

Deployment Pipeline

Professional deployment usually follows this workflow.

Developer → Git Commit → Git Push → GitHub → GitHub Actions → Build → Tests → Docker Image → Docker Registry → Production Server → Users

Everything is automated.

Continuous Integration (CI)

CI means every code change is automatically verified.

Example

Push Code → Install Dependencies → Run Tests → Build → Success

No manual verification required.

Continuous Deployment (CD)

CD automatically publishes successful builds.

Example

Build → Docker Image → Production → Application Updated

GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions automates workflows.

Example

Push → Workflow → Install Node → Install Packages → Run Tests → Build → Deploy

Typical GitHub Actions Workflow

Developer Pushes Code → Checkout Repository → Setup Node.js → Install Dependencies → Run ESLint → Run Tests → Build React → Create Docker Image → Push Docker Image → Deploy

Hosting Platforms

Popular React hosting providers

Platform Description
Vercel Optimized for React and Next.js
Netlify Static hosting with CI/CD
GitHub Pages Free hosting for static sites
Firebase Hosting Google's hosting solution
AWS S3 + CloudFront Enterprise-grade hosting
Azure Static Web Apps Microsoft cloud hosting

Production Folder Structure

Example

Production Server
│
├── nginx
├── frontend
├── backend
├── docker-compose.yml
├── logs
└── ssl

Logging

Applications should log important events.

Examples

  • User Login
  • Application Error
  • API Failure
  • Deployment
  • Authentication Error

Logs help diagnose production issues.

Monitoring

Production applications should be monitored.

Common metrics:

  • CPU Usage
  • Memory Usage
  • Response Time
  • Error Rate
  • Active Users
  • API Latency

Popular tools:

  • Grafana
  • Prometheus
  • Datadog
  • New Relic

Deployment Checklist

Before deployment:

✅ Run tests

✅ Remove console logs

✅ Build successfully

✅ Verify environment variables

✅ Optimize images

✅ Check API URLs

✅ Enable HTTPS

✅ Configure caching

✅ Enable compression

✅ Verify routing

Common Deployment Mistakes

❌ Hardcoding API URLs.

❌ Committing .env.local.

❌ Storing secrets in frontend code.

❌ Deploying without tests.

❌ Ignoring HTTPS.

❌ Serving development builds.

❌ Forgetting SPA routing configuration in Nginx.

❌ Large unoptimized bundles.

❌ Missing caching headers.

Complete Enterprise Deployment Flow

Developer → Write Code → Git Commit → Git Push → GitHub Repository → GitHub Actions → Install Dependencies → Run Tests → Run Build → Create Docker Image → Push Docker Image → Production Server → Docker Compose → Nginx → Spring Boot → MySQL → Users Access Website

Architecture Overview

                Internet
                    │
                    ▼
               HTTPS Request
                    │
                    ▼
                 Nginx
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
     React Frontend     Spring Boot API
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
     Static Files         Business Logic
                              │
                              ▼
                           MySQL

Best Practices

✅ Use Vite for modern React applications.

✅ Keep development and production environments separate.

✅ Store configuration in environment variables.

✅ Never expose secrets in frontend code.

✅ Use Docker for consistent deployments.

✅ Serve React with Nginx in production.

✅ Automate builds using GitHub Actions.

✅ Run automated tests before deployment.

✅ Enable HTTPS and compression.

✅ Monitor production systems continuously.

Chapter Summary

Deployment transforms a React application from local development into a production-ready system accessible to users worldwide.

Modern React applications typically follow this lifecycle:

  1. Develop locally with Vite.
  2. Build optimized static files.
  3. Configure environment variables.
  4. Package the application with Docker.
  5. Serve it using Nginx.
  6. Automate testing and deployment with GitHub Actions.
  7. Monitor the application in production.
← Previous chapter15 · Testing React ApplicationsNext chapter →17 · React Security Best Practices
17

React Security Best Practices

Introduction

Security is one of the most important parts of modern web development.

A React application is not only a user interface. It communicates with:

  • Backend APIs
  • Databases
  • Authentication systems
  • File storage
  • Third-party services

A security mistake in the frontend can expose:

  • User information
  • Authentication tokens
  • Business data
  • Application functionality

Professional React developers must understand common security risks and how to protect applications.

The Security Model of a React Application

A React application usually follows this architecture:

User Browser → React Application → HTTPS Request → Spring Boot Backend → Database

Important rule:

The frontend is never trusted.

Everything important must be verified by the backend.

Frontend Security vs Backend Security

Frontend Security

Responsible for:

  • User experience
  • Hiding unavailable UI
  • Input validation
  • Preventing accidental mistakes

Examples:

  • Disable button
  • Show error message
  • Validate form

Backend Security

Responsible for:

  • Real authorization
  • Data protection
  • Permissions
  • Authentication
  • Business rules

Example:

Even if a user modifies JavaScript:

isAdmin = true

The backend must reject unauthorized requests.

Authentication vs Authorization

These concepts are different.

Authentication

Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Example:

Username + Password → JWT Token → User Logged In

Authorization

Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Example:

  • Admin
  • Can delete users
  • Employee
  • Cannot delete users

JWT Authentication Flow

Modern React + Spring Boot applications commonly use JWT.

Flow:

User → Login Form → auth.api.ts → POST /login → Spring Security → Generate JWT → Return Token → React Stores Token → Future Requests Include Token → Backend Validates Token

JWT Structure

A JWT contains three parts:

Header.Payload.Signature

Example:

xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

Header

Contains information about the token.

Example:

{
"type":"JWT",
"algorithm":"HS256"
}

Payload

Contains user information.

Example:

{
"id":10,
"role":"ADMIN"
}

Important:

The payload is encoded, not encrypted.

Do not store secrets inside JWT.

Signature

Used to verify that the token was not modified.

Where Should We Store JWT?

Common options:

localStorage

Example:

localStorage.setItem(
"token",
jwt
);

Advantages:

  • Simple
  • Easy access

Disadvantages:

  • Vulnerable to XSS attacks

Cookies

HttpOnly Secure Cookies are often safer.

Advantages:

  • JavaScript cannot access token
  • Better protection against XSS

Disadvantages:

  • Requires CSRF protection

Enterprise Recommendation

For sensitive applications:

  • HttpOnly Cookie
  • +
  • Secure Flag
  • +
  • SameSite Policy

is usually preferred.

Axios Interceptors

Axios interceptors automatically attach tokens.

Example:

Request → Axios Interceptor → Add Authorization Header → Backend

Header:

  • Authorization:
  • Bearer TOKEN

Protected Routes

React can protect pages visually.

Example:

  • Dashboard
  • ↓
  • Check User
  • ↓
  • Logged In?
  • Yes → Show Page
  • No → Login

Example:

<ProtectedRoute>

<Dashboard />

</ProtectedRoute>

Important Security Rule

Protected routes in React are NOT real security.

Why?

Because users can modify frontend code.

Real protection:

  • React Protection
  • +
  • Spring Security Authorization

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Applications usually have roles.

Example:

  • ADMIN
  • MANAGER
  • EMPLOYEE
  • CUSTOMER

Permission Example

  • ADMIN
  • ✓ Create Employee
  • ✓ Delete Customer
  • ✓ View Reports
  • EMPLOYEE
  • ✓ Update Order Status
  • ✗ Delete Customer

XSS Attack

Cross-Site Scripting

XSS happens when attackers inject malicious JavaScript.

Example:

User enters:

<script>
alert("Hacked")
</script>

If displayed incorrectly:

Browser Executes Script

React Protection Against XSS

React escapes content automatically.

Example:

<div>

{username}

</div>

React converts:

<script>

into safe text.

Dangerous HTML

Avoid:

dangerouslySetInnerHTML

Example:

<div
dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{
__html:data
}}
/>

This bypasses React protection.

Only use with trusted content.

Sanitization

If HTML must be displayed:

Use sanitizers.

Example:

User Input → Sanitize → Safe HTML → Display

Libraries:

  • DOMPurify

CSRF Attack

Cross-Site Request Forgery

An attacker tricks a logged-in user into sending unwanted requests.

Example:

User is logged in.

Attacker creates:

Fake Website → Send Delete Request → User Account

CSRF Protection

Solutions:

  • SameSite Cookies
  • CSRF Tokens
  • Backend Validation

SQL Injection

This happens on the backend.

Example:

Bad query:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE name='input'

Attack:

' OR 1=1

Protection:

  • Prepared Statements
  • JPA
  • Hibernate
  • Validation

React Responsibility

React should:

  • Validate input
  • Avoid unsafe HTML
  • Send correct data

Backend must:

  • Validate again
  • Protect database

Input Validation

Never trust user input.

Examples:

Email:

test@gmail.com

Password:

Minimum 8 characters

Phone:

Correct format

Validation Layers

Professional applications validate at multiple levels.

React Validation → API Validation → Spring Validation → Database Constraints

File Upload Security

File uploads are dangerous.

Attack examples:

  • Malicious files
  • Huge files
  • Wrong file types

Safe Upload Process

User Selects File → Check Size → Check Extension → Check MIME Type → Upload → Store Securely

Example Restrictions

Images:

Allowed:

  • jpg
  • png
  • webp

Maximum:

5 MB

Environment Security

Never expose:

  • DATABASE_PASSWORD
  • SECRET_KEY
  • PRIVATE_API_KEY

inside React.

Bad:

VITE_SECRET_PASSWORD=123

Anyone can see it.

HTTPS

Production applications must use HTTPS.

Without HTTPS:

Browser → Network → Attacker Can Read Data

With HTTPS:

Encrypted Connection

Content Security Policy (CSP)

CSP controls what resources the browser can load.

Example:

Allow:

  • Company Domain
  • Trusted CDN

Block:

Unknown Scripts

Security Headers

Important headers:

  • Content-Security-Policy
  • X-Frame-Options
  • X-Content-Type-Options
  • Strict-Transport-Security

Usually configured in Nginx or backend.

Dependency Security

React projects use many packages.

Example:

npm install package

A package may contain vulnerabilities.

Check:

npm audit

Fix:

npm audit fix

Keeping Dependencies Updated

Old packages may contain:

  • Security vulnerabilities
  • Bugs
  • Performance issues

Regular updates are important.

Error Handling Security

Never expose internal errors.

Bad:

  • Database connection failed:
  • password=123456

Good:

Something went wrong.
Please try again.

Logging Security

Never log:

  • Passwords
  • Tokens
  • Credit cards
  • Private information

Bad:

console.log(userToken);

Security Checklist

Before production:

✅ Use HTTPS

✅ Validate user input

✅ Protect routes

✅ Use backend authorization

✅ Avoid dangerous HTML rendering

✅ Protect JWT tokens

✅ Secure file uploads

✅ Remove sensitive logs

✅ Audit dependencies

✅ Configure security headers

✅ Keep packages updated

Enterprise Security Flow

User → React Application → Input Validation → HTTPS → Axios → JWT Authentication → Spring Security → Authorization Check → Business Logic → Database → Response → Safe UI Update

Common Security Mistakes

❌ Trusting frontend permissions.

❌ Storing secrets in React.

❌ Using localStorage without understanding risks.

❌ Using dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data.

❌ Skipping backend validation.

❌ Uploading files without restrictions.

❌ Exposing error details.

❌ Ignoring dependency vulnerabilities.

❌ Using HTTP in production.

Chapter Summary

Security in React applications is based on one main principle:

Never trust the client.

React is responsible for creating a secure user experience, but the backend is responsible for enforcing security.

A professional React application should combine:

  • Secure authentication
  • Proper authorization
  • Safe data handling
  • Input validation
  • HTTPS
  • Secure token management
  • Dependency monitoring
  • Protected backend APIs

When React and Spring Boot security practices work together, the application becomes safer, more reliable, and ready for enterprise production environments. Understanding deployment and DevOps practices is essential for building enterprise-grade React applications that are reliable, scalable, and maintainable.

18

State Management in React Applications

Introduction

State management is one of the most important concepts in React.

Every React application needs to remember information while the user interacts with it.

Examples:

  • Current user
  • Shopping cart items
  • Selected language
  • Theme preference
  • Form values
  • Notifications
  • Table filters
  • Server data

This information is called State.

Understanding state management is essential for building professional React applications.

What is State?

State is data that can change over time and affects the user interface.

Example:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Current state:

count = 0

After clicking:

count = 1

React updates the UI automatically.

State vs Normal Variables

Normal variable:

let count = 0;

count++;

React does not know that the value changed.

The UI will not update.

State:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

setCount(count + 1);

React knows:

State Changed → Re-render Component → Update UI

Types of State in React

Modern applications usually have several types of state.

  • Application State
  • Server State
  • Component State
  • URL State
  • Form State

Component State

State that belongs to one component.

Example:

function Button(){

const [loading,setLoading] = useState(false);

}

Used for:

  • Modals
  • Toggles
  • Inputs
  • Local UI changes

Example

Customer Modal:

Open Modal → User Enters Data → Close Modal

The state belongs only to that component.

Sharing Component State

Sometimes multiple components need the same state.

Example:

Parent
 ├── CustomerForm
 └── CustomerPreview

Both need:

customerData

Solution:

Move state to the common parent.

This is called:

Lifting State Up

Lifting State Up Example

Before:

  • CustomerForm
  • has name

After:

CustomersPage

has customer state

       |
       |
  --------------

Form        Preview

Props Drilling Problem

Passing data through many components:

App → Layout → Page → Component → Child → Button

Example:

<Component user={user}/>

After many levels:

<Button user={user}/>

This becomes difficult to maintain.

This problem is called:

Props Drilling

Context API

React provides Context API to share global data.

Example:

AuthContext → User Information → Available Everywhere

Context Example

Create:

AuthContext.tsx

Store:

{
 user,
 login,
 logout
}

Use:

const {user}=useAuth();

Common Contexts

Enterprise applications usually have:

  • AuthContext
  • ThemeContext
  • LanguageContext
  • NotificationContext

Context Limitations

Context is useful, but it is not a complete state management solution.

Problems:

  • Large contexts cause re-renders
  • Harder debugging
  • Complex updates become difficult

For large applications, external state libraries are often used.

Server State vs Client State

This is one of the most important concepts.

Client State

Data that belongs to the frontend.

Examples:

  • Sidebar Open
  • Theme
  • Modal Visible
  • Selected Tab

Managed by:

  • useState
  • Context
  • Zustand
  • Redux

Server State

Data that comes from backend.

Examples:

  • Customers
  • Orders
  • Employees
  • Reports

Managed by:

  • React Query
  • SWR
  • Apollo Client

Why Server State is Different

Server data has:

  • Loading
  • Errors
  • Cache
  • Synchronization
  • Refreshing

Example:

Customers Table → Backend Changes → Frontend Should Update

React Query handles this automatically.

React Query State Management

Example:

const {
data,
isLoading,
error
}=useQuery({
queryKey:["customers"],
queryFn:getCustomers
});

React Query manages:

  • Data
  • Loading
  • Error
  • Cache
  • Refetch

Redux

Redux is a popular state management library.

Architecture:

Component → Action → Reducer → Store → Component

Redux Store

The store contains global state.

Example:

Store
│
├── auth
├── cart
├── settings
└── notifications

Redux Actions

Actions describe what happened.

Example:

{
 type:"LOGIN",
 payload:user
}

Reducers

Reducers decide how state changes.

Example:

function authReducer(state,action){

switch(action.type){

case "LOGIN":

return action.payload;

}

}

Redux Toolkit

Modern Redux uses Redux Toolkit.

It simplifies:

  • Store creation
  • Reducers
  • Actions
  • Async logic

Redux Architecture

Example:

Login Button → Dispatch LOGIN Action → Auth Slice → Update Store → Components Re-render

Zustand

Zustand is a lightweight state management library.

Example:

const useStore=create((set)=>({

user:null,

setUser:(user)=>set({user})

}));

Advantages:

  • Simple
  • Less code
  • Fast
  • Easy learning curve

Redux vs Zustand vs Context

Feature Context Redux Toolkit Zustand
Small Apps Excellent Good Excellent
Large Apps Limited Excellent Very Good
Debugging Medium Excellent Good
Boilerplate Low Medium Very Low
DevTools Limited Excellent Good

Form State Management

Forms have their own state.

Example:

  • Name
  • Email
  • Phone
  • Password

Managing large forms with useState becomes difficult.

React Hook Form

Professional applications commonly use:

React Hook Form

Advantages:

  • Fast
  • Less re-rendering
  • Easy validation
  • Works with Zod

Form Architecture

Example:

CustomerForm → React Hook Form → Zod Validation → Submit → Service → API

URL State

Sometimes state belongs in the URL.

Example:

/customers?page=2&search=john

Benefits:

  • Shareable links
  • Browser history support
  • Refresh keeps state

Used for:

  • Search
  • Pagination
  • Filters

Local Storage State

Some data should survive browser refresh.

Examples:

  • Theme
  • Language
  • User Preferences

Example:

localStorage.setItem(
"theme",
"dark"
);

Session Storage

Similar to localStorage.

Difference:

localStorage → Permanent → sessionStorage → Removed after browser closes

State Management Architecture Example

Laundry Management System:

  • React App
  • |
  • | |
  • Client State Server State
  • | |
  • Context/Zustand React Query
  • | |
  • Theme/Auth/UI Customers/Orders
  • |
  • Components

Real Enterprise Example

User opens Dashboard.

Flow:

Dashboard Page → useDashboard() → React Query → dashboard.service.ts → dashboard.api.ts → Backend → Database → Cache Result → Display Charts

Authentication:

Login → Auth Service → JWT → Auth Context → Protected Routes

Theme:

Theme Button → Theme Context → Update CSS Variables → UI Changes

Choosing the Right Tool

Use:

useState

For:

  • Small local changes
  • Modal state
  • Inputs

Context API

For:

  • Authentication
  • Theme
  • Language

React Query

For:

  • API data
  • Backend communication
  • Caching

Redux Toolkit

For:

  • Very large applications
  • Complex global state
  • Multiple teams

Zustand

For:

  • Medium applications
  • Simple global state

Common State Management Mistakes

❌ Putting everything in Redux.

❌ Using Context for huge frequently changing data.

❌ Storing server data manually in state.

❌ Duplicating the same state in multiple places.

❌ Passing props through many levels.

❌ Keeping unnecessary global state.

❌ Forgetting to reset state.

State Management Best Practices

✅ Keep state as close as possible to where it is used.

✅ Separate client state from server state.

✅ Use React Query for backend data.

✅ Use Context for simple global values.

✅ Use Redux/Zustand only when needed.

✅ Avoid unnecessary global state.

✅ Normalize complex data structures.

✅ Keep state predictable.

State Decision Tree

  • Need to store data?
  • |
  • ▼
  • Is it from backend?
  • Yes No
  • | |
  • ▼ ▼
  • React Query Is it shared?
  • |
  • Yes No
  • | |
  • ▼ ▼
  • Context/Zustand useState

Chapter Summary

State management is the foundation of interactive React applications.

Professional React applications usually divide state into different categories:

  • Component State for local UI behavior.
  • Context State for simple global information.
  • Server State managed by React Query.
  • Global Client State managed by Redux Toolkit or Zustand.
  • Form State managed by React Hook Form.
  • URL State for shareable navigation data.

The goal is not to use the biggest state management library.

The goal is to choose the correct tool for each type of data.

A well-designed state architecture makes React applications easier to understand, faster, and more scalable.
